Bilateral communications were front and center in Mexico the week of Sept. 7, with developments running the gamut from encouraging to combative. U.S. President Donald Trump’s remark that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs beyond “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” caught fire over the weekend, unleashing a fresh round of provocations from Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the days that followed.

Mexico, however, continued to highlight trade and security collaboration with its northern neighbor, though the PISA test results and next year’s midterm elections sparked more conversations at home. Meanwhile, the annual inflation rate ticked up to 3.26% — as expected according to Banxico, which forecasts inflation of 3.5% by the end of 2026. President Claudia Sheinbaum remained optimistic through it all, especially as her administration makes its plans for 2027. Overhead, punishing heat baked Mexico’s northern border states even as monsoon rains drenched the Pacific coast and center of the country.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

2027 budget takes shape

On Monday, Finance Minister Édgar Amador Zamora submitted a 10.6-trillion-peso (US $627.8 billion) budget proposal for 2027 to Congress, an increase of about 1% in real terms over this year. Amador framed the package around “five pillars” — economic growth, protecting government priorities, strengthening revenue, more efficient spending and fiscal discipline. The government is banking on those pillars to shrink the budget deficit to 3.9% of GDP next year from an estimated 4.1% in 2026, even as public debt climbs to 55% of GDP. No new taxes or fuel-price hikes are planned.

Health care gets a 10.9% real-terms boost to 1.1 trillion pesos, largely for IMSS-Bienestar infrastructure and medicine supply, while education rises about 7% to 1.3 trillion pesos to fund new schools. Pension and welfare programs get just over 1 trillion pesos, and debt servicing alone eats up 1.6 trillion pesos — roughly one of every seven pesos the government spends. Security agencies see an 11.6% bump to 331.4 billion pesos, while Pemex funding falls 69.2% as the state oil company pushes toward self-sufficiency.

The National Electoral Institute (INE) is the biggest percentage winner of all, with an 87.5% real-terms increase ahead of 2027 midterm elections, while the Energy Ministry, the National Human Rights Commission and the Federal Electricity Commission absorb the steepest cuts. Sheinbaum said the following day that she is “very satisfied” with the package and that growth could exceed the official forecast of 1.5-2.5%, citing anticipated stability in trade relations with the U.S. and Canada.

Homicides continue to fall

Security officials reported this week that daily homicides fell 53% in August compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration, making it the least violent August since 2015.

More than 67,000 people have been arrested for high-impact crimes since Sheinbaum took office, though Security Minister Omar García Harfuch cautioned that “the job is not done.” Days later, from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the president highlighted a 63% drop in Chiapas’s homicide rate since Gov. Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar took office, alongside nearly 10,000 arrests in the southern state. The same briefing revealed the discovery of a clandestine hospital the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) used to treat injured members.

Olmeca Refinery notches record month

Pemex’s Olmeca Refinery in Tabasco posted its best month yet for fuel production in July, averaging 252,498 barrels per day, a 78.8% jump over June. Gasoline output rose even more sharply, up nearly 128% month-over-month, after equipment fires forced repairs earlier in the year. Despite the milestone, the plant — which began operating approximately two years ago — is still running at roughly two-thirds of its 340,000-bpd capacity.

Fox and PRI’s Alito Moreno join forces

In a striking political reunion, former President Vicente Fox met with PRI leader Alejandro “Alito” Moreno to discuss “the need to build a strong opposition” ahead of 2027 midterms — 26 years after Fox became the first opposition candidate to sweep the once-dominant PRI out of the presidency, and years after he called the party “black vipers, vermin and tadpoles.”

Morena, for its part, dismissed the pairing as “the reorganization of the power elite,” saying in a statement that “they change the names, they invent new organizations, but behind the facade, it’s the same old faces.” The PRI, which ruled Mexico for 71 years, now holds just two of the country’s 32 governorships — the same number as the much smaller Citizens Movement (MC) party.

At her Monday press conference, Sheinbaum branded the reunion “PRIAN” politics dating to the “neoliberal” era of former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, and called Fox a “traitor of democracy” — a jab tied to his role in Mexico’s disputed 2006 election.

Bilateral high points

Trade and security cooperation produced some of the week’s more encouraging bilateral news. Mexico’s exports to the U.S. hit a monthly record in July: US $60.55 billion worth of goods were sent north, pushing Mexico’s share of the $332.92 billion U.S. import market above 18%.

Along the border, Mexican and U.S. forces carried out “High Eagle,” a binational operation to detect and disable drones cartels use to surveil authorities near Tijuana and San Diego. And though bad weather grounded Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s flight to Mexico City on Wednesday, he and Sheinbaum still held a video call on USMCA negotiations that Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard described as “cordial” and “very useful,” with talks on steel, aluminum and automotive tariffs continuing ahead of a fourth bilateral review round.

Bilateral low points

Other exchanges were considerably more combative. Over the weekend, Trump proposed to rename New Mexico “New America,” despite having no legal authority to rename a U.S. state, drawing pushback from the state’s Democratic leaders. Later in the week, from Ecuador, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio doubled down on claims that cartels control “vast territories” of Mexico, hinting the threat may eventually have to be “confronted one way or the other.” Sheinbaum shot back on Thursday morning, telling Rubio to keep Mexico out of U.S. midterm politics and calling his remarks electorally motivated. Rounding out the week, U.S. Vice President JD Vance labeled the Mexican flag “a symbol of the far left” after a protester interrupted his convention speech in Dallas, telling the man to “get your ass over there” if he loved Mexico so much.

Poor PISA scores spark a debate over screens

New results from the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), given to 7,843 students across 297 Mexican schools, showed that four in 10 15-year-olds — 41.8% — scored below the basic level in science, math and reading, more than double the 19.7% OECD average and Mexico’s worst showing since 2009.

Mexican students averaged 388 points in math, 408 in reading and 414 in science, all well below OECD averages of 463, 461 and 482, and the country has shed seven points in both math and reading since the 2022 test. The decline wasn’t unique to Mexico — the OECD’s education director called it part of a “dramatic” global drop, particularly in reading — and Mexican students still reported unusually high curiosity (80%, versus a 24% global average who called school “a waste of time”). Education International, the global teachers’ federation, pinned the broader slide on shrinking attention spans, heavy AI use and a worldwide teacher shortage. China, Singapore, South Korea, Estonia and Canada topped the rankings.

Education Minister Mario Delgado blamed excessive screen use for the drop in reading comprehension — arguing that “screens make it easy to ‘read’ or consume images” — while defending the New Mexican School curriculum model and promoting traditional games like yo-yos, marbles and spinning tops as a substitute for phone time. He conceded the PISA sample was “statistically representative” even as he questioned whether the test amounts to a comprehensive evaluation of Mexican education. Sheinbaum later told reporters Mexico will roll out new math and reading textbooks next year, including poems and short stories, and push a “return to pencil and paper,” tying the effort to new national guidelines already restricting cellphone use in schools.

Education Ministry, UNESCO team up on AI in schools

Also this week, Mexico’s Education Ministry signed a letter of intent with UNESCO to guide the “responsible” rollout of artificial intelligence in classrooms, with the U.N. body offering technical assistance, teacher training and research support. Officials said the goal is to ensure AI supports, rather than substitutes for, teaching and critical thinking, and the deal also opens the door to new rules on cellphone use in schools.

Mexico prepares for El Grito and Independence Day

With the country’s 216th independence anniversary approaching, more than 18,000 members of Mexico’s armed forces are readying for the Sept. 16 military parade through Mexico City, featuring drones, horses, dogs and a float marking the country’s World Cup hosting duties this past June and July. The holiday kicks off the night before, with Sheinbaum leading the Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony and Tejano band Intocable headlining a concert in the Zócalo.

Festivities and gritos will ring out from cities across the country, including in Sinaloa, whose capital city of Culicán will hold a public celebration of Independence Day for the first time in two years.

Points of 🇲🇽 pride

A 20-year-old engineering student from a Chihuahua farming family, Luis Ángel Robles Morales, won a national innovation award for an irrigation filter that is already helping 500 drought-stricken farmers use water more efficiently.

Forward Julián Quiñones and Club América’s Scarlett Camberos earned historic Ballon d’Or nominations, marking the first time two Mexican players — and a Mexican club — have featured on the shortlist for world soccer’s top individual honor.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Witnessing the explosive sledgehammer ritual in San Juan de la Vega, Guanajuato
World.content:
A door in the street cracked open just enough for a hand to slip through. A kid, maybe 15, curled his fingers toward himself: come here, come here, then pulled back into the dark. I looked around the street. Nobody. I stepped inside.

The house looked like a drug kitchen. Two folding tables stretched across the room, their surfaces dusted white and yellow. On one side, a bucket of potassium chlorate. On the other, sulfur. Three kids stood around the tables, working the powders together with their bare hands. One kid looked up at me and grinned, then went back to scooping powder into small plastic bags.

Josué was the one who had waved me in from the doorway. One of the boys had no hands. Both arms ended at the wrists. I didn’t want to ask. I asked anyway. He told me it happened during the explosions, a few years back. He said it the way someone tells you about a stolen bicycle, part of life.

Don Juan David, Josué’s father, walked into the room. He greeted me with a handshake and a smile, glanced at the tables of explosive powder where their children worked, and walked back out.

A dangerous tradition

Every year, on Shrove Tuesday, the townspeople of San Juan de la Vega pack homemade explosives onto sledgehammers, carry them to the streets and open fields, and slam them against the ground. People lose limbs. This time, something was different. For the first time in the town’s history, authorities had banned the use of explosives during the carnival.

Families wanted to talk. Each family insisted theirs was the true story. The carnival, they all agreed, celebrates San Juan de la Vega, a saint who saved the town from gold robbers centuries ago. The explosives reenact the gunshots from his battles.

Every family also wanted to make sure we knew that the big explosions, the ones the town is famous for, are not the real tradition. The real tradition is small. Modest. A respectful crack of gunpowder in honor of the saint. Kids started making bigger and bigger explosives, destroying city piping. Everything breaks, they said, shaking their own heads. This is not what we are.

A man named Aquino de la Vega was moving silver shipments by mule along the Camino Real when bandits started robbing him. He prayed to San Juan Bautista. The robbers stopped. Aquino vowed he would honor the saint every year, forever, and so would his sons.

Six families still carry that vow. Each one is tied to a barrio. The families fund the music, the food, the processions. They keep the image of the saint in their home for a year.

Adrenaline and danger

The word I heard more than any other was adrenalina. The afternoon before the carnival, I found Josué sitting on a curb outside a corner store, rolling a cigarette. He was quiet.

“I’m always scared before I do it,” he told me. “But once I blow up one, I can’t stop. The adrenaline is too strong. I want to keep going.”

I asked about the dangers, and stories came easily: a man who burned, another who was paralyzed, people who lost fingers, hands, arms, legs. Accidents happen because the explosives are powerful enough to send 25-kilogram sledgehammers flying through the air. A hammer goes up, a hammer comes down, and sometimes there is a head in the way.

“Police always try to take them away,” one man said, sitting in a plastic chair outside his house, two kids playing in the dirt beside him. “But they will never stop the tradition. Nothing will change.”

On the afternoon before the main event, the streets were empty. Doors closed. No music. No voices.

Boom. The first hammer hit the ground as soon as night fell.

The sound moved through me. The ground shook under my feet. My ears whistled, even from 100 meters away. My chest vibrated. Windows cracked. The pipes beneath the street groaned and split.

Then came another. And another.

Parades took the streets. Villagers singing, dancing, playing instruments, carrying the image of San Juanito through the town. Following them in the back, kids dressed as soldiers, some in boots and gas masks, others with no gloves, no protection of any kind. Everyone carried sledgehammers and backpacks stuffed with explosives.

Defying the ban

I found Josué in the crowd. Face covered in soot, eyes wide. He swung a hammer down and the detonation threw him sideways. He got up laughing and loaded another charge.

Around midnight, the first police cars appeared.

The crowd froze. About 10 men climbed out with SWAT gear, assault rifles and bulletproof vests. They walked toward the kids with the backpacks. The boys scattered.

I saw a grandmother crack her front door open. She let the kids shove their backpacks full of explosives through the gap; she closed the door, and she stood in front of it. When the police asked to enter, she stood immobile like a statue until they were gone.

The police confiscated what they could, caught a few guys, and left. Within minutes, the parades reformed. The hammers came back out. The explosions picked up where they had stopped.

At around 3 a.m., we walked back toward town to catch some sleep. I did not sleep. The bed shook after every boom. Even with earplugs, my ears hurt. It went on until 7 a.m.

We walked outside. Over 10 police cars patrolled the town. They had shut everything down. But beyond the edge of town, we could hear it. Boom. Boom.

We followed the sound.

Moving to the tracks

The townspeople had moved to the train tracks. Flat, open land, sand, rocks and gravel, not a piece of shade anywhere. They placed explosives on the rails and waited for trains to roll over them. Between trains, they took turns blowing up hammers on steel bars laid flat against the ground.

There, away from the police, the hammers got bigger.

It was noon. The sun was directly overhead. People packed more and more powder onto the sledgehammers and took turns. Huge hammers flew tens of meters into the air.

I watched a kid swing a hammer down. The explosion threw him back onto the ground. The hammer launched upward, spinning, and came down on his head. The ring of steel on skull. He tried to stand. Blood ran from his scalp, down his face, into his eyes. His friend pulled off his own shirt, wrapped it tight around the kid’s head, and hauled him onto the back of a motorcycle. They disappeared down the road.

Nobody stopped. The next person stepped up.

The next morning, the market opened in the square as always. People walked slowly, said good morning to each other. A dog slept in a doorway. The church bell rang at 8.

Here was Josué, down the road. He waved.

I went to say goodbye to Don Juan David. He pulled me into a hug that lasted a long time. He held on. We had barely talked. When he finally let go, his eyes were wet. He thanked me. He begged me to come back next year.

“Sí, San Juanito permite,” he said. If San Juanito allows it.

Mattia Astori and Daniele Colucci make Sacratos, a documentary project on extreme rituals with photos, interviews, articles and videos. They’ve worked in Mexico, India, Bolivia, Thailand and Italy.

World.title: Turtle power: Volunteer to protect Mexico’s sea turtles
World.content:
Turtle camps can be found all over Mexico’s coastline, including the Gulf Coast, allowing volunteers to liberate baby turtles.

With the fifth-longest coastline in all of Mexico — a country that is internationally known and beloved for its beach offerings — Veracruz is certainly a sea-loving state, boasting some 450 miles of Gulf Coast access. For the record, Baja California Sur, a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides, has the longest total coastline at more than 1,350 miles of beach.

Historically, Veracruz is celebrated for its seafood and coastal tropics, as well as being the site of Mexico’s largest and oldest port with access to the Atlantic Ocean.

But what has been lost in the greater narrative is that, as part of its cultural significance along the Gulf Coast, Veracruz has also become one of Mexico’s leading states for turtle conservation.

The legacy of turtle conservationism in Mexico

The earliest federal efforts to focus on sea turtle nesting in Mexico began in 1962, led by the National Institute of Biological and Fisheries Research on both of Mexico’s ample coasts. In 1963, the Center for Turtle Culture opened on Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo.

Shortly after, in 1966, Rancho Nuevo — located in Tamaulipas, just north of Veracruz — was among the first turtle conservation camps to formally open in Mexico. The National Commission of Protected Natural Areas outlined the importance of these efforts from the mid-1960s; the investments significantly helped to maintain the growth of Mexico’s turtle populations by increasing local awareness and participation. During that time, the National Sea Turtles Conservation Program was founded as a result.

Rancho Nuevo, along with the other turtle conservation camps that would spring up all over Mexico’s beaches — from the Gulf to the Pacific — has become a crucial element of turtle protection efforts since then, utilizing a mix of dedicated turtle conservationists and public volunteers. Responsibilities include the protection of nesting sites via monitoring and safeguarding turtle nests, and assisting (or “liberating”) fresh turtle hatchlings to ensure they make it to the sea.

Milestones in national protection rights

Since the 1960s, Mexico has become a global leader in turtle conservancy; in 2025, Mexico was recognized as an exemplar for its turtle protection efforts. Currently, Mexico federally operates 26 turtle conservation centers, in addition to various independent organizations and nonprofits extending across 13 coastal states. Officials announced a record of more than 34 million newborn olive ridley turtles that reached the ocean in a single season, in Oaxaca’s Morro Ayuta region alone.

In 1990, federally backed turtle protection rights gained further ground when then-President Carlos Salinas de Gortari decreed an end to the commercial harvesting of all sea turtles and related products. The landmark move shifted former turtle hunting communities — such as areas in Mazunte, which had among the highest rates of turtle slaughter — into epicenters of turtle conservation. Mazunte opened the Mexican Turtle Center in 1991, aiding the area’s turtle population and ecotourism alike.

Mexico’s role as a sanctuary for sea turtles

According to a 2008 report from the Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat), “Mexico is the country with the largest number of sea-turtle species worldwide. Seven of the eight species known … nest in Mexican beaches, both in the Pacific and in the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean littorals: loggerhead turtle, white or green turtle, black turtle, hawksbill turtle, Kemp’s ridley, olive ridley and leatherback turtle. Two of them, Kemp’s ridley and black sea turtle, nest exclusively in Mexican beaches.”

A more recent investigation from 2023, published in Revista Mexicana de Biodiversidad, revealed that southeastern Mexico, including Veracruz, is the most diverse region for turtle conservation in the country: “According to our results, southeastern Mexico supports three-fourths of the families — and more than half of the genera — found nationwide in Mexico. These findings highlight southeastern Mexico as a region of high importance for the composition of land and freshwater turtles at the national level … Oaxaca, Chiapas and Veracruz stand out as the states with the highest species richness and endemism, respectively. These three states are located within the region considered the richest in total herpetofauna, a result of complex orography, diverse habitats and environments, and the biogeographic history of Mexico.”

An afternoon with turtle conservationists in Veracruz

Jeanne A. Mortimer, a world-renowned marine biologist known as “Madame Torti” who specializes in sea turtle conservationism, once wrote that “The importance of the central coast of Veracruz (for turtle nesting) may be attributed to the fact that the beaches are easily accessible from the ocean without great obstacles like rocks, pronounced slopes or coastal developments that prevent the movement of the adult females along the length and breadth of the beaches.”

It partially explains why Veracruz has been able to cultivate a long-lasting ethos and engagement around turtle protection, with civic initiatives like Fundación Yépez and the Veracruzano Center for Research and Conservation of the Sea Turtle having launched decades ago. Additionally, Veracruz boasts Veracruz Reef System National Park, which played a role in a major environmental ruling by Mexico’s Supreme Court to conserve sea turtle habitats by restricting the construction of industrial ports in endangered areas (although reports that the ruling hasn’t been properly enforced have been published).

Vida Millenaria is among Veracruz’s most prominent turtle conservation groups. The project began in Tecolutla in 1974 as a personal mission for Fernando Manzano, whom locals began to call “Papá Tortuga,” or Turtle Father. Over half a century later, his efforts have expanded to include other members.

To date, the nonprofit has protected and released thousands of baby turtles each year. Visitors arrive year-round to receive public education and help to release newborn turtles into the water along the beaches on the city’s northern outskirts, about a 20-minute drive from the town’s center, along a mostly deserted dirt path.

Camping under the stars in Tecolutla

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kate Levasseur (@katelevass)

I personally drove out to experience it for myself. Depending on your budget, you can rent a group-sized or personal tent near the beach at a campsite that includes outdoor showers, bathrooms and a common area for campers and volunteers who arrive at different hours of the day to participate in the turtle release. The camp area is shaded by palm trees and is relatively cool due to the strong coastal breeze.

The camping experience adds a layer of memory-making, as you sleep beneath the moonlight on a private, mostly isolated beach while the waves wash ashore in the near distance. A rotation of Vida Millenaria workers takes turns patrolling the area on ATVs around the clock, mostly to keep an eye on the turtles and their nests. (Note: If you decide to camp overnight, be sure to bring plenty of supplies, water and food, as a one-way trip back into town requires more than 20 minutes of off-roading to reach the edge of Tecolutla). There, you can enjoy a paradisiacal beach to yourself, undisturbed, until the next day.

A volunteer brigade assembles

Early in the morning, around 7:30 a.m., volunteers of all ages begin to arrive and assemble at the center of camp. A local expert introduces the nonprofit’s history, and a musician plays music dedicated to sea turtles. Maps and visuals are used to show and explain a brief history of turtle conservation in the state, and an adult-sized turtle replica stands in as a faux mascot for guests to take pictures with.

Afterwards, participants are escorted to the nearby souvenir shop, where everything is turtle-related (of course) and handmade. Each purchase grants a set of baby turtles for group liberation — so the more things you buy, the more turtles you’re able to liberate (prices start around 150 pesos and include turtle plushies, stuffed animals, mugs, shirts, etc.). For breakfast, a local volovanero (a savory pastry vendor common in Veracruz) brings a freshly baked batch for about 50 pesos each.

Releasing hatchlings into the wild

Then, the finale: Everyone strolls down to the beach together, lines up, and is given baby turtles to release into the ocean together. It’s a spectacular sight to see upwards of 50 small creatures — more or less, depending on the volunteer group’s size that day — crawling their way into the waves for the first time. They are swept away, their tiny heads occasionally poking out from the shimmering waters before completely disappearing into the distance by the dozens.

Of course, if you’re nowhere near Veracruz, you can search for your nearest beach. You’ll likely discover a turtle conservation group awaiting your participation. It makes a memorable weekend trip — and most importantly, it helps to keep an essential part of Mexico’s ecosystem intact.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: MND goes all in on Mexico City: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Mexico City is having a long-overdue and well-deserved moment in the spotlight. People from all over the world of all ages are discovering the city and everything it has to offer. Entire neighborhoods are being influenced and transformed by the influx of new foreign residents and tourists. Some locals lament the changes, others celebrate them. We had one of our local CDMX writers reflect on it here.

As of late, I now hear from several people a week who have just visited the city for the first time and were blown away by how awesome it is. I can’t help but smile. When I first visited the city over 30 years ago, it was love at first sight — the history, the energy, the people, the contrasts. I would always tell people that it was one of my very favorite cities in the world and have gushed about it in articles and podcasts:

The team at Mexico News Daily is excited to announce that, starting this week, we will be further increasing our coverage of Mexico City. In addition to our regular daily content that very frequently covers news happening in the city, we are now going to begin a weekly MND Local CDMX feature that will give readers even more detailed news and information.

The idea behind this new weekly feature article is to provide the next level of news and information about the city. Perhaps most importantly, we are being very thoughtful in who we are writing for and what should be included. The goal is to write it for a wide audience: those currently living in the city, those considering moving to the city, or others just interested in learning more and being better informed for planning future trips. We hope to inspire first-timers to come check the city out, and those who have been there to come back again soon!

It is NOT written to help you understand what to do in the next 24 hours. It is NOT meant to replace local event calendars and local social media pages. It IS written to help you learn more about the city and better plan your time there. We will give you insight into new openings to be aware of, important events to plan for and new trends shaping the city. We hope to introduce you to new people, new places and new things to check out — all in an effort to inspire you to spend more time discovering this wonderful city.

World.title: ‘Confidently Wrong About Tipping in Mexico’: A new podcast from MND
World.content:
Many people say religion, abortion and politics are topics one should avoid discussing in public. I think I would add tipping to that list! Tipping, both in Mexico and the U.S., was a pretty straightforward affair for years — that is, until the pandemic. What used to be a generally accepted 15% in the U.S. became … 18%? 21%? 24% or more? No purchase, no matter how minor, seemed free of a tip request.

Here in Mexico, tipping has also gotten more complicated for a number of reasons. Since the COVID pandemic, there has been increased awareness about the wages of service workers, and many people have raised their standard tip from 10% to 15%.

More foreigners spending more time in Mexico has also put upward pressure on tipping practices. This trend has not always been well-received by some locals who feel that they are being pressured to tip more or receiving lower quality service due to what their tip is perceived to be. Obviously, that creates an uncomfortable situation.

There is also the debate as to the rationale behind higher tips. Some people say, “If I have the money and I want to give it, who cares?” Others, meanwhile, seek to be cognizant of local norms, seeing that as a form of respect for the culture.

So who’s right? What is standard? And who else besides restaurant servers in Mexico are supposed to be tipped?

Check out our recent article here: Mexico and My Money: The tricky business of tipping in Mexico

And the latest episode of our Confidently Wrong podcast here:

Confidently wrong about tipping in Mexico: Episode 8 - Season 3

World.title: Mexico’s 2027 election cycle has begun: What to know
World.content:
Listen to this article

The 2026-2027 election cycle began on Thursday, and though the stakes are high for the control of Congress, the majority of governorships and all 16 Mexico City borough leaders, the process has already been marred by accusations about the autonomy and transparency of the agency in charge.

A record 102 million Mexicans are eligible to participate in the June 6, 2027, vote. The National Electoral Institute (INE) said it will set up 176,141 polling places, some 6,000 more than during the 2024 federal elections.

Controversy flared up during the agency’s opening electoral session, however, when INE Councilor Arturo Castillo challenged the institution’s credibility.

“The INE seems to have abdicated its role of overseeing and arbitrating elections,” he said, describing a scenario of premature campaigning and irregularities that he said could compromise confidence in the outcome.

Castillo also criticized INE President Guadalupe Taddei for appointing 12 new executive directors over the past year without the consensus of the General Council, some of whom did not meet legal requirements for their appointment.

Two other INE councilors raised questions about new procedures and past oversights, while representatives of opposition political parties complained about what they see as the failure to enforce electoral regulations.

These denunciations contrasted with Taddei’s assertion that the INE was ready to organize the election, while insisting the playing field is level.

What’s at stake in next June’s election

Beyond the selection of more than 20,000 public officials, the vote will serve as a national referendum on the governing project of Morena and the performance of President Claudia Sheinbaum. It will also determine the relative strength of opposition forces ahead of the 2030 presidential election.

While Morena seeks to consolidate its territorial dominance and protect its legislative majority in the Chamber of Deputies (all 500 seats are on the line), some parties will be battling for political survival. The election will also see 17 states choose new governors.

The once-dominant PRI is fighting to remain one of the top five parties in Congress, while the conservative PAN is desperate to preserve its hold on three governor’s mansions.

These two parties also hope to remain relevant in Mexico City, where PRI-PAN alliances control five of the capital’s 16 borough halls, while the PAN aims to maintain its status as the No. 2 party in the Mexico City Congress.

Two new political parties will make their debut in the upcoming elections: PAZ (a party linked to the evangelical church) and Somos México (a center-left party that emerged from opposition to reforms of the INE championed by Morena).

Although the election cycle has officially begun, the formal candidate selection process is not due to begin until Jan. 4, with parties permitted to hold primaries through Feb. 12. After that, the formal campaign season will take place from April 4 through June 2.

Complaints about alleged irregularities

Criticism of the INE is primarily related to alleged violations of the campaign schedule regulations.

Ahead of the 2018 elections, Morena designated so-called state coordinators who were tasked with guiding the party in the run-up to gubernatorial elections. Since they were then inevitably nominated as candidates, critics say their actions as state coordinators should be regarded as campaign violations.

At the same time, office-holders seeking re-election or aiming for a new post have been known to stage public events and rallies before the official campaign season, proceedings that could be seen as violating election law.

With reports from El País, Animal Político, El Universal, Texas Public Policy Foundation and Lider Empresarial

World.title: Brazil’s Casas Bahia Is in Court-Supervised Reorganisation With US$3.4 Billion of Claims
World.content:
BRAZIL · RETAIL

Key Facts — The filing Sunday 16 August 2026, at the central civil court in Sao Paulo, by the parent and nine subsidiaries.

— The size About 17.3 billion reais, roughly US$3.4 billion, of obligations fall inside the process.

— The shield A judge granted a 180-day stay on 31 August, running from 19 August 2026 to 15 February 2027.

— The quarter A second-quarter accounting loss of 10.1 billion reais, some US$1.98 billion, mostly non-cash.

— The adjusted number The adjusted loss was 978 million reais, about US$192 million, up 76 percent on a year earlier.

— The catch Negative equity of 8.2 billion reais, roughly US$1.61 billion. The balance sheet has to be rebuilt, not just refinanced.

This is reorganisation, not liquidation. The company keeps trading, keeps its stores open and gets six months of protection from creditors while it negotiates.

A shopping street in central Sao Paulo. The retailer sells furniture and appliances to lower-income households across Brazil. (Photo: “Crowded shopping street in central Sao Paulo” by Wilfredor, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

Casas Bahia, one of Brazil’s largest household goods retailers, is in court-supervised reorganisation. It filed on Sunday 16 August 2026.

The application went to the central civil court in Sao Paulo. It was made by the parent company and nine subsidiaries.

Around 17.3 billion reais of obligations, roughly US$3.4 billion, fall inside the process. That is what the company now has to renegotiate.

What This Is and Is Not

Recuperacao judicial is the Brazilian equivalent of Chapter 11 in the United States. It is a reorganisation with the company still running.

It is not bankruptcy and it is not liquidation. Stores stay open, staff stay employed and the business keeps trading.

The point of the process is time. A court freezes enforcement so a plan can be negotiated with creditors.

Getting this wrong in English is common and it is damaging. A company in reorganisation has not gone bust.

The Shield

On Monday 31 August a judge in the specialist bankruptcy and recovery court granted the stay. It runs for 180 days.

The period is backdated to 19 August 2026 and expires on 15 February 2027. During it, creditors cannot seize assets or enforce collections.

That protection was needed quickly. Within days of the filing, creditors had already frozen around nine million reais, some US$1.77 million.

The shares rose 40 percent on the ruling, to 0.56 reais, about US$0.11. That is the arithmetic of a very low base.

The company provides consumer electronics, home appliances, furniture, and other domestic items. It also engages in the manufacture, industrialization, and sale of wood-based furniture; ownership and management of equity interests; management of logistics operations; and provision of…

How It Got Here

The second-quarter results are the reason. The accounting net loss was 10.1 billion reais, roughly US$1.98 billion.

That headline figure is misleading on its own. It is heavily non-cash, and the adjusted loss was 978 million reais, about US$192 million.

The adjusted loss was still 76 percent worse than a year earlier. Net financial debt stood at 1.2 billion reais, some US$236 million.

The number that actually matters is equity. Shareholders’ funds were negative by 8.2 billion reais, roughly US$1.61 billion.

The Sao Paulo courts. The reorganisation is being supervised by a specialist bankruptcy and recovery court. (Photo: “Edifício do Tribunal de Justiça de São Paulo (4)” by Fernanda Grillo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

The Explanation the Company Gives

Management points at interest rates, restricted credit and financing costs. It also cites pressure on consumption and on working capital.

Casas Bahia sells appliances and furniture largely on instalment credit. High rates hit both the cost of funding and the customer’s ability to pay.

The company confirmed 298 store closures in its results. That count was itself disputed in Brazilian coverage, so treat it as the company’s own figure.

Headcount has also been cut. No redundancy total has been confirmed in a company disclosure.

The Share Price Puzzle

The stock was at 0.76 reais, about US$0.15, on Friday 11 September, up 4.11 percent on the day. It has roughly doubled since the end of August.

Nothing disclosed explains that. No new filing, ruling or transaction was announced in the intervening fortnight.

The context is brutal. The shares are down about 82 percent this year.

The 52-week range runs from 0.34 reais to 4.90, some US$0.07 to US$0.96. The low end is where they have been trading.

Net debt sits at more than twelve times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Trading at this level is a bet on the plan, not on the business as it stands.

What Happens Next

The company must present a reorganisation plan to creditors. They vote on it, and a court then either confirms or rejects it.

The nine subsidiaries inside the filing include the logistics arms and the furniture manufacturer. That means the whole operating chain is covered.

The February deadline is not absolute. Brazilian courts routinely extend the protection period where negotiations are progressing.

For customers, nothing changes for now. For suppliers and bondholders, the negotiation is where the outcome will be decided.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Casas Bahia gone bankrupt?

No. It is in recuperacao judicial, a court-supervised reorganisation similar to Chapter 11. Stores remain open and the company continues trading.

How much debt is involved?

About 17.3 billion reais, roughly US$3.4 billion, of obligations fall inside the process.

When did it file?

Sunday 16 August 2026, at the central civil court in Sao Paulo, together with nine subsidiaries.

What protection does it have?

A 180-day stay granted on 31 August 2026, running from 19 August to 15 February 2027, during which creditors cannot enforce claims.

How bad are the results?

A second-quarter accounting loss of 10.1 billion reais, an adjusted loss of 978 million reais, and negative shareholders’ equity of 8.2 billion reais, roughly US$1.61 billion.

World.title: Brazilian Farming Group SLC Agricola Raises About US$101 Million in Rural Notes
World.content:
BRAZIL · AGRIBUSINESS

Key Facts — The issue 515,480 rural product notes at 1,000 reais each, about 515.5 million reais or roughly US$101 million.

— The date Approved Friday 11 September 2026. Trade date: Friday 11 September 2026.

— The terms Maturity 15 September 2033, with principal repaid in two equal instalments from 2031.

— The rate 95.5 percent of the interbank rate, swapped into dollar appreciation plus 6.15 percent a year.

— The upgrade JPMorgan moved the stock to overweight on 9 September and raised its target to 23 reais, about US$4.52.

— The catch First-quarter net income fell 53 percent. The upgrade is a bet on the next crop, not the last one.

Grain and cotton prices have turned. One of Brazil’s largest listed farmers spent the week collecting the benefit in both the debt and equity markets.

Soybean production in Brazil. The company farms soy, cotton and corn across several states. (Photo: “Soy Production In Brazil – 46200453244” by SentinelHub, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

SLC Agricola approved a rural note issue on Friday. The total is about 515.5 million reais, roughly US$101 million.

The instrument is a cedula de produto rural with financial settlement. It is a Brazilian farm-sector security that settles in cash rather than in grain.

There are 515,480 notes at a nominal 1,000 reais each, about US$196. They are sold to professional investors only.

The Terms

The notes mature on 15 September 2033, seven years out. Principal is repaid in two equal instalments, the first in September 2031.

The headline rate is 95.5 percent of the accumulated interbank deposit rate. That is then swapped into dollar appreciation plus 6.15 percent a year.

The swap is the interesting part. A farmer selling soy and cotton earns in dollars, so dollar-linked debt matches the revenue.

Bradesco guarantees the issue in full and its investment bank is underwriting it. Proceeds go to production, commercialisation, processing, working capital and investment.

The Week Before It

On Wednesday 9 September JPMorgan raised its rating to overweight from neutral. It lifted its price target from 18 reais to 23, about US$3.54 to US$4.52.

The shares rose 7.72 percent that morning to 18.15 reais, roughly US$3.56. The bank named the company its top pick in the sector.

It preferred it to 3tentos, Sao Martinho and Adecoagro. Its argument was that Brazilian agribusiness is coming out of a three-year squeeze on margins and leverage.

The case rests on prices. Soybeans were up 13 percent on the month and 26 percent on the year.

Corn was up 16 percent on both measures. Cotton has gained 29 percent so far this year.

Farmland at Alto Taquari, Mato Grosso. The company’s land portfolio was revalued at 13.53 billion reais, some US$2.66 billion, in June. (Photo: “Alto Taquari” by Coordenação-Geral de Observação da Terra/INPE, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)

The company was founded in 1977 and is headquartered in Porto…

What the Shares Did

SLC Agricola shares were at 17.94 reais, about US$3.52, on Friday, down 2.66 percent on the day. Trade date: Friday 11 September 2026.

The weekly picture is the opposite. It gained 9.75 percent over the five sessions, the best performance on the Brazilian index.

Over twelve months it is up about 24 percent. The 52-week range runs from 12.62 reais to 19.32, roughly US$2.48 to US$3.79.

The Number That Argues the Other Way

First-quarter net income was 236 million reais, some US$46 million. That was down 53 percent on the same quarter a year earlier.

The broker case is therefore forward-looking. It depends on the combination of prices and costs holding through the coming harvest.

Two specifics were cited. The timing of fertiliser purchases and the company’s hedging book are both said to protect margins.

On the numbers used, the stock trades at about 5.9 times expected 2027 earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. The free cash flow yield is put at 6.2 percent.

The Land Question

SLC Agricola farmland was revalued in June at 13.53 billion reais, roughly US$2.66 billion. That was an increase of just one percent.

The small move is the signal. Brazilian farmland values have flattened after years of rapid appreciation.

For a business that owns much of what it farms, that matters twice. It affects the balance sheet and it affects the cost of expanding.

Nothing new was announced on land or acquisitions this week. The 13.6 percent planted-area increase circulating online refers to the 2025 to 2026 season, not the coming one.

Why It Matters

Brazilian farming depends less on domestic interest rates than on the dollar and the weather. Both moved in its favour this week.

A dollar-linked seven-year note at these terms says lenders agree. So does a bank raising its target by almost a third.

The counterweight is a weak first quarter and a flat land market. The next results are the test of which reading is right.

What are the terms?

How have the shares performed?

They ended the week at 17.94 reais, about US$3.52, up 9.75 percent over five sessions and roughly 24 percent over twelve months.

What is the risk?

First-quarter net income fell 53 percent to 236 million reais, some US$46 million, and the farmland portfolio rose only one percent in the June revaluation.

World.title: Petrobras Announced a Fuel Price Rise and Cancelled It Four Hours Later
World.content:
BRAZIL · ENERGY

Key Facts — The announcement Wednesday 9 September at 20:44. Gasoline to distributors up 0.19 reais a litre, about US$0.04.

— The reversal Thursday 10 September at 00:53, roughly four hours later. The revised price was a cut of the same size.

— Why A subsidy expired and a tax cut replaced it. The two moves netted out the other way.

— Diesel The government announced a further 1.00 real a litre subsidy, some US$0.20, on 9 September.

— The credit A decree opened 6.6 billion reais, roughly US$1.30 billion, to pay for the fuel subsidies.

— The catch The diesel increase has not happened. The company says it is waiting for the legal texts.

Brazilian fuel pricing now runs through a stack of temporary decrees. When one expires and another lands the same week, even the company gets confused.

The Duque de Caxias refinery in Rio de Janeiro state. Refinery gate prices are what the company sets. (Photo: “REDUC Vista do Morro do Céu” by Filipo Tardim, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Petrobras raised the price of gasoline late on Wednesday night. By one in the morning it had taken the increase back.

The first notice went out at 20:44 on 9 September. It put gasoline to distributors up by 0.19 reais a litre, about US$0.04, to 3.24 reais, some US$0.64.

The correction came at 00:53 on 10 September. The revised figure was 3.05 reais a litre, roughly US$0.60.

That is a cut of 0.19 reais, about US$0.04, not a rise. The company said the change corresponded only to the suspension of a discount.

Why Both Statements Were True

Two Petrobras-relevant policy changes landed in the same 24 hours. One removed money from the price and the other put more back.

A temporary decree that had subsidised gasoline by 0.44 reais a litre, some US$0.09, expired. On its own that pushes the price up.

At the same time the government cut two federal levies by 0.63 reais a litre, about US$0.12. That takes the total tax load on gasoline down to 0.16 reais, roughly US$0.03.

The tax cut is larger than the lost subsidy. Net of both, the price falls.

The arrangement runs from 10 September to 5 October. After that the question reopens.

The Diesel Half

Diesel is the more important number for Petrobras and for Brazil. It sets freight costs and therefore food prices.

On 9 September the government announced a new subsidy of 1.00 real a litre, some US$0.20, for road diesel. That sits on top of an existing 1.12 reais, about US$0.22.

Together that is roughly 2.12 reais a litre, around US$0.42, of public money in the price. A decree opened 6.6 billion reais, some US$1.30 billion, of extraordinary credit to fund it.

Of that, 5.607 billion reais, roughly US$1.10 billion, is earmarked for diesel. The remainder covers other fuels.

The tax on hydrous ethanol was also taken to zero. That is worth about 0.19 reais a litre, some US$0.04.

A filling station in Mato Grosso. What drivers pay depends on taxes and distributor margins as well as the refinery price. (Photo: “Posto de Combustível – Vila Rica – Mato Grosso” by Túllio F, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Petróleo Brasileiro S.A. – Petrobras explores, produces, and sells oil and gas in Brazil, China, the United States, the Americas, Asia, Europe, Singapore, and internationally. It operates through three segments: Exploration and Production; Refining, Transportation & Marketing; and Gas & Low Carbon Energies. The Exploration and Production segment explores, develops, and produces…

The Increase That Has Not Happened

Petrobras is expected to raise the refinery price of diesel by about 1.00 real a litre, roughly US$0.20. The subsidy is designed to absorb it.

In principle distributors would pay the same as before. The consumer would notice nothing.

It has not been done. Petrobras says on the record that it is waiting for the legal texts to be published first.

Everything beyond that comes from unnamed sources. Treat reports that the increase has already taken effect with care.

Why the Company Wants the Rise

Brent crude has been above US$100 a barrel. Domestic refinery prices have not followed.

Petrobras sells diesel well below what an importer would pay. The company’s own pricing policy is meant to track international levels loosely.

This is the oldest argument in Brazilian energy policy. Holding pump prices down is popular, and the cost lands on a company the state controls but does not wholly own.

Minority shareholders have sued over exactly this in the past. Using subsidies rather than suppressed prices is the government’s answer to that objection.

What to Watch

The first thing is publication. Until the decrees appear in the official gazette, Petrobras will not move on diesel.

The second is 5 October, when the current gasoline arrangement lapses. A second expiry without a replacement means a real increase at the pump.

The third is the subsidy itself. The finance ministry can adjust, suspend or extend it, which makes it a policy lever rather than a commitment.

For anyone living in Brazil, the practical effect this month is nil to slightly positive. Pump prices are not going up because of any of this.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Petrobras announce?

Petrobras announced a 0.19 reais a litre increase in gasoline to distributors on the night of 9 September 2026, about US$0.04, then a reversal about four hours later.

Why did the price change twice?

A subsidy of 0.44 reais a litre, some US$0.09, expired, while a larger tax cut of 0.63 reais, about US$0.12, took effect. Net of both, gasoline fell rather than rose.

Has diesel gone up?

No. Petrobras says it is waiting for the government’s legal texts to be published before implementing anything.

How much is the government spending?

A decree opened 6.6 billion reais of extraordinary credit, roughly US$1.30 billion, of which 5.607 billion reais, some US$1.10 billion, is earmarked for diesel.

How long does this last?

The current gasoline arrangement runs to 5 October 2026. The diesel subsidy can be adjusted, suspended or extended by the finance ministry.

World.title: Banco Patagonia, Owned by Banco do Brasil, Buys 28 Branches in Argentina
World.content:
ARGENTINA · BANKING

Key Facts — The deal Announced on 28 August 2026. The buyer takes over the seller’s retail banking business, not the bank itself.

— The buyer Banco Patagonia, which is 80 percent owned by Brazil’s state-controlled Banco do Brasil.

— The seller Banco Industrial, known as Bind, which is exiting consumer banking to focus on corporate clients.

— The perimeter 28 branches, about 200,000 customers and a pension payment book covering 396,307 retirees.

— The approvals Argentina’s central bank, the securities regulator, the competition authority and the pension agency.

— The catch No price has been disclosed. A figure of about US$60 million circulating is a market estimate.

This is a carve-out, not a takeover. The seller keeps its licence, one branch and its corporate business, and walks away from retail banking.

Buenos Aires. The branches being transferred are concentrated in the capital and the surrounding province. (Photo: “Corrientes Buenos Aires at Night” by Luis Argerich, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

Banco Patagonia is taking over the consumer banking business of a smaller Argentine rival. The agreement was announced on 28 August 2026.

The buyer is 80 percent owned by Banco do Brasil, the Brazilian state-controlled lender. The seller is Banco Industrial, known in Argentina as Bind.

Get the shape of it right. This is not one bank buying another.

What Is Being Sold

Bind is selling its retail banking operation as a business unit. It keeps its banking licence and its corporate business.

It will retain a single branch in downtown Buenos Aires. Its stated plan is to focus on corporate and business clients and on partnerships with financial technology firms.

The transferred perimeter is specific. It covers 28 branches across the city of Buenos Aires, the surrounding province, Cordoba, Santa Fe and Tucuman.

Around 200,000 customers move with them. Staff transfer with their length of service recognised.

The Part That Matters Most

The most valuable item is not the branches. It is the pension and payroll book.

That covers 396,307 retirees whose payments run through the seller. In Argentina a pension payment relationship is a stable, recurring customer base.

Deposits move across as well. Across its whole business the seller reports 8.75 million savings accounts and 332,509 debit cards.

Not all of that is in the sale. The figures give a sense of the scale of the institution behind it.

Its Banking segment offers various products and services, including…

The Price Nobody Has Confirmed

No purchase price has been disclosed by either party. A figure of about US$60 million is being repeated in coverage.

That number is a market estimate, not a term sheet. The outlet that published it said explicitly that this is what the market reckons.

Its workings are visible. Branches valued at one to two million dollars each, customers at roughly 120 dollars a head, pension relationships at about 60.

There is a benchmark. Banco Columbia changed hands for a little over US$40 million with 36 branches and 400,000 customers.

A Buenos Aires street corner. Branch networks have become the currency of Argentine bank consolidation. (Photo: “Av. Corrientes & Junín, Once, Buenos Aires (28042883004)” by Andrew Milligan sumo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

What Still Has to Happen

Four approvals are required. They come from the central bank, the securities regulator, the competition authority and the pension agency.

The pension agency matters because of the retiree payment book. Transferring that function is not a purely commercial decision.

The full branch transfer is expected by January 2027. Until then nothing changes for customers.

Why a Brazilian Bank Is Buying in Argentina

Banco do Brasil has held its Argentine subsidiary since 2010. Its presence there has been steady rather than expansionary.

Argentine banking has been consolidating as smaller institutions find retail unprofitable. Branch networks and payment books are what change hands.

For the buyer the logic is scale in a market it already knows. For the seller it is an exit from a business it no longer wants.

The wider read is about Brazilian capital moving sideways into the region. This is a subsidiary’s purchase, not a headquarters decision, but the ownership chain runs to Brasilia.

Argentine retail banking is a low-margin business in a high-inflation economy. Anyone buying into it is taking a view on the next several years, not the next several months.

Banco Patagonia already ranks among the larger private banks in the country. Adding 28 branches strengthens its position outside the capital.

Nothing in the announcement suggests job cuts. Staff move across with their seniority intact.

The seller has run a retail network for decades. Walking away from it is a judgement about where Argentine banking margins now sit.

Banco Patagonia, 80 percent owned by Banco do Brasil, is buying the retail banking business of Banco Industrial, known as Bind. The bank itself is not being sold.

How big is the deal?

28 branches, about 200,000 customers, transferred deposits and a pension payment book covering 396,307 retirees.

How much is it worth?

No price has been disclosed. A figure of about US$60 million circulating in coverage is a market estimate, not a confirmed number.

When does it complete?

The full branch transfer is expected by January 2027, subject to four regulatory approvals.

What happens to Bind?

It keeps its licence, one downtown Buenos Aires branch and its corporate business, and shifts toward corporate clients and fintech partnerships.

World.title: Puerto Rico Had 15 Load Shedding Events in Two Months, the Grid Operator Says
World.content:
PUERTO RICO · ENERGY

Key Facts — The figure 15 manual load shedding events in July and August 2026, reported by the grid operator.

— The comparison The whole May to October 2025 season produced 16.

— The demand August peak demand reached about 3,234 megawatts, the highest in four years.

— The supply Installed capacity is above 6,500 megawatts. Roughly 3,200 are actually available after outages.

— The gap A structural shortfall of 700 to 850 megawatts, on the operator’s own numbers.

— The catch The figure was filed by the company arguing for 800 megawatts of new temporary generation.

The number comes from the company asking regulators to approve 800 megawatts of emergency generation. That does not make it wrong, but it is worth knowing.

Puerto Rico went through 15 rounds of deliberate load shedding in July and August. The figure comes from the company that runs the island’s transmission and distribution network.

It was submitted in a filing to the energy regulator. The whole of the previous summer season, from May to October 2025, produced 16.

Two months have therefore almost matched six. That is the point the operator is making.

The Arithmetic of the Shortage

Installed generating capacity on the island is above 6,500 megawatts. That number is close to meaningless in practice.

Only about 4,100 megawatts are actually available. After forced outages and scheduled maintenance the usable figure falls to roughly 3,200.

Peak demand in August reached about 3,234 megawatts. That was the highest in four years.

The gap is therefore structural rather than occasional. The operator puts the shortfall at 700 to 850 megawatts.

What a Bad Day Looks Like

Take Saturday 12 September. Three units were offline: two at Costa Sur and one at the AES plant.

Available capacity was about 2,495 megawatts against projected demand of 2,950. That is a negative reserve of 355 megawatts.

The 355 figure already assumes a demand-reduction programme worth roughly 100 megawatts. Without it the gap is 440.

When the reserve goes negative, load shedding is the tool. Customers are cut in rotation to keep the system from collapsing.

How It Got Here

One event stands out. A catastrophic failure at Aguirre Unit 1 in February 2025 removed a critical baseload generator.

The fleet was already old. Most of the island’s firm generation runs on ageing oil and gas plants.

The replacement plan was temporary generation. That is where the politics start.

The Palo Seco plant. Most of the island’s baseload generation comes from ageing oil and gas units. (Photo: “Staff Delegation Tours Palo Seco Power Plant, Puerto Rico” by South Atlantic Division (SAD) USACE, via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.)

The Cancelled Contract

On 18 August the power authority cancelled a contract with a company called Power Expectations. It covered 400 megawatts.

The reported value was US$5.9 billion. The governor’s public position on it was that it should be cancelled.

The company has sued in federal court to have the contract reinstated. That litigation is active.

The cancellation left a hole. On 19 and 20 August the energy regulator ordered the operator to update its statement of what temporary generation the island needs.

That order is what produced the filing containing the 15-event figure. The sequence matters when you read the number.

Reading the Number Honestly

The load shedding count is the operator’s own. It was filed by a company asking a regulator to approve about 800 megawatts of emergency capacity.

That does not make it false. Regulatory filings carry consequences for inaccuracy.

It does mean the figure serves an argument. A second, independent count has not been published.

The operator’s worst case is stark. It describes up to 47 days of interruptions if demand rises ten percent and another baseload unit is lost.

The Political Fight

Relations between the government and the operator are poor. The governor has publicly accused it of wanting to sow chaos.

The legislature is summoning the power authority’s head over the failed temporary generation deal. The regulator has been demanding status updates and calendar dates for months.

None of that adds a megawatt. The winter months bring lower demand and some relief.

The test comes next summer. Unless firm capacity arrives before then, the same arithmetic produces the same result.

More: Latin America news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many outages were there?

15 manual load shedding events in July and August 2026, according to the grid operator’s filing to the energy regulator.

Is that unusual?

Yes. The entire May to October 2025 season produced 16, so two months in 2026 nearly matched six months in 2025.

Why is there not enough power?

Installed capacity exceeds 6,500 megawatts but only about 3,200 are usable after outages and maintenance, against August peak demand of about 3,234.

What happened to the emergency generation plan?

A 400-megawatt contract with Power Expectations, reported at US$5.9 billion, was cancelled on 18 August 2026. The company is suing to reinstate it.

Who produced the 15-event figure?

The grid operator itself, in a filing supporting its request for about 800 megawatts of temporary generation.

Sources: Metro Puerto Rico, El Nuevo Dia, NotiCel, El Vocero.

World.title: Puerto Rico Panel Drops the Criminal Case Against a Former Elections Chief
World.content:
PUERTO RICO · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The date Friday 11 September 2026.

— The decision The special prosecutor panel archived the criminal investigation for lack of sufficient evidence.

— The subject Jessika Padilla Rivera, former alternate president of the State Elections Commission.

— The allegation Authorising a one-off payment of US$177,586.49 to exempt staff from the 2024 general election budget.

— The panel Decided by Leila Rolon Henrique and Olga Birriel Cardona. The panel president recused herself.

— The catch Archiving is not exoneration. The file went on to the ethics office and three other bodies.

An investigation into a payment of about US$177,600 to election-office staff has ended without charges, and with two of the three panel members deciding it.

The Capitol in San Juan. The special prosecutor panel is an independent body created by statute. (Photo: “Capitol of Puerto Rico at dusk” by Amaury Laporte, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.)

The body that handles corruption cases against senior officials in Puerto Rico has closed one of them. It archived the criminal investigation of a former elections official on Friday.

The subject is Jessika Padilla Rivera. She was the alternate president of the State Elections Commission.

The reason given is evidentiary. Prosecutors concluded the material was not sufficient to sustain a criminal accusation.

What She Was Investigated For

The allegation concerned a payment to staff. It was a one-off disbursement of US$177,586.49 to exempt employees of the commission.

The money came from the operating budget for the 2024 general elections. It was described as a non-recurring single payment.

The claim was that she authorised and disbursed it without proper authority. That would have amounted to misappropriation of public funds.

Why It Was Dropped

The independent special prosecutors assigned to the file recommended archiving it. They reported contradictions and deficiencies in the testimony they gathered.

Those gaps meant the elements of the offence could not be established. Without them there is no case to put before a court.

The panel accepted that recommendation. Two of its three members made the decision.

They are Leila Rolon Henrique and Olga Birriel Cardona, both former judges. The panel president, Ygri Rivera Sanchez, was recused from the matter.

It Is Not Over Everywhere

Archiving a criminal file does not end the matter administratively. The panel referred it onward.

It went to four bodies: the Office of Government Ethics, the presidency of the elections commission, the budget office and the treasury. Any of those can act on its own rules.

Administrative and ethical standards are lower than the criminal standard. A payment that cannot be prosecuted can still be found improper.

No objection to the decision had been published by Saturday. That may change once the referred bodies respond.

Old San Juan. The elections commission is one of several agencies whose officials fall under the panel’s jurisdiction. (Photo: “San Juan – Calle de San Francisco” by Jack Delano, via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.)

What This Panel Is

It is an independent statutory body. Its job is to decide whether allegations against high-ranking officials justify appointing a special prosecutor.

The structure exists to take those decisions away from the executive branch. A governor cannot direct it and cannot dismiss its members at will.

Panel members serve fixed terms set in law. That independence is the whole point of the design.

It is worth stating clearly because the mechanism is unusual. Most jurisdictions in the region leave such cases with the ordinary prosecution service.

The Other File

The panel has a separate and much larger matter in progress. On 10 September it assigned another prosecutor to an investigation that includes Francisco Domenech.

Domenech was the governor’s chief of staff. He and Itza Garcia left the office of the secretary of governance in late July.

Their departures came while that investigation was under way. Neither has been charged.

That case is unrelated to the elections payment. The two are being handled separately and should not be read together.

Why It Matters

Puerto Rico has spent years dealing with federal and local corruption prosecutions. The panel’s decisions get read politically whichever way they go.

Friday’s outcome will be read by some as a system working and by others as one failing. The document itself says something narrower.

It says the evidence collected did not meet the criminal threshold. That is a statement about the file, not a verdict on the conduct.

The referred bodies now decide whether anything administrative follows. Those processes are slower and rarely make headlines.

More: Latin America news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the panel decide?

It archived the criminal investigation of Jessika Padilla Rivera on 11 September 2026, finding the evidence insufficient to sustain a charge.

What was the allegation?

That she authorised a one-off payment of US$177,586.49 to exempt elections commission staff from the 2024 general election operating budget without proper authority.

Does archiving mean she was cleared?

No. It means the criminal threshold was not met. The file was referred to the ethics office, the commission presidency, the budget office and the treasury.

Who made the decision?

Panel members Leila Rolon Henrique and Olga Birriel Cardona. The panel president, Ygri Rivera Sanchez, was recused.

Is this connected to the Domenech investigation?

No. That is a separate matter, to which the panel assigned another prosecutor on 10 September 2026. Nobody has been charged in it.

Sources: NotiCel, Periodico La Perla, Metro, El Nuevo Dia.

World.title: Colombian Power Company Grupo Energía Bogotá Starts Paperwork for a US Listing
World.content:
COLOMBIA · ENERGY

Key Facts — The step On Friday 11 September the board called an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting to authorise a US registration.

— The instrument American depositary shares, which let foreign investors hold the stock through a US-traded certificate.

— The exchange Not confirmed. The company says a US exchange, not New York specifically.

— The owner The city district holds 65.7 percent. Pension funds hold about 21.5 percent between them.

— The purpose A wider international shareholder base, more liquidity and easier access to foreign financing.

— The catch Nothing is listed yet. Shareholders must vote, and the US securities regulator must register it.

This is a depositary receipt programme, not a share sale, and not yet a listing. The company has been careful about that distinction. Headlines have not.

Bogotá. The city district is the majority shareholder in the utility that carries its name. (Photo: “57 – Bogota – Décembre 2008” by Martin St-Amant (S23678), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

The Colombian power company Grupo Energía Bogotá moved a step closer to a United States listing on Friday. Its board called an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting to authorise the registration.

It is the energy utility majority-owned by the city of Bogotá. It operates transmission and gas distribution businesses in Colombia, Peru, Brazil and Guatemala.

Nothing has been listed and nothing has been sold. What happened is a corporate authorisation step.

What Is Actually Proposed

The instrument is an American depositary share. That is a certificate traded in the United States that represents shares held in the home market.

It is the standard route for a Latin American company that wants American investors without moving its primary listing. The shares themselves stay on the Colombian exchange.

The company first disclosed the idea on 20 April 2026. It told the Colombian financial regulator it had begun exploratory activities toward a US registration.

That filing said plainly it was not an offer to sell. It made the plan conditional on corporate approvals, regulatory registration and exchange approval.

Which Exchange

The company has not named one. Its own wording refers to a United States exchange.

A good deal of coverage has written New York. That is an inference rather than a disclosure.

No registration statement with the US securities regulator has been published. No timetable has been given either.

Who Owns It

The city district of Bogotá held 65.7 percent as of the end of September 2025. That makes the capital’s government the controlling shareholder.

Colombian pension funds hold about 21.5 percent between them. Porvenir has 9.9 percent and Protección 7.8 percent.

Corficolombiana holds 5.2 percent. The remaining 7.6 percent is spread across other private investors.

The Liévano Palace, seat of the city government. A separate proposal to sell part of the city’s stake has drawn objections in the council. (Photo: “Palacio Liévano en la lluvia” by Aztlek, Luis Alejandro Bernal Romero, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

The Separate Argument About Selling

There is a second proposal that people keep confusing with this one. The city is evaluating the sale of 9.4 percent of its holding.

That would be about 863 million shares, valued at roughly 2.56 trillion pesos, some US$826 million. The district would still hold about 56.3 percent afterwards.

The legal basis is a 2016 council agreement allowing the city to divest up to 20 percent. Selling 9.4 percent would stay inside that ceiling.

This is where the political objection sits. In March a city councillor called the sale another historic emptying of public assets.

The council placed the possible sale under review the same month. No comparable objection to the depositary receipt programme has been recorded.

Why a Company Does This

The company gives three reasons: a broader global shareholder base, better liquidity and easier access to international financing. Those are the standard ones.

A US listing also brings American disclosure obligations. For a state-controlled utility that is a meaningful change in how much it has to publish.

The practical benefit is the investor pool. Many large funds cannot easily hold Colombian local shares but can hold depositary receipts.

The risk is the same as for any emerging-market issuer. A US listing exposes the share price to sentiment about Colombia as a whole.

What Happens Next

Shareholders must vote at the extraordinary meeting. No date for it has been published.

After that, a registration would have to be filed and accepted in the United States. An exchange would have to approve the listing.

Only then would the certificates trade. Each of those steps can take months.

For now the correct description is a process that has started. Anything more definite is ahead of the facts.

More: Latin America news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the company announce?

Its board called an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting on 11 September 2026 to authorise registering with the US securities regulator for a depositary share programme.

Is it listing on the New York Stock Exchange?

Not confirmed. The company refers to a United States exchange without naming one.

Is the city selling the company?

No. A separate proposal would sell 9.4 percent of the city’s stake, leaving it with about 56.3 percent and still in control.

Who owns the Colombian power company?

The city district holds 65.7 percent, pension funds about 21.5 percent, Corficolombiana 5.2 percent and other private investors 7.6 percent.

When would trading begin?

No timetable has been published. A shareholder vote, a US registration and an exchange approval all have to come first.

Sources: Valora Analitik, Bloomberg Línea, Portafolio, La República, Concejo de Bogotá.

World.title: Colombia Seizes Three Properties From Former Presidential Candidate Zuluaga
World.content:
COLOMBIA · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The date Friday 11 September 2026, ordered by the national prosecution service.

— The assets An apartment in Bogota, a one-third share of another Bogota home, and a property in Pensilvania, Caldas.

— The value About 3,664 million pesos, roughly US$1.18 million at the official rate.

— The process Civil asset forfeiture, which runs separately from the criminal case.

— The background An alleged US$1.61 million Odebrecht payment for 2014 campaign advertising, never declared.

— The catch There is no conviction. He was charged in 2023 and did not accept the charges.

This is a freeze, not a verdict. The criminal case against the former candidate has not reached trial and he has never accepted the charges.

The Palace of Justice in Bogota. The criminal case has been working through the courts since 2023. (Photo: “Palacio de Justicia de Colombia, Bogotá” by Bernard Gagnon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Colombian prosecutors froze three properties linked to Oscar Ivan Zuluaga on Friday. He was the runner-up in the 2014 presidential election.

The order came from the prosecution service’s asset forfeiture directorate. It was handled by the special task group working on the Odebrecht file.

The measures are an embargo, judicial custody and suspension of the right to dispose of the assets. In plain terms, nothing can be sold.

What Was Frozen

There are three properties. One is an apartment in Bogota and one is a one-third share of another home in the city.

The third is in Pensilvania, in the department of Caldas. Together they are valued at about 3,664 million pesos, roughly US$1.18 million.

All three were registered in his own name. They were transferred to family members in June 2023, his wife among them.

Prosecutors say the freeze stops any sale while forfeiture proceeds. The relatives who received the transfers have not been charged with anything.

What Forfeiture Is, and Is Not

Asset forfeiture in Colombia is a civil action against property, not against a person. It asks whether an asset has a lawful origin.

It runs on a separate track from the criminal case. A freeze in one does not establish guilt in the other.

This distinction gets lost quickly in headlines. Zuluaga has not been convicted of anything.

The Underlying Allegation

The case concerns the 2014 presidential campaign. Prosecutors allege a payment of US$1,610,740 from the Brazilian construction group Odebrecht.

The money is said to have moved between June and July 2014 through an entity registered in Panama. It allegedly paid for campaign advertising.

The advertising work is attributed to the Brazilian publicist Duda Mendonca. The payment was never reported to electoral authorities.

Odebrecht admitted paying bribes across Latin America in a 2016 settlement with United States prosecutors. Colombia has been working through the consequences ever since.

Pensilvania, in the coffee-growing department of Caldas. One of the three frozen properties is here. (Photo: “Pensilvania caldas – panoramio (5)” by Jimmy Gómez N, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

Where the Criminal Case Stands

Zuluaga was formally charged on 10 July 2023. The counts are falsification of a private document, procedural fraud and illicit enrichment.

His son David Zuluaga Martinez was charged with procedural fraud. Neither accepted the charges.

Defence attempts to annul the proceedings were rejected in April 2024. A Bogota appeals tribunal rejected them again on 25 June 2024.

The formal indictment was filed on 5 August 2024. The case has not reached a verdict.
