His lawyer said in 2023 that the defence would prove innocence with evidence and disprove every charge. No comment on Friday’s freeze had been published by Saturday.

Why It Matters

Zuluaga came second to Juan Manuel Santos in 2014. He was the candidate of the party led by former president Alvaro Uribe.

The Odebrecht scandal touched both campaigns in that election. It has produced years of litigation and very few final judgments.

Friday’s order is a procedural step, not a conclusion. It signals that prosecutors intend to pursue the assets whatever happens in the criminal court.

For readers outside Colombia, the useful point is the two-track system. Property can be frozen and even forfeited on a civil standard while a criminal case is still unresolved.

Colombia created that system in the 1990s to strip assets from drug organisations. It has since been applied to corruption cases as well.

The burden in a forfeiture case sits on the origin of the asset. Owners must show the money behind a property was lawful.

More: Latin America news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did prosecutors seize?

Three properties: a Bogota apartment, a one-third share in another Bogota home, and a property in Pensilvania, Caldas, worth about 3,664 million pesos, roughly US$1.18 million.

Has Zuluaga been convicted?

No. He was charged in July 2023 with falsification of a private document, procedural fraud and illicit enrichment, and did not accept the charges.

What is the case about?

An alleged US$1.61 million payment from Odebrecht in mid-2014, routed through a Panama-registered entity to fund presidential campaign advertising and never declared.

Is the seizure the same as the criminal case?

No. It is a civil asset forfeiture action against the property itself, which runs on a separate track from the criminal proceedings.

Are his family members accused?

No. The properties were transferred to relatives in June 2023, but none of them has been charged.

Sources: El Tiempo, Vanguardia, Cambio, Pulzo, El Espectador, Infobae.

World.title: Costa Rica Whisky Fest Returns Today with Tastings, Jazz and a Bit of History
World.content:
Whisky may not be the first drink associated with Costa Rican culture, but a growing community of collectors, curious beginners and serious enthusiasts is giving the centuries-old spirit a distinctly local stage. Whisky Fest 2026 takes place today at Campo Lago in Lindora, bringing together more than 50 brands for an evening built around tasting, food, music and the stories behind what is in the glass.

The second edition is expected to attract as many as 1,500 people, more than double the 700-plus who attended the inaugural festival last year. The main festival is listed to begin at 7 p.m., although guided tastings start earlier in the afternoon. This year’s festival leans heavily into atmosphere. The event is designed around the American Prohibition era, with dark wooden stands, warm lighting and the feel of the speakeasies that operated secretly in the United States during the 1920s and early 1930s.

Ten whisky distributors and importers will have dedicated spaces, representing dozens of labels. Visitors can move between them at their own pace, sample whisky by the glass and purchase bottles directly from participating companies. But organizers are trying to make the experience about more than simply drinking whisky.

Five expert-led tastings are planned, including sessions aimed at people still learning the difference between styles and more detailed experiences for experienced drinkers. Food pairings are part of the tasting program, reflecting a broader shift toward treating whisky much like wine: something to smell, compare, discuss and understand rather than simply order at a bar.

That approach represents an interesting turn in Costa Rica’s own relationship with whisky. A University of Costa Rica study of alcohol consumption and leisure from 1900 to 1930 found clear social divisions in drinking patterns. Aguardiente and chicha were associated with the broader population, while whisky, champagne and wine were more commonly linked to Costa Rica’s wealthier classes.

More than a century later, whisky remains a premium product, but the culture around it has changed. Tastings, specialty retailers, collector groups and events such as Whisky Fest increasingly emphasize where a whisky comes from, how it is made, how barrels affect its flavor and why bottles from Scotland, Ireland, the United States, Japan and elsewhere can taste remarkably different.

The evening also includes contemporary jazz from Costa Rican singer Rayssa Jiménez and her band, followed by DJ Slechta. A dedicated food area will offer dishes intended to accompany the spirits. Organizers have also included a designated-driver program that provides food and nonalcoholic drinks to participants who agree not to drink alcohol and water will be available throughout the event.

Whisky Fest operates as a private promotional event rather than through traditional ticket sales. Adults 18 and older can purchase the event’s limited-edition commemorative glass online for ₡15,000 plus VAT. Possession of the glass includes complimentary admission, subject to capacity. Buyers receive a QR code and collect the glass at the event.

The festival is entirely cashless and for newbies, the organizers’ concept is deliberately informal: carry a glass, visit the different houses, ask questions and compare what is being poured. For experienced whisky drinkers, the attraction is the concentration of brands and distributors in one place.

Either way, the rapid expansion of Whisky Fest says something about how Costa Rica’s food and drink culture continues to evolve. A spirit once closely associated here with imported luxury is increasingly being approached as something to explore, study and share.

World.title: Buying Property in Costa Rica – What Foreign Buyers Need to Know
World.content:
Foreigners can own land in Costa Rica on the same terms as citizens, with one significant exception, and the country has spent two decades marketing that openness to North American and European buyers. What the marketing rarely covers is the machinery underneath the purchase: the registry checks that reveal a lien nobody disclosed, the tax that arrives every January on a house the owner never considered luxurious, and the water letter that decides whether a lot can be built on at all.

Two developments have changed the calculus for foreign buyers this year. The tax incentives attached to Law 9996, the statute that drew thousands of investors and retirees to Costa Rica after the pandemic, expired on July 14. And the colón has climbed to its strongest level against the dollar in the history of the Central Bank’s published series, which quietly raises the real cost of everything a dollar-holding buyer pays for locally.

What follows is the ground the purchase actually stands on.

Foreign ownership is unrestricted except at the water’s edge

A foreign national can buy titled property in Costa Rica with a valid passport. No residency, no visa, no local partner, no minimum purchase. The property registers in the buyer’s name at the Registro Nacional with full rights of use and disposal, which distinguishes Costa Rica from a number of countries that restrict foreign landholding outright.

The exception is the coast. Under the Maritime Terrestrial Zone Law, Law 6043, the first 200 meters (656 feet) inland from the ordinary high tide line belong to the state. The first 50 meters (164 feet) of that strip is public zone and cannot be occupied or built on by anyone. The remaining 150 meters (492 feet) is restricted zone, where the municipality grants concessions rather than title.

A concession is a lease from the state, not ownership. It carries a term, it carries renewal risk, and a foreign national cannot hold a majority interest in one without at least five years of legal residency in Costa Rica. The workaround many buyers are offered, holding the concession through a company with majority Costa Rican ownership, puts a substantial asset in someone else’s hands on paper.

Anyone shown a beachfront property should establish before anything else whether the seller holds title or a concession. The two words are often used interchangeably in listings. They are not interchangeable in law.

The registry tells the truth that the listing does not

Every property in Costa Rica carries a folio real number, and the Registro Nacional record attached to it is public. It shows the registered owner, the recorded boundaries, the fiscal value, and any annotation against the property: mortgages, liens, easements, litigation, embargoes.

Unpaid municipal taxes and outstanding obligations travel with the property rather than the seller. A buyer who closes without municipal tax certifications inherits the arrears.

The survey plan, or plano catastrado, is the second document to pull. Mismatches between the registered plan and the fences, driveways and structures actually on the ground are common, particularly on rural and subdivided parcels, and they surface as boundary disputes years later. A licensed surveyor walking the property against the plan is inexpensive relative to what it prevents.

Where a property is being sold through the transfer of a company’s shares rather than a transfer of title, the buyer acquires the company’s entire history along with the land, including any debt or litigation it carries. That structure lowers the transfer tax, which is why it is offered, and it is only safe after a corporate due diligence review that many buyers skip.

What closing actually costs

The property transfer tax, the impuesto de traspaso, is 1.5 percent, assessed on whichever is higher, the declared sale price or the registered fiscal value. Documentary stamps and Registro Nacional recording fees add roughly 0.5 to 0.8 percent. Only a notary public, who in Costa Rica is a lawyer with specific notarial authority, can draft and register a transfer. Notary fees follow a schedule set by the Colegio de Abogados and generally run 1 to 2 percent of the price, plus value added tax on the fee.

Total closing costs therefore land in a band of roughly 3.5 to 5 percent of the purchase price for a straightforward residential transaction, rising toward the upper end where financing or corporate structures are involved. Custom in the market is to split these costs between buyer and seller, but custom is not law and the split is negotiable.

Escrow through an agent registered with SUGEF, the financial regulator, typically costs a further 0.25 percent or a flat fee near $1,000. It is the single cheapest piece of protection in the transaction and should not be waived.

Buyers are sometimes encouraged to declare a sale price below what is actually paid, since the taxes key off the declared figure. The saving is small, the practice is tax fraud, and the understated value becomes the buyer’s cost basis when the property is later sold, converting a modest gain into a large taxable one.

The taxes that arrive every year afterward

Municipal property tax is 0.25 percent of the registered fiscal value annually, payable to the municipality where the property sits. Owners must file a property declaration every five years; where they do not, the municipality assigns a value on its own initiative.

The solidarity tax, widely known as the luxury home tax, is the one that surprises foreign owners. For 2026 it applies where the value of the construction and fixed installations reaches ¢143 million, a threshold set by Executive Decree 45358-H and published in La Gaceta on December 19, 2025. At the Central Bank reference sell rate of ¢450.06 on September 11, that is approximately $318,000 of construction value, before the land is counted at all.

Rates run progressively from 0.25 to 0.55 percent once the threshold is crossed, the declaration is filed every three years on form D-174, and payment falls due by January 15 each year. The tax reaches concession holders and occupants of the maritime zone as well as titled owners.

Rental income from Costa Rican property is taxed at 15 percent applied to 85 percent of gross receipts, which accounts for a presumed expense deduction requiring no receipts. Owners whose principal activity is renting may instead elect the general regime and deduct documented expenses.

Capital gains on a sale are taxed at 15 percent of the difference between the sale price and the adjusted acquisition cost. Property acquired before July 1, 2019 carries a one-time alternative of 2.25 percent of the gross sale price, available only on the first transaction after that date. A taxpayer’s habitual residence is exempt under the income tax law.

All of these obligations now run through TRIBU-CR, the tax administration platform that replaced ATV in October 2025. Owners holding property through a Costa Rican company also owe the annual corporate tax each January, and the Registro Nacional will not issue corporate standing certificates or record documents for a company that has not paid it, which can freeze a sale at the worst possible moment.

Water decides what can be built

Electricity and road access are negotiable problems. Water is not. Construction permits in Costa Rica require a water availability letter from the local ASADA or from AyA, the national water utility. Where the local system has no capacity, the letter is refused, and a lot that cannot obtain one is effectively unbuildable regardless of what the listing says about services.

Availability is genuinely constrained in parts of Guanacaste and along the Pacific coast, where development has run ahead of supply. A drilled well is not a substitute in most cases, since wells require concessions from the Dirección de Agua. The letter should be in hand, current and in the buyer’s favor before money moves, not promised as a formality to be handled after closing.

Personal name or corporation, and why the answer shifted

Holding Costa Rican property through a local company, an S.A. or an S.R.L., has been standard advice for years, offering liability separation, privacy, estate planning benefits and a cheaper exit by share transfer. The costs are the annual corporate tax, the accounting obligations and an annual beneficial ownership declaration to the transparency registry.

That calculation changes for anyone intending to use the purchase to support an investor residency application. Current immigration practice requires the qualifying property to be registered in the applicant’s personal name at the Registro Nacional rather than inside a company. Buyers who structure into a corporation first and consider residency afterward frequently find they have disqualified the asset and face a second transfer, with a second round of transfer tax, to fix it.

The order of operations matters more than the structure. Decide the residency question before the deed is drafted.

The residency question nobody has answered

Law 9996, the Law for the Attraction of Investors, Rentiers and Pensioners, was enacted in July 2021. It lowered the minimum qualifying investment for investor residency from $200,000 to $150,000 and attached a package of tax incentives, including duty-free import of household goods and up to two vehicles and a 20 percent reduction in the property transfer tax. Those incentives ran for five years and expired in July of this year.

What expired alongside them is contested. Most English-language guidance now states flatly that the investor threshold has reverted to $200,000. No Costa Rican authority has said so.

Ramón María Yglesias Piza, an attorney with the Costa Rica Bar Association, published an analysis in August arguing that the reversion does not follow from the text. His reading is that Article 12 of the law, the only provision setting an expiration term, refers exclusively to the tax benefits in Article 5 and never mentions the investment amount set in Article 8. The implementing regulations, he notes, reproduce the $150,000 figure as a condition of the investor subcategory without attaching any sunset to it, and reserve the expiry language for the tax benefits.

He argues further that the $200,000 figure originated in a regulation to the General Migration Law rather than in a statute, and that a statute outranks a regulation, so the lower amount set by Law 9996 should not silently revive the higher one. Where an administrative rule imposing a burden is incomplete, he writes, the doubt is resolved in favor of the applicant.

Yglesias is explicit that this is not settled. There is no case law, and the contrary reading, that the $200,000 base rule was merely suspended and has now returned, is defensible. His recommendation to anyone weighing capital against this question is to file a written inquiry with the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería and obtain a documented answer before committing funds.

Two points are not in dispute. The Article 5 tax exemptions are gone for applications filed after July 14. And eligibility under Law 9996 is determined by filing date rather than approval date, so applications submitted on or before that date retain the benefits even if approval comes later.

Financing is possible and rarely worth it

Costa Rican banks will lend to foreign buyers, generally only to legal residents, at loan-to-value ratios well below North American norms and at interest rates that make the arithmetic unattractive. Approval timelines run long.

Most foreign purchases here close in cash or on financing arranged in the buyer’s home country. Seller financing is common in the market and can work, but it belongs in a properly drafted and registered instrument rather than a handshake.

What a stronger colón does to the budget

The dollar closed at ¢447.93 on the Monex market yesterday, the lowest level since the Central Bank’s published series began in December 2007. The Central Bank reference sell rate today was ¢450.06.

Listings are quoted in dollars, so the headline price appears unaffected. Almost nothing else about ownership is. Property tax, the solidarity tax, municipal fees, notary fees, construction labor, materials, maintenance, security and condominium fees are all colón obligations, and a dollar covers roughly six percent less of them than it did in March.

For a buyer planning to build, that gap lands squarely on the construction budget, where it compounds over a project that may run eighteen months. Estimates prepared before this year should be repriced rather than trusted.

Before any money moves

The sequence that protects a buyer is unglamorous and rarely followed in full. Retain an attorney who represents the buyer alone and is not connected to the seller, the listing agent or the developer. Pull the Registro Nacional folio real and read the annotations. Match the survey plan against the physical property with a licensed surveyor. Obtain municipal tax certifications. Secure the water letter. Confirm whether the property is titled or held under concession. Place funds with a SUGEF-registered escrow agent. Decide the ownership structure only after deciding whether residency is part of the plan.

Costa Rica remains one of the more straightforward markets in the region for a foreign buyer, with genuine legal protection for registered owners and transaction costs well below those in the United States or most of Europe. The difficulties that arise here are almost never caused by the law itself. They are caused by buyers who moved money before they finished reading.

This article is general information, not legal or tax advice. Property, tax and immigration matters in Costa Rica turn on specific facts and should be reviewed with a licensed Costa Rican attorney and an accountant before any purchase.

World.title: Costa Rica Independence Day 2026 Brings a Tuesday Holiday and Rain
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Independence Day is Tuesday, September 15 so some holidays here get moved to the nearest Monday to make a long weekend, but this one does not. The Labor Ministry has confirmed it stays on the 15th. That means Monday the 14th is a regular workday, and the celebrations run across both evenings.

This year marks 205 years of independence so expect a torch relay over the weekend, lantern parades Monday night, school parades Tuesday and rain on and off the whole time. The Independence Torch crosses from Nicaragua at Peñas Blancas around 11 a.m. Sunday, according to the Ministry of Public Works and Transport. About 22,000 students will carry it roughly 378 kilometers (235 miles) to Cartago, the Ministry of Public Education says.

The relay passes through Liberia, Cañas, Esparza, Palmares, Naranjo, Alajuela and Heredia before reaching San José on Monday evening. The national anthem will be sung at 6 p.m. at Plaza de la Democracia. The flame is due at the ruins in Cartago around 8 p.m. You can track it live at antorcha.mep.go.cr.

If you drive in San José or Cartago on Monday evening, plan around the relay. From about 5 p.m., traffic police will stop cars on Paseo Colón and Avenida Segunda so the runners can cross. Police will do the same at the Fuente de la Hispanidad, the Montes de Oca church, Curridabat and La Galera, and they will control traffic around Cartago’s central park.

The runners are on foot, so each stop lasts only as long as it takes them to pass. At rush hour, though, even short stops back up quickly. Leave early or stay off those roads between 5 p.m. and 8 p.m. On Tuesday morning, expect closures near Parque Nacional and the Legislative Assembly. President Laura Fernández will attend the main civic ceremony there. Traffic police will also be working civic events across the country.

Monday night is the desfile de faroles or the lantern parade. Children carry handmade lanterns through town centers, and Cartago holds its traditional parade that evening. Most towns hold school parades with marching bands on Tuesday. Check with your municipality for start times.

Bring an umbrella to all of it sinceThe National Meteorological Institute (IMN) says tropical wave No. 42 reaches Costa Rica this afternoon, and wave No. 43 follows on Saturday. Both are moving through a humid, unstable atmosphere, and IMN expects that pattern to last through at least Wednesday, September 16.

On the Pacific side, most of the rain falls in the afternoon, with scattered downpours and thunderstorms in the South and Central Pacific. The Caribbean and the Northern Zone are more likely to get rain overnight and in the morning. In the Central Valley, IMN expects occasional showers that become more frequent early next week. That is right when the lantern parades and school parades take place.

Wind is part of the picture too and IMN recorded gusts of 30 to 50 km/h (19 to 31 mph) in mountain areas on Friday, and up to 75 km/h (47 mph) in the North Pacific. IMN also warned earlier this week about saturated soils. Ground soaked by weeks of rain gives way more easily, so landslides and falling branches become more likely after a heavy afternoon storm.

If you are driving to Guanacaste or Puntarenas, Route 1 at Cambronero, near San Ramón, is still closed. A truck damaged the temporary bridge there earlier this week, and MOPT says repairs could take up to two months. Take Route 27 instead. Cars and other smaller vehicles can also use Monte del Aguacate or the local road between Río Jesús and Piedra Blanca.

If someone works for you, the 15th is a paid day off. That includes a housekeeper, a nanny or a gardener. The Ministry of Labor and Social Security (MTSS) says no worker can be required to work that day, and no one can be penalized for refusing. What you owe depends on how you pay. If you pay monthly or every two weeks, the holiday is already built into the wage. You pay the usual amount even if the person takes the day off. If you pay weekly for work outside a commercial business, add one day’s wage for the holiday on top of the days worked.

If the worker agrees to work on the 15th, the day is paid double. In practice, that means one extra day’s wage on top of what you would normally pay. Any overtime that day is paid at triple the regular hourly rate. The rule has a simple purpose. The law treats Independence Day as a day everyone is entitled to take off without losing income and is why working it costs double.

Hotels, restaurants, bakeries, theaters and gas stations are among the businesses the law allows to open on the holiday. Many other shops and most government offices will be closed, so call ahead before you plan errands for Tuesday. The celebrations run from the torch’s arrival on Sunday through Tuesday’s parades. Leave extra time on the road, carry rain gear, and check the latest IMN and MOPT updates before you set out.

World.title: International News: Guatemala ends criminal proceedings against Indigenous authorities
World.content:
International News: Guatemala ends criminal proceedings against Indigenous authorities

By Zoila Palma: Amnesty International has welcomed a decision by Guatemala’s judiciary to close criminal proceedings against four Indigenous authorities who were charged following their participation in peaceful protests during the national strike in October 2023.

The case involved Luis Pacheco, Héctor Chaclán and Basilio Puac of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán, and Esteban Toc of the Indigenous Mayor’s Office of Sololá. They faced charges including unlawful association, terrorism, obstruction of justice, sedition and obstruction of criminal prosecution.

Amnesty International said the proceedings were unfounded and linked to their work defending human rights and the rule of law.

“This unfounded prosecution and all the human rights violations it led to should never have happened. Luis Pacheco and Héctor Chaclán should never have been imprisoned. This ruling is a first step towards ending the arbitrary actions against them,” said Astrid Valencia, Amnesty International’s Deputy Research Director for the Americas.

The organization named Pacheco and Chaclán prisoners of conscience in May 2026 after they spent more than 15 months in pretrial detention.

Amnesty International warned that the criminalization of Indigenous authorities for peacefully exercising their rights threatens Indigenous Peoples’ community organization and systems of representation.

The organization is calling on Guatemalan authorities to prevent further arbitrary prosecutions and ensure full reparation for Pacheco, Chaclán, Puac and Toc, their families and communities, including investigating and prosecuting those responsible for allegedly misusing the criminal justice system against them.

World.title: Panton blasts latest diesel price increase, asks “When is enough, enough?”
World.content:
Panton blasts latest diesel price increase, asks “When is enough, enough?”

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Leader of the Opposition Tracy Taegar Panton is criticizing the latest increase in the price of diesel, warning that Belizean families and businesses are being pushed to their limits by rising costs.

In a statement on Saturday morning, Panton said the price of diesel increased again at midnight and questioned what measures the Government intends to introduce to ease the burden.

“When is enough, enough?” Panton asked.

She described the situation as “unbearable,” “unconscionable” and “completely unacceptable.”

Panton argued that higher fuel and energy costs are affecting virtually every part of the economy, including agriculture, tourism, transportation, small businesses and consumers.

She also rejected what she expects will be the Government’s explanation that external inflationary pressures are responsible for higher prices.

According to Panton, Belize’s productive sector is struggling, tourism is flat and entrepreneurs are finding it increasingly difficult to sustain and grow their businesses.

She also highlighted the transportation sector, saying operators are struggling to meet their obligations and maintain reliable services even with exclusive licences.

Meanwhile, she said ordinary Belizeans continue to face a rising cost of living.

“We are still waiting to hear the practical solutions this Government will implement to cushion the impact of rising fuel and energy costs,” Panton said.

She warned that the burden on Belize’s working class and taxpayers is becoming increasingly difficult to bear and ended her statement by urging Belizeans to “stay awake.”

World.title: Deadly motorcycle crash claims life of Guinea Grass man
World.content:
Deadly motorcycle crash claims life of Guinea Grass man

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 25 year old motorcyclist lost his life following a traffic accident in Orange Walk Town on Thursday night.

Police say the accident occurred at around 9:40 p.m. near the intersection of Munioz Street and Otro Benque Road.

When officers arrived, they found a white Ford E350 van on Munioz Street and a man lying several feet away with serious injuries.

Initial investigations indicate that the van, driven by 61 year old Antonio Novelo, was travelling along Otro Benque Road toward Trial Farm Village and was making a left turn onto Munioz Street.

Police say 25 year old Lorenzo Antonio Castro of Guinea Grass Village was travelling behind the van on a motorcycle and allegedly attempted to overtake it as the van was turning.

The motorcycle collided with the driver’s side of the van, causing Castro to fall from the motorcycle.

Castro was transported to the Northern Regional Hospital, where he succumbed to his injuries while receiving medical treatment. He was pronounced dead at 10:25 p.m.

Police reported that the motorcycle had no licence plate and that no insurance or licence sticker was found during initial checks. Investigators also reported that the motorcycle was travelling without a light.

Both vehicles were impounded for inspection, while the van driver was detained pending further investigation.

Castro’s body remains at the Northern Regional Hospital morgue awaiting a post mortem examination.

Police investigations continue.

World.title: 13 year old cyclist injured in Orange Walk hit and run
World.content:
13 year old cyclist injured in Orange Walk hit and run

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in Orange Walk are investigating a hit and run traffic accident that left a 13 year old boy injured on Friday evening.

According to police information, the minor was riding a bicycle along San Jose Drive at around 6:45 p.m. when he was struck by a vehicle while passing 9 De Octubre Street.

The boy told police that he suddenly felt a hard impact to the right side of his body, causing him to fall onto the pavement and then into an empty lot.

He reportedly identified the vehicle as a gold Ford Ranger single cab pickup with a licence plate ending in 84.

Police say the driver did not stop and continued on.

The minor sustained injuries to the right side of his body, including his right elbow and ankle. A doctor later classified the injuries as harm.

His bicycle also sustained damage to the seat and both wheels, estimated at $350, while the screen of his Samsung A05 phone, valued at $250, was broken.

The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: Two women charged after confrontation with police in San Pedro
World.content:
Two women charged after confrontation with police in San Pedro

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Two women have been charged following a confrontation with police officers on Barrier Reef Drive in San Pedro Town on Thursday night.

According to police information, officers were conducting mobile patrol at around 10:00 p.m. when they stopped near Isla Ceviche to conduct a business check.

While the police vehicle was parked, officers reportedly heard a screeching sound and noticed that a bicycle being carried by another vehicle had made contact with the right rear view mirror of the police mobile.

Police approached the driver and requested his licence before informing him that he would be detained for traffic offences.

During the interaction, police allege that a woman standing nearby began recording the incident and directed insulting words in Spanish toward a female police corporal.

Police subsequently attempted to detain the woman for using insulting words.

According to investigators, a second woman then intervened, allegedly grabbing the first woman and preventing officers from escorting her to the San Pedro Police Station.

Police say the confrontation continued at the station, where the second woman allegedly pushed the corporal and grabbed the front of her uniform during a struggle.

On Friday, police formally arrested and charged 30 year old Aleida Michell Trujillo with aggravated assault and obstructing a police officer.

Antonia Bardales Carcamo, 48, was charged with using insulting words.

Both women reportedly chose to remain silent after being cautioned.

World.title: Woman calls police after ex partner threatens to kill her in San Pedro
World.content:
Woman calls police after ex partner threatens to kill her in San Pedro

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 41 year old man has been charged with threat of death after allegedly threatening to kill his former common law partner during an incident in San Pedro Town.

According to police information, the woman reported that she was at her home in the DFC area at around 9:00 p.m. on Thursday, September 10, when her former partner arrived.

She told police that the two have been separated for approximately one year and alleged that he has repeatedly visited her home and caused problems.

The woman said the man appeared to have been drinking and attempted to enter her house, but she prevented him from doing so.

According to her report, an argument followed and the man allegedly threatened her multiple times in Spanish, saying, “Te voy a matar,” which translates to “I will kill you.”

The woman told police she feared for her life and the safety of her daughters and called for assistance.

Police responded to the area and later detained the man.

On Friday, September 11, police formally arrested and charged Wilson Garcia, 41, with threat of death.

Garcia was cautioned and reportedly chose to remain silent.

World.title: Napoles FC to honor Jaheed Lopez in special tribute at tonight’s game
World.content:
Napoles FC to honor Jaheed Lopez in special tribute at tonight’s game

By Zoila Palma: Napoles FC will honor the memory of former player Jaheed Lopez during its First Division match against San Pedro Pirates tonight at the FFB Stadium in Belmopan.

Lopez, a proud son of Punta Gorda, wore the number 22 jersey during his time with Napoles FC. The club said the match will be about more than football as players, fans, and members of the football community come together to remember the young athlete, whose life was tragically cut short this week.

Before kickoff, a moment of silence will be observed in Lopez’s memory.

Then, during the 22nd minute, the club is asking everyone inside the stadium to rise for a full minute of applause in celebration of his life, his time with the club, and the memories he leaves behind.

All First Division teams have been invited to attend free of charge as the football community stands in solidarity with Lopez’s family and loved ones.

The match kicks off at 7:30 p.m., with general admission set at BZ$10.

Napoles FC said, “Football brings us together in competition, but moments like these remind us that we are one football family.” Rest in peace, Jaheed. Once Napoles, always Napoles.

World.title: Jaheed Lopez remembered as rising Football talent after tragic accident
World.content:
Jaheed Lopez remembered as rising Football talent after tragic accident

By Zoila Palma: The Punta Gorda community, the University of Belize (UB) student community and the football community across Belize are mourning the death of 21-year-old Jaheed Lopez, a promising footballer whose life was cut short in a tragic traffic accident on Wednesday.

Lopez was reportedly returning from farm work in Armenia Village when he stopped along the roadside to help remove a fallen tree.

At around 4:30 p.m., an 18-wheeler truck carrying sand and gravel was reportedly overtaking when it became unstable and overturned, crushing Lopez underneath.

His death has sent shockwaves through Belize’s football community, particularly as he had recently received a sports scholarship from UB that would have provided him with a full ride through school.

UB Athletic Coach Joseph Waight recalled Lopez as a player who brought excitement and unity to the team. “He actually scored in one of our matches, and in the ATLIB tournament, that gave us the opportunity to play for a final match the following day,” Waight said. “Jaheed will definitely be missed on our team because, you know, he brings that excitement to the game. He brings his personal skills onto the field and, like I said, that unity he bonds within the group.”

Wingz Police FC, where Lopez was affectionately known as “Jude Bellingham,” also paid tribute to the young footballer. The club said, “Jaheed was more than just a footballer. He was more than just a teammate. He was family,” describing him as a dedicated, humble and committed player who remained loyal to the club through its journey from the Second Division back to the First Division.

Verdes FC also remembered Lopez as “a true VERDES FOR LIFE,” describing him as “a noble and exemplary young man.”

Coach Waight said Lopez’s legacy extends beyond football, adding that the young athlete’s message was to “continue to work for what we wanted,” because he always strove to become better. “That was his message to everybody: to continue to be different and get better at what you do in order to attain your goals that you have set in life,” Waight said.

World.title: Shabba Ranks files lawsuit against publishing arm of Greensleeves Records
World.content:
Shabba Ranks

Iconic dancehall trailblazer and deejay, Shabba Ranks, has filed a lawsuit against the publishing arm of Greensleeves Records, in a move to reclaim the rights to several of his crossover hits as well as the 1990 song Dem Bow.

According to a report in Billboard magazine, Shabba Ranks (born Rexton Gordon) filed the suit on Friday (Sept. 11), and it aims to reclaim compositions including the Billboard Hot 100 hits Slow and Sexy, Housecall, Mr Loverman and Let’s Get It On.

Shabba Ranks’ catalogue also includes the 1990 song Dem Bow, the namesake for reggaetón’s iconic dembow rhythm that is currently at the centre of a long-running copyright infringement lawsuit entangling the entire genre.

Friday’s lawsuit, meanwhile, centres on copyright termination — the provision of United States (US) copyright law that enables authors to claw back their intellectual property decades after signing it away.

Shabba Ranks first notified Greensleeves in 2023 that he wanted to exercise his termination right, but the publisher said no. According to Greensleeves, his 1989 publishing deal stipulated that his compositions were “works made for hire,” which are explicitly excluded from the copyright termination statute.

Shabba, however, is contesting the validity of that work-for-hire provision, and he wants a judge to declare that his copyright termination is effective regardless.

“The compositions are not and could not have been works made for hire under the US Copyright Act, regardless of the language of the assignment,” wrote Shabba Ranks’ attorneys at Reitler Kailas & Rosenblatt.

“Gordon was never at any time an employee of [Greensleeves], and musical compositions are not recognised in the US Copyright Act as a type of work that can be deemed a work made for hire simply by agreement between the hiring party and a non-employee author.”

Copyright termination is a hot topic in music law in the United States at present.

Pioneering rap outfit Salt-N-Pepa is battling Universal Music Group (UMG) over the provision in a case that has caught the industry’s attention.

Meanwhile, all three major labels are currently trying to get the Supreme Court to reverse a controversial recent ruling that extended the termination right overseas.

Shabba Ranks, raised in Seaview Gardens, rode high in the late 1980s into the mid-1990s with a steady streak of hit songs. He signed with Epic Records and scored back-to-back wins at the Grammy Awards when As Raw As Ever and X-tra Naked won the Best Reggae Album awards in 1992 and 1993, respectively.

Both albums have been certified gold by the Recording Industry Association of America.

World.title: Seville beaten in Ultimate 100m final
World.content:
US' Kenneth Bednarek (2R) wins ahead of US' Ronnie Baker (L), Botswana's Letsile Tebogo (2L) and Jamaica's Oblique Seville in the men's 100m final during the World Athletics Ultimate Championship at the Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre, in Budapest on September 12, 2026. (Photo by Jewel SAMAD / AFP)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Oblique Seville just failed to add the World Athletics Ultimate Championships title to his World Championships and Diamond League titles after placing second in the men’s 100m final on Saturday’s second day at the National Athletics Center in Budapest, Hungary.

American Kenny Bednarek spoiled the party after he ran a season’s best 9.85 seconds (-0.6m/s) to beat the Jamaican who repeated the 9.90 seconds he ran to lead the semi-finals.

Another American Ronnie Baker was third in 9.93 seconds.

Jonielle Smith was fourth in the women’s 100m with 10.94 seconds (-0.2m/s), the same time awarded to her compatriot Tina Clayton while Lavanya Williams was seventh in 11.07 seconds.

American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden ran a world-leading 10.62 seconds to win the trophy, just beating Julien Alfred of St Lucia- 10.74 seconds with Sha’Carrie Richardson of the USA third in 10.76 seconds.

National record holder Nickisha Pryce was third in the women’s 400m final, running 49.56 seconds as favourite Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic won with 49.07 seconds, coming from fourth place over the last 120 metres to take the trophy.

Norway’s Henriette Jaeger was second in 49.28m.

In the other final that included a Jamaican, Diamond League winner Tajay Gayle was fifth in the men’s long jump with a best of 7.90m (-0.1m/s), getting only three jumps as only the top four advanced to the fourth and final round.

Gayle improved with each jump, starting with 7.52m (1.0n/s); he then had a 7.72m (-0.2m/s) jump in the second round.

Meanwhile, Commonwealth Games champion Sanique Walker who ran a big personal best of 53.77 seconds and Rushell Clayton, advanced to Sunday’s final of the women’s 400m hurdles.

Walker lowered her personal best from 54.00 seconds that she set while winning at the Commonwealth Games to place third in her semi-final, running from lane nine, behind Americans Jasmine Jones who ran a season’s best 52.77 seconds and Anna Cockrell, 53.31 seconds.

Clayton was fourth in her semi-final with 53.84 seconds after she came off the seventh hurdle in seventh place.

Emma Zapletalova of Slovakia won with 52.93 seconds, followed by Panama’s Gianna Woodruff- 53.73 seconds and Belgium’s national record holder Paulien Couckuyt- 53.81 seconds.

Commonwealth Games gold medalist Navasky Anderson just missed advancing to the men’s 800m final, finishing fifth in the first semi-final in 1:44.83, just behind Kenya’s Emmanuel Wanyoni who got fourth place in 1:44.43 and a place in the final.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Build better, faster
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (right) engages in a lively discussion with Donald Mullings (left), chairman, M&M Jamaica Limited; Martin Miller (second left), managing director, National Housing Trust (NHT); and NHT Chairman Linval Freeman during Friday’s ground breaking for the construction of 700 houses at Greater Bernard Lodge in St Catherine. The houses are being built will under a partnership agreement with the NHT, the Housing Agency of Jamaica, and M&M Jamaica Ltd. Photo: Garfield Robinson

BREAKING ground Friday for the construction of 700 new homes at Greater Bernard Lodge in St Catherine, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness challenged local contractors to embrace technology and invest in equipment that can accelerate the pace of delivery.

“The building technologies that we are using today are outdated and expensive. We need more of our private contractors and our private developers to start using modern technology. It’s not just to build the houses more cost-effectively, but we have to move away from building the matches boxes, the heat boxes, to building things that look modern, aesthetically pleasing and sustainable. That is my challenge today to our developers,” Holness said, adding that he expects that within the next 18 months he will be back at the location to present keys to the owners of the new units.

“The role of Government is to use legislation, and fiscal incentives, and moral suasion to guide and sometimes direct the private developers into the underserved areas of the market. But we are seeing an influx of overseas private contractors who have solved the problem of being able to build quickly and deliver quickly at a reasonable price because they have integrated significant technology and equipment into their operations,” Holness said.

“Almost every day we are getting proposals. The only thing they want from us would be land. But I am thinking that I want my local contractors to do this. I want my local contractors to develop the capability to deliver these houses quickly. I can’t just give away everything to overseas and foreign investors. I want my local contractors to benefit, but at the same time I want the people to get houses,” the prime minister said.

The units — 280 one-bedroom and 420 two-bedroom houses — will be built under a partnership agreement with the National Housing Trust (NHT), the Housing Agency of Jamaica (HAJ), and M&M Jamaica Limited, across two parcels of land.

They will form the D2 and D3 phases of the Greater Bernard Lodge housing development programme and will include paved roads, storm water drains, perimeter walls, street signs, and other essential amenities.

The $11.62-billion project will expand the supply of housing available to NHT contributors.

Arguing that the practise of squatting will persist if enough isn’t done to provide shelter for the many Jamaicans who have no home for themselves, Holness reiterated that his Administration remains committed to its election promise of building 70,000 houses.

“So, the 70,000 is very ambitious. I’m hanging my hat where I will have to stretch to reach it,” he said.

“We have been stretching. The NHT was tasked to build 42,000 of that, and my last check showed that they have seen their way in terms of what they have already constructed — what is in contracts, what is in procurement, and what is in planning. They are over 40,000, so they have seen the slate of what they should construct. The chairman told you that since the start of the year we have broken ground for 2,000. We are now at over 8,000 houses under construction or out of construction,” the prime minister said.

Lynvale Freeman, the NHT chairman, said that Friday’s ground-breaking represented not just the turning of soil but the expansion of homeownership in Jamaica. He said it was important to do it in St Catherine because of its close proximity to Kingston, among other important factors.

“The common goal is to build as many houses at the lowest price point,” Freeman said.

World.title: ‘EDUCATION EMERGENCY’
World.content:
La Sonja Harrison, president of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association, speaking at a meeting of the Rotary Club of Kingston at Jamaica Pegasus hotel on Thursday. Garfield Robinson

DECLARING that Jamaica is facing an “education emergency”, president of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association (JTA) La Sonja Harrison is urging the Government to implement a five-year national learning recovery and acceleration plan to tackle the existing gaps in the sector.

But Harrison is adamant that the five-year initiative must put educators at the forefront of the conversation.

“If it is as educators, we are the first responders, we are the people on the ground, I am saying that there can be no conversation about how we go nationally without the teachers in a meaningful way. And I’m not talking about us, leaders of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association, I’m talking about the people who are on the ground, the foot soldiers, and the people on whom you will depend [on] anyway to carry out whatever vision you have for education.

“Those persons need to be invited at the table from the beginning of the conversation, not at the tail end,” Harrison told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday following a meeting of the Rotary club of Kingston at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel.

“We have TREND [Transforming Education for National Development], and we have ETOC [Education Transformation Oversight Committee], because they continue to update the nation quarterly concerning same. So ETOC will have some educators represented there, but is it reflective of the system, the people who work in the trenches of the system, and are they at the table for the conversation and posit the solutions that they would see ideal and realistic, in transforming the education system?”Harrison questioned.

In her presentation Harrison highlighted several disruptions faced by the education sector and argued that the urgency displayed by the Government in rebuilding structures and restoring operations has not been given to recovering learning.

“COVID-19 interrupted the education system of an entire generation. Then came Hurricane Beryl [July 2024], Hurricane Melissa [October 2025]. In between, there have been floods…fires, infrastructural failures, and teacher shortages, and that is just since 2019, we have not even gone back decades,”

“We have spent considerable time recovering buildings, and those recovery of buildings have certainly not been to the standard that we are desirous of, and the pace, the alacrity. Because for us to be able to report as a nation that 40 of some 600 plus schools have been rebuilt, that’s 6.67 per cent of our schools that have been retrofitted to provide an atmosphere for safe, comfortable learning of our children,” Harrison frowned.

Pointing to the Government’s emergencies in education plan, including the modification of objectives from the National Standards Curriculum, (NSC) post-Hurricane Melissa, Harrison charged that establishing such a plan after a disaster is ineffective.

“We need to identify those who have fallen behind. We need targeted initiatives. We need additional instructional support where necessary. We need stronger literacy and numeracy initiative benchmarks to support. We need trained teachers and interventionists at varying levels of the system. And we need to measure whether children are actually catching up. Attendance is not recovery. Promotion is not recovery. Completing a grade is not recovery. Learning is recovery. Teachers cannot be expected to recover six years of educational disruption with the same resources, same staffing, and in some cases under staffing, and after these weather challenges and with worsening infrastructure,” said Harrison.

“The Government is going to tell you that we have the emergency in education stuff, but it has to be proactive in nature. It can’t be that it is when the event happens, then we come up with something that will help to take us through another event. So we have to sit down and look and say how are we going to, one, ensure learning, how are we going to engage teachers, how are we going to engage parents.

“Jamaica needs a national foundational learning emergency plan. I deliberately use that language. Not another programme project to treat with the illiteracy problem. Not another intervention to treat with learning gap, as this is just not another education challenge. It is an emergency. Because when children are progressing through our schools without mastering reading, comprehension, writing, and numeracy, we’re not simply dealing with an academic problem. We’re compromising Jamaica’s future,” Harrison charged.

World.title: Garbage truck obstacle
World.content:
Falmouth Mayor C Junior Gager addressing Thursday’s regular monthly meeting of the Trelawny Municipal Corporation.

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — A derelict garbage truck is standing in the way of plans by the Trelawny Municipal Corporation (TMC) to establish temporary headquarters, prompting Falmouth Mayor C Junior Gager to give the vehicle’s owner an ultimatum to remove it or face having it towed.

Gager, who is also chairman of the TMC, told Thursday’s regular monthly meeting of the corporation that the truck is occupying the spot earmarked for two newly acquired containers, which are to be converted into offices and a meeting room.

He said repeated attempts to locate the owner have failed, despite the corporation obtaining contact information for a person believed to be associated with the vehicle.

“We have a garbage truck that is parked on the premises of the Trelawny Municipal Corporation for some time now. We have tried all that we can. It seems to be maybe a private contractor. We have tried to reach him. We cannot reach him,” Gager said.

With the project considered urgent, Gager said the TMC would not allow the abandoned vehicle to delay the work.

“If the truck isn’t removed within maybe another day or two, we’ll be taking it out and we’ll be placing it in an open land,” he warned.

The ultimatum comes as the TMC continues to operate from makeshift facilities following severe damage inflicted by Hurricane Melissa to its previous location at the historic Falmouth Courthouse last October.

The local authority is currently operating from containerised units on the grounds of its Roads and Works premises, while other functions have been squeezed into the Roads and Works building. Its monthly meetings are being held at the Port Authority of Jamaica’s conference room at the Falmouth Port.

Gager said the two recently purchased containers are to be retrofitted to provide badly needed office and meeting space, with the work expected to be completed within about a month.

“I would be happy if next month we can move in and have our council meeting there, because you see this room is getting so small, and we want a little more space,” Gager said.

He disclosed that a portion of the funding needed is already available and that technical officers, including the acting chief engineering officer, are being mobilised to expedite the work.

“We have some funding, and we are working with it. But we are going to make sure that next month, when you come back here it is nearly finished, or it is finished, or maybe in another two weeks,” Gager told his fellow councillors.

He described the facility as a temporary but potentially long-term investment, saying it could be used for other purposes even after the corporation establishes permanent headquarters.

The mayor also disclosed plans for an official opening of the facility once the work is completed, with Local Government Minister Desmond McKenzie expected to be among those invited.

World.title: Sher Luxury Doll takes a ‘Victory Lap’ into music production
World.content:
SHER... I want to leave a legacy, so when my family looks back at my journey dem si seh I was a trying person.

NOBODY saw Sher Luxury Doll’s latest move coming. But, according to the dancer-turned-entrepreneur and now music producer, that was precisely the point.

After building a name in dancehall as a dancer and choreographer before expanding her reach through the locally popular Luxury Beauty brand, Sher has stepped confidently into another arena with Victory Lap, her debut project as a producer.

For Sher, the unexpected transition is less about abandoning one identity for another and more about refusing to limit what she can become.

“Nobody saw this coming, but that’s me. I like surprising people,” she said. “From hairdresser, to dancer, to entrepreneur, to producer — I always want to grow and challenge myself. Trying new things keeps my brain active, and from me small I don’t like to do one thing.”

That desire to continually evolve has become one of the defining threads of her journey. While each career move has seemingly carried her into unfamiliar territory, Sher said she is motivated by the legacy she hopes to leave behind.

“I want to leave a legacy, so when my family looks back at my journey dem si seh I was a trying person,” she shared. “I like to master things and prove to myself that I can and push myself beyond the measures and limits people put on me.”

Interestingly, her venture into production began with a casual conversation and an idea she initially expressed in jest. While speaking with a close associate about the need for more female-centred songs in dancehall, Sher jokingly declared that she would take matters into her own hands. Her colleague, however, immediately took her seriously.

“I was on the phone with someone I work with closely, and we were just having a regular conversation saying we miss the girl songs in dancehall and we need more,” she recalled. “I was saying I was going to make it happen, but I was saying it as a joke. Instantly, him seh him have some riddims and him ago send me dem.”

Once she received the riddims the joke quickly became a mission. Sher began contacting artistes, coordinating recordings and quietly laying the groundwork for what would eventually become Victory Lap.

“When him send me dem, me link the artistes dem, and dem did very open to the idea. When me get half of the songs on the current playlist him see seh a serious thing,” she said, noting that work on the project began around February or March. “I was doing a lot of work behind the scenes.”

Victory Lap currently features eight tracks, with contributions from AI Milly, Jahvillani, Chronic Law, Felony 19, Rytikal, Ding Dong, Renee 6:30 and Deno Crazy. Sher said several other artistes have also expressed an interest in joining the project. Despite being a newcomer to production, she encountered little resistance when approaching established entertainers. She believes the reputation she has built for taking her work seriously helped the artistes trust her vision.

World.title: Melissa puts PE on pause in some western Jamaica schools
World.content:
Carisbrook Primary and Infant School Principal Patrick Malcolm leads the Jamaica Observer on a tour of the compound on Monday. Naphtali Junior

As temporary classrooms take over playing areas of some schools in St Elizabeth, principal of Carisbrook Primary and Infant School Patrick Malcolm is warning that physical education (PE) is becoming an unfortunate casualty of the push to get damaged schools functioning again.

According to Malcolm, this reflects a wider tendency to treat PE and sport as less important than academic subjects, despite their role in developing healthy, well-rounded children.

The concern is particularly acute at Maggotty High School, where temporary classrooms have left the school without enough space to conduct practical PE sessions, and properly facilitate its netball and football programmes.

Maggotty High’s Principal Sean Graham said the school has been forced to make a significant adjustment, with practical PE sessions put on hold for the current term while administrators work around the loss of playing space.

“The PE teacher expressed concern in terms of how she will facilitate training… because the school does not have a big enough play field. We also facilitate some level of football training here as well, especially for the junior team. So, those are going to be compromised, and we are going to have to find other ways to work it out,” Graham told the

Jamaica Observer on Monday.

He said the school understands the urgency of getting students back into suitable classrooms, but stressed that the temporary arrangement cannot be allowed to become prolonged.

“But we have to figure it out. Because the most important thing is to have the students here. All PE sessions for this term have to be theory-based. So, that is why I really still have to insist that by December, temporary classrooms have to be gone, because we don’t have the space to facilitate physical education, practical, plus the netball training and so on,” added Graham.

The situation is not confined to the high-school level.

At Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School, temporary classrooms are also being constructed on the school’s netball court, forcing administrators to look elsewhere for space for physical activity.

Principal Pauvine Watson-Barrett, who also spoke with the Observer on Monday, said the school intends to use its grassy areas rather than abandon PE altogether, although the loss of the hard surface presents its own challenges.

But Malcolm is adamant that the issue goes beyond finding alternative spaces.

He believes the temporary loss of playing areas exposes a long-standing failure to give physical education the same consideration afforded to subjects such as mathematics and English.

Malcolm, who is also president of the St Elizabeth Football Association, pointed to Carisbrook’s own experience as evidence of the determination required to keep sport alive despite inadequate facilities.

The school has 137 students, including 30 infants, and has built a strong sporting programme despite limited resources.

Malcolm said the school has trophies, medals and plaques reflecting its achievements, while its football field — which he said is the only one in the area capable of accommodating a 200-metre track — is also shared with the wider community.

He charged that the school’s sporting success has often come despite, rather than because of, the resources available to it.

“This is the myopicness of the people around. We all want to be bright, maths and English people, but we don’t want to be fit and strong. So we’re going to be doctors, but sick doctors. We’re going to be teachers, but sick teachers. Sports is such that the impact of it can be felt everywhere in this country,” he said.

Malcolm questioned the decision to place temporary classrooms on playing areas when alternative spaces may be available, particularly at Middle Quarters.

“When you put a temporary classroom on the court, what are you suggesting to those who are interested in PE? That they’ll sit down and do nothing for the next two months, three months?…and it’s just sad because there is more space that they could use,” he said.

He argued that the recovery effort should not treat sport as an optional extra, particularly at a time when children are already coping with disruption caused by Hurricane Melissa and the rebuilding of their schools.

“Somebody has to get up and start to show a little bit more appreciation for sports and physical education in this country. We cannot do without it. It is the stress buster. It is where we go for a break, and if the students are not encouraged to do this, then we are in trouble,” Malcolm added.

He also linked the decline in physical activity to broader concerns about the health of Jamaican society, arguing that schools have a critical role to play in encouraging children to remain active.

“Later on, we’re going to have a sick society… Look at the size of some of the teachers we have around. Look at the size of the society. I mean, probably two-thirds of the society is overweight. We better fix that, and the only way we can fix that is with physical education,” argued Malcolm.

World.title: PFJL boss confident of securing premier league title sponsorship deal
World.content:
Professional Football Jamaica Limited CEO Owen Hill (right) talks to television host Garfield Jones during the media launch of the Jamaica Premier League at TVJ’s Lyndhurst Road base on Thursday.Photo: Karl Mclarty

OWEN Hill, chief executive officer of the Professional Football Jamaica Limited (PFJL), remains confident that a deal will soon be struck to confirm the title sponsor of the Jamaica Premier League (JPL) which kicks off on Sunday.

At the press launch on Thursday at the offices of

TVJ, Hill confirmed that long-time headline sponsor Wray & Nephew and JPL have ended their contractual agreement.

Although Hill stopped short of naming the prospective sponsor, the Wisynco Group is understood to be involved through its Legend Beer brand. Wisynco recently posted on

Instagram that it was “powering a new chapter for Jamaica Premier League”, while also referencing a J$300-million commitment over five years to Jamaican football.

“It’s unfortunate that we don’t have a title sponsor on the dotted line and we’re very close,” he said.

“The league kicks off on Sunday,” Hill said, noting that four matches are scheduled for the opening day, with another two set for Monday.

Hill explained that PFJL has a contractual obligation to begin the season within a specific window, making it necessary for the league to move forward while the sponsorship negotiations continue.

He was quick to point out that negotiations have been taking place at the boardroom level on a daily basis as both sides work through the final details of what could become a significant long-term partnership.

“We’ve been in the boardroom every single day. We’re hammering all those fine points within a five-year conversation,” he said.

While the agreement had not been signed at the time of his comments, Hill insisted that the league is close to securing a major commercial partnership.

“I’m positive that it’s going to be a bigger, better league as we go forward,” he said.

According to Hill, the plan is not only to secure a new presenting partner but also to attract additional supporting partners, with the ultimate aim of creating greater financial stability for the league and its 14 clubs.

“We will be having a new presenting partner and some supporting lead partners,” he noted.

Hill stressed that PFJL is seeking more than a short-term sponsorship arrangement, saying the objective is to build a sustainable football economy in Jamaica.

“We’re building a football economy and that requires strategy and it also requires some assurance from our commercial partners,” he explained.

“The league’s 14 clubs must be developed as economic engines capable of creating value for their communities, players, sponsors and international football markets,” Hill added.

A major part of that vision is positioning the JPL as a pathway for Jamaican players to secure opportunities in professional leagues overseas.

“We are a source market for football. People come here and we need to get them out into more professional leagues,” Hill said.

For that to happen, he said improvements are needed in areas such as infrastructure, marketing, player nutrition, support services and the overall professionalism of the domestic game.

Hill also highlighted the importance of television exposure, noting that PFJL has deliberately built the JPL around broadcast visibility and improved production.

“We’ve built the product specifically around exposure and television and broadcast,” he said.

The league is also expected to benefit from improvements to playing surfaces and expanded television and production coverage as PFJL continues to develop the competition.

“Those investments can have a wider impact on Jamaican football, including strengthening the national team and helping the country work towards its long-term ambition of qualifying for the 2030 FIFA World Cup,” said Hill.

“Definitely, we are ready,” he said. “The teams are ready. The players are excited. I think all the pieces are coming together.”

For PFJL, the success of the upcoming season will therefore extend beyond the league’s commercial performance. Hill said progress will also be measured by the number of players advancing into national-team programmes and professional leagues overseas.

With the JPL set to begin as scheduled, PFJL will continue its final negotiations in the hope of securing the anticipated long-term partnership and taking another step towards establishing a stronger and more sustainable football economy in Jamaica.

On Sunday, champions Portmore United were expected to kick start the defense of their title against Waterhouse FC but that game has been postponed.

However, there will be four games on as Dunbeholden FC host Cavalier FC; promoted Humble Lion FC travel to Tivoli Gardens FC, Mount Pleasant FA face debutants Tru-Juice FC at Bramwell Clarke Sports Complex and Montego Bay United tackle Chapelton Maroons FC at Jarrett Park. All games are to begin at 3:30 pm.

On Monday, there will be a double-header at Stadium East as Molynes United take on Treasure Beach FC at 5:30 pm before Racing United face Arnett Gardens at 8:00 pm.

World.title: Will Lagarde bite the apple? ECB President leaves everyone guessing in Normandy
World.content:
On stage, she even encouraged reporters who made the trip to Normandy to cover her potential political comeback to pack up early, promising that they would be disappointed.

But there are signs suggesting that the ECB chief, who entered into politics during the presidency of France's apple-loving Jacques Chirac, is increasingly willing to weigh in on the campaign.

While she promised to stay at least until the end of the year, Lagarde previously refused to rule out leaving before the end of her term, which ends in October 2027.

Earlier this week, she announced that she would publish her first autobiography, Lady First, in January. She also waded into the French presidential debate by rejecting French far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s proposal to wipe out government debt.

Her presence at the apple festival in the 15th-century Manoir de la Fortière — an unconventional locale for a central banker's speech — might be yet another signal. Opening the event, Morin said that he tried to invite her for years but never managed to make it work. Until this year.

Christine Lagarde at the Fête de la Pomme, France, on September 12, 202. | Giorgio Leali/POLITICO

“Everyone is happy to have you here and I realized to what extent you have an exceptional reputation,” said Morin, who worked with Lagarde when they both served as ministers under conservative president Nicolas Sarkozy, including during the 2008 financial crisis.

World.title: Trump says he would ‘love’ to see a united Ireland
World.content:
Donald Trump and Taoiseach Micheál Martin listen to a question from the media at Farmleigh House in Phoenix Park in the Irish capital Dublin on September 12, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images

“It’s going to happen eventually,” the U.S. president said in Dublin during a golf-focused trip to the long-divided island.

DUBLIN — U.S. President Donald Trump waded into another age-old conflict Saturday, declaring on a golf-focused visit to Ireland that he’d like to see the island unified — the nightmare scenario for Northern Ireland’s British unionists.

Sitting beside Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin after an overnight flight from Washington, Trump said he couldn’t understand why Northern Ireland — the part of the island that remained in the U.K. when the rest of Ireland won independence over a century ago — hadn’t already joined the Republic of Ireland.

“I’d love to see it unified. I think it’d be great. A great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually,” Trump said, gesturing to Martin, who has spent years trying behind the scenes to build better relations with unionists, to little avail. “You’ve got the right man over here to get it moving. But I think it would be a fantastic thing. Now the U.K. will have something to say about it obviously. But I think it’d be a great thing. How can it be bad?”

World.title: Farage’s Reform UK gets two £36M donations from crypto billionaires
World.content:
Delo argued in an opinion piece for The Telegraph that Reform needed the injection to make the election “a fair fight.” Delo, who was already one of Reform’s largest donors, said he wanted to give Reform “a level playing field” at the next general election.

The paper on Saturday also published an opinion piece from Harborne, where he called his donation “a philantropic gift to our country.”

Farage thanked the two men for their contributions. “Both men know that we are the only party that can turn the country around,” he said in a statement.

Reform UK was leading the polls since April 2025 , according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls. But the party has now slumped slightly behind Labour, with new Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the helm and after a bizarre by-election where Farage defeated satirical candidate Count Binface.

The right-wing force is currently rushing to get battle-ready amid speculation Burnham could trigger an early general election, though one is not due until 2029. Reform UK is on the hunt for potential candidates to run as MP, and has only about 100 star candidates considered ready to run at the moment.

World.title: Portugal wants EU cash to pay for firefighting goats
World.content:
José Manuel Fernandes Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries of Portugal at the European Council in Brussels in Belgium on 9 December 2024. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

As budget negotiations intensify, capitals are reaching for a new argument to keep money in the farming pot: climate change.

Portugal’s minister for agriculture has a burning desire for the next EU long-term budget: more goats.

José Manuel Fernandes wants Brussels to help pay shepherds to let goats, cows and sheep graze on shrubs in areas at high risk of wildfires — a low-tech approach that experts say the EU has been ignoring for too long. Portugal and some regions in Spain are already running their own programs.

“We are using our national money, but it is work that we are doing for all the European Union,” Fernandes told POLITICO at an informal meeting of ministers in Dublin, arguing that preventing fires helps lower carbon emissions.

World.title: EU delays key tobacco tax vote until after Swedish election
World.content:
The European Commission proposed increasing levies on cigarettes and setting minimum rates on newer products like vapes, heat-not-burn tobacco and nicotine pouches in July last year.

The plan has become a flashpoint for Sweden, which has a long tradition of using snus — a pouch of tobacco that sits between the gums. As such, Stockholm has strongly opposed raising taxes on similar nicotine pouches.

Delaying the vote gives extra time for Sweden to appoint a new finance minister and for the capitals to negotiate a way out of the current stalemate.

The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the talks, confirmed the vote has been pushed from October to November's ministerial meeting.

Four diplomats granted anonymity to speak candidly about the sensitive negotiations said the postponement is meant to give Sweden's next government extra time to change its mind.

A spokesperson for the Irish presidency said they will "continue[s] to engage bilaterally with the aim of securing unanimous political agreement at the November ECOFIN" meeting of finance ministers.

World.title: Escaping the AI safety nightmare: What can governments do?
World.content:
A case in point is that OpenAI agents hacked a German website back in May to use it as a messaging board, Reuters reported last week. OpenAI had not publicly announced the incident and responded to the Reuters reporting on X saying: “We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment.”

“[Reporting] timelines are going to need to be dramatically shortened [for incidents], and so we need much better continuous monitoring capabilities,” said Imogen Stead, AI policy manager at London-based think tank the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, adding that the data will be needed in real time “and that will be true for governments and for labs.”

Speaking at a London event for U.K. lawmakers arranged by campaign group ControlAI on Monday, computer scientist Stuart Russell said that the most concerning aspect of the Hugging Face incident for him was that “by running a thousand agents communicating with each other, they were able to generate behaviors that no one agent could do by itself,” referring to investigations showing the incident was far more severe than OpenAI first acknowledged.

“But [in] the evaluations, standard testing is done with a single AI system, not with a thousand,” he told lawmakers, so now the industry must anticipate the possibility of many agents all collaborating at once.

Out of alignment

Beyond avoiding any obvious mistakes in testing, there are issues in the culture of AI testing that are more deeply embedded.

The concept of the alignment of AI models or agents — i.e. making sure AI systems do what they're told by human users and don’t go off-piste — has been one of the cornerstones for AI safety in the industry’s eyes.

World.title: ‘Abuse of power’: Von der Leyen rapped after backing space mega deal
World.content:
“Endorsing a merger at a conference covered by the media, without any substantive review, is an abuse of power and misconduct,” the French MEP wrote on X.

Von der Leyen was referring to Project Bromo, a joint venture between satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales to compete, at least in part, with the Starlink satellite-internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which recently went public in the U.S. and is valued around $2 trillion.

“These are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow,” von der Leyen said.

Her words would have been music to the ears of the summit host, French President Emmanuel Macron, who has publicly backed the project together with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

But they raised red flags with the antitrust community in Brussels, where the project has yet to be formally notified or assessed by the EU executive’s competition department led by Executive Vice President Teresa Ribera.

“What is the point of Competition Commissioner Teresa Ribera and the Directorate General for Competition if it is the president of the Commission who unilaterally decides a case?” Yon-Courtin asked.

World.title: 'Woman Unknown' wins Golden Lion award at the 83rd Venice Film Festival while 'Naza' wins special jury prize
World.content:
“Woman Unknown,” a drama about Denmark in the aftermath of the Nazi occupation directed by May el-Toukhy, won the prestigious Golden Lion at the 83rd Venice Film Festival on Saturday.

 

El-Toukhy was the only woman to have solely directed a film in the main competition this year.

Her film centres on a young Marie, played by Mathilde Arcel, whose Best Actress win makes it a rare double victory. Marie is a nanny and housemaid who is about to marry her wealthy employer in the immediate aftermath of the war. But she harbours a secret past intimate relationship with a German soldier that threatens to upend her reputation.

South Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong’s poetic portrait of class and labour, “Possible Love,” won the Silver Lion grand jury prize, the runner-up award. “Possible Love” is Lee’s first film in eight years, following his acclaimed 2018 title “Burning.”

“NAZA,” a harrowing documentary about military strategies employed in the war in Gaza from Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was awarded a special jury prize.

“It is really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film,” Abraham said.
