World.title: Poland and other V4 countries will block EU climate policies that raise energy costs, warns Tusk
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that the Central European Visegrád Group (V4) would seek to block any European Union climate policies that push up energy prices. Speaking after a meeting with the leaders of the other V4 countries, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, Tusk said that they could not accept policies that further weakened competitiveness at a time when they were already facing high electricity costs. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Bratysława ⤵️ Polska i grupa #V4 nie pozwoli na żadne zmiany i na żadne propozycje instytucji europejskich, czy innych państw, które mogłyby wpłynąć na pogorszenie sytuacji energetycznej w naszych państwach. Ceny energii w tym regionie muszą spaść. pic.twitter.com/BFnRx8Clse — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 10, 2026 In recent months, Poland and some other member states have been pushing for a softening of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), a cap-and-trade scheme launched in 2005 that makes polluters pay for carbon emissions in sectors such as power generation and heavy industry. They have also secured a postponement of the introduction of ETS2, which will cover emissions from road transport and buildings. “Whether we are talking about ETS1, ETS2, or other proposals, anything that brings a risk of more expensive energy for us will be blocked by us,” said Tusk on Thursday at a press conference alongside the other V4 prime ministers, as well as Ireland’s Micheál Martin. “Poland and the V4 will not allow any changes or any proposals from European institutions or other countries that could worsen the energy situation in our countries,” he added. “Energy prices in this region, including in Poland, must fall.” Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Tusk argued that high energy prices pose a threat not only to Central European economies but also to the competitiveness of the EU as a whole. “We can forget about any dreams of competing with China or the United States if our energy prices remain as they are right now,” warned Tusk. Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico likewise said the V4 countries were united in their approach to the emissions trading system. “We will be very active, and we will also engage in discussions outside the meetings of the European Council and the Council of Europe to discuss what steps to take to bring down these energy prices,” he said. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš also expressed frustration with rising energy costs. “All of us in our industrial region pay a lot of money for emissions allowances. And what did the commission tell us in 2020? That the price of this allowance in 2030 will be €26.50. Right now, it’s €80,” he said. According to the Eurostat data, households in Poland paid €27.09 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh), including taxes and levies, for electricity in the second half of 2025. That was the 11th highest figure in the EU and below the figure of €28.96 across the bloc as a whole. However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in costs of living, Polish households faced the second-highest electricity prices in the EU, at 37.15 PPS per 100 kWh, behind only Romania (49.52 PPS) and the Czech Republic (39.16 PPS). The effects of ETS on electricity bills has moved to the centre of political debate this year after the main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from the system, saying it makes “Poles a cash machine for the EU’s absurd leftist climate policy”. The opposition-aligned conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, has also twice sought to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policies, including ETS, arguing they are too expensive. Both his efforts were rejected by the government’s majority in parliament. While the government has rejected the idea of withdrawing from ETS – which it says would result in large, ongoing fines being levied against Poland – it has pushed for reforms to the system. In July, the European Commission outlined proposals to soften ETS in response to pressure from countries such as Poland, allowing industries to continue emitting CO2 for longer while providing more financial support for investment in clean technologies. Yet there are also a number of other EU member states that argue against weakening ETS, saying it would penalise those who moved early to cut emissions. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Just before the European Commission unveiled its proposal in July, Poland’s climate minister, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, said she had assembled a coalition of 10 countries calling for ETS reform and a more realistic emissions-reduction path. They also want ETS funding mechanisms to account for national differences, including energy mixes and GDP per capita, to ensure a fairer transition for lower-income countries starting from a more challenging position. Poland, for example, has a historical reliance on coal, which it still uses to produce around half of its electricity, helping make it one of the EU’s biggest emitters. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. For more, read our full report: https://t.co/XjD9hfhabo pic.twitter.com/WklP7dYL78 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 2, 2026 However, the country has made significant progress in expanding renewables in recent years, particularly solar and onshore wind. In 2025, renewables accounted for just over 29% of Poland’s electricity generation, almost three times the share recorded a decade earlier. Further progress is expected this year, after Poland began to generate electricity from offshore wind farms for the first time. Under a national energy and climate plan approved by the current government in June, it plans by 2040 for Poland to generate 18-21% of power from offshore wind and 22-27% from onshore wind. A further 15-16% will come from nuclear, 14-18% from solar, 7-8% from gas and 0-5% from coal. Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". World.title: Polish far-right leader Braun vandalises Ukrainian monument with hammer
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland dedicated to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two partisan formation that fought against the Soviet Union but was also responsible for massacring Poles. Braun declared that the monument, which was also recently vandalised by other unknown perpetrators, should be removed as it “insults the memory of victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles” and “glorifies Nazism”. The incident comes amid recent tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, and in particular the fact that the UPA continues to be honoured in Ukraine. Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️ Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ — Grzegorz Braun (@GrzegorzBraun_) September 10, 2026 The monument in question is located in the village of Liski, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and marks the burial site of 41 UPA soldiers killed while fighting against the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, in 1946, in the aftermath of World War Two. The area previously had a large ethnic-Ukrainian population. The memorial was vandalised last month, when it was sprayed with black paint and its arch was damaged. On Monday this week, further damage was discovered to the inscription on the monument. Police announced that they had launched an investigation into vandalism, property damage and ethnic hatred, but had not yet identified the perpetrators, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). On Wednesday evening, Braun published a video showing himself and another man using a hammer to repeatedly strike the front of the monument, causing visible damage to the stone, which contains the names of the killed UPA soldiers. They also appear to attempt to remove a separate plaque. During the video, Braun, who is a member of the European Parliament and finished fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, claimed that local residents are “afraid they would be set on fire” if they attempted to remove the memorial themselves. It is not clear when the video was recorded. Shortly after Braun published it, local police in Hrubieszów county, where the monument is located, issued a statement saying that officers were investigating damage to the monument. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka shared their statement and declared that “the perpetrators will not go unpunished”. Sprawcy zniszczenia pomnika w Białymstoku nie pozostaną bezkarni. Policjanci zabezpieczają dowody i przesłuchują świadków. https://t.co/7HCApuhPZ1 — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) September 10, 2026 Braun, who regularly carries out stunts intended to demonstrate his anti-Ukrainian, antisemitic and anti-LGBT views, and is already facing multiple legal cases over such incidents. He is currently on trial for attacking a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament using a fire extinguisher. Last month, he was charged with the crime of denying Nazi crimes for claiming that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake”. He was also charged with theft over incidents in which he tore down Ukrainian and European Union flags, and with vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition. If convicted, some of the crimes Braun is charged with carry potential years-long prison sentences. Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, which recently called for a “normalisation of relations with Russia”, enjoys support of around 8-9%, according to polling averages. That could make it a key player in deciding who can form a government after next year’s parliamentary elections. Figures from Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun's party celebrated Russia Day at the Russian embassy and presented a letter hailing Russia's development, blaming "globalists" for the Ukraine war and calling for normalisation of Polish-Russian relations https://t.co/SU3gEdVod0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2026 At the time of writing, there had been no response from Ukrainian authorities to Braun’s latest stunt. However, when the same monument was vandalised last month, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw issued a statement expressing its “deep indignation”. “Regardless of the difficult and tragic chapters of our shared history, burial and memorial sites should remain outside the realm of political disputes and be treated with respect,” they wrote. The embassy also expressed “particular concern that this incident occurs against the backdrop of a rising number of hostile acts toward Ukrainians in Poland, including reports of aggression and attacks on Ukrainian citizens” “Any attempts to shift historical disputes into the realm of vandalism, intimidation or hostility toward modern Ukraine and Ukrainians are dangerous and must be met with an appropriate legal response,” they added. Poland and Ukraine have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. His Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, responded by stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. Tensions have since cooled, and Ukraine has made moves to defuse the crisis. However, significant differences remain, in particular over memory of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the killing of around 100,000 Polish civilians. Poland regards the episode as a genocide. Ukraine strongly rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Recent months have also seen a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland, including a series of cases of verbal or physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported anti-Ukrainian hate crimes were up 30% in the first half of this year. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine responded to the dismantling of a UPA monument in Poland by introducing a ban on exhumations of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres on its territory. It is believed that tens of thousands still remain buried in unmarked mass graves. However, last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Kyiv allowed such exhumations to resume, and since then the remains of dozens of victims have been found, researched and reburied. Earlier this month, Poland also granted Ukraine permission to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. World.title: Polish train drivers announce go-slow protest after deadly crash at rail crossing
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Following a crash between a train and a truck at a rail crossing that left one passenger dead and both drivers with serious injuries, Poland’s main train drivers’ union has announced a go-slow protest that will take place on Friday. They note that they have long been warning about a lack of sufficient safety measures at rail crossings, and say that a “red line has now been crossed”. In the wake of Wednesday’s tragedy, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has pledged that the government will introduce “very tough” new punishments for those who violate regulations at crossings. Poczułam takie jakby silne hamowanie, takie bardzo silne i nagle takie bujanie i do człowieka dociera, że zaraz się wykoleimy – mówiła pasażerka pociągu Intercity "Koziołek", jadącego z Lublina do Szczecina, który wykoleił się w miejscowości Sokolniki Suche w Mazowieckiem.… pic.twitter.com/enyjD2Wo6K — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 9, 2026 On Wednesday morning, a train travelling between the cities of Lublin and Szczecin partially derailed in the village of Sokolniki Suche in central Poland after colliding with a heavy goods vehicle that, initial findings suggest, had entered the tracks at a rail crossing despite warning lights flashing. The crossing had no barriers. The train was carrying at least 114 people, including three crew. One passenger in the first carriage, a 39-year-old woman, died in hospital from her injuries, prosecutors announced later on Wednesday. Four others, including the drivers of both the train and the truck, remain hospitalised in serious condition. Prosecutors say that, from the evidence collected so far, they will launch an investigation into the crime of unintentionally causing a rail disaster, which carries a prison sentence of six months to eight years. However, they have not yet been able to interview either driver due to their health conditions. On Thursday, the head of the Polish train drivers’ union, Leszek Miętek, announced that a protest would begin at midnight and last through the whole of Friday. “We are appealing to train drivers to travel at a safe speed of 20 km/h (12.4 mph) across every level crossing in Poland,” he said, adding that he had “received reports from across the country” that “there’s full support for this type of action”. Miętek noted that the Polish labour code allows employees to refrain from work if they believe it poses a threat to their life or health. While drivers would not go that far, they want to demonstrate in a bid to prompt “action from those responsible for safety.” He warned that train delays should be expected on Friday. Związek Zawodowy Maszynistów Kolejowych mówi "dość" i ogłasza ogólnokrajowy protest po tragicznej katastrofie w Sokolnikach Suchych. However, “a red line has [now] been crossed”, he added, quoted by news website Interia. Miętek noted that, for over 18 months, the union has been running a campaign, titled “I Want To Live”, focused on safety. Just two days before the accident, it had issued a special appeal to drivers over “growing safety concerns on Polish railways”. “We have been doing everything we can in parliament and at the infrastructure ministry to make sure this problem is noticed,” added Miętek, who also welcomed the fact that, following Wednesday’s accident, Tusk has pledged to take action. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Katastrofa kolejowa w Sokolnikach miała miejsce na przejeździe kolejowym, dlatego natychmiast rozpoczniemy prace nad zaostrzeniem przepisów dla tych, którzy wjeżdżają na przejazdy kolejowe, mimo zapór i czerwonych światel. pic.twitter.com/BgaZQLEPbR — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 9, 2026 In those remarks, the prime minister lamented that the accident in Sokolniki Suche was “yet another case of such a catastrophe happening at a rail crossing”. “We must immediately begin urgent work on tightening regulations,” he continued. He revealed that one proposal being considered is suspending for three months the licence of any driver who ignores red lights at rail crossings. However, critics noted that the ministry had already announced such plans in July 2025, and had failed to implement them since then. – Chcemy wprowadzić przepis, na podstawie którego każdy kierowca, który wjedzie na przejazd drogowo-kolejowy kiedy jest zapalone czerwone światło, straci prawo jazdy, zostanie mu ono zatrzymane na trzy miesiące. However, 24% of Poland’s accidents took place at rail crossings, compared to 16% in Germany. In total, Poland had by far the highest number of deaths caused by accidents at rail crossings (45), ahead of Germany (26), France (20) and Hungary (18). When taking into account the size of countries’ rail networks, Poland had 4.3 rail deaths (from all causes, not just accidents at crossings) per thousand kilometres of track, which was the fifth-highest figure in the EU, behind Portugal (6.2), Hungary (5.8), Slovakia (5.7) and Lithuania (4.6). Last week, in dramatic scenes captured on camera, a train carrying almost 300 passengers hit a truck at a rail crossing in Gdańsk, luckily resulting in no injuries. World.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia. The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded. In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed. Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid. Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”. That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government. In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.” The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred. “We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.” With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”. Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked. “A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”. In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission. “NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added. Błaszczak to stan umysłu. Mało im było niszczenia SAFE, to dziś były szef MON podważył sens istnienia NATO wskazując, że Wojsko Polskie nie powinno bronić Litwy, Łotwy czy Estonii. Przyjaźń tego skompromitowanego środowiska z Orbanem to nie był przypadek… — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) September 1, 2026 On Wednesday, Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, visited Latvia, including the base in Ādaži where a Polish military contingent has been based since 2017 as part of a multinational NATO brigade. “Poland and Latvia face similar threats in the security domain,” said Sikorski. “We must speak with one voice and take our security seriously. Only such actions can guarantee effective protection against the threat from Russia.” “We do not want an escalation of the conflict, but Putin must know that we are not going to sit idly by and wait for his next step,” he continued. “We understand that the defence of our allies also contributes to Polish security. We stand ready to share the burden of defending the eastern flank.” 📍 Ādaži 🇱🇻 Continuing visit to Latvia, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs @sikorskiradek visited the base of the Polish Military Contingent. World.title: Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: Poland secures further $4bn financing from US to buy American military equipment
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”. The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”. .@UnderSecT took part in the signing of a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee—an important step in U.S.-Polish security cooperation. Poland’s significant investments in its defense capabilities and the U.S. defense industrial base reflect our shared… pic.twitter.com/Dz3huAp8pj — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) September 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery. The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”. In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself. Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”. “Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”. This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”. 💬 Obecna umowa została zawarta na korzystniejszych warunkach niż dwie poprzednie umowy z gwarancjami pożyczkowymi dzięki subsydiowaniu części kosztów finansowania w ramach grantu przyznanego w tym celu przez Rząd USA. To kolejny wyraz bardzo bliskiej, transatlantyckiej… pic.twitter.com/Ipd4cYDeFo — Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego 🇵🇱 (@BGK_pl) September 9, 2026 The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year. President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending. They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement. However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”. Amerykański sprzęt wojskowy ponownie wzmocni Wojsko Polskie i bezpieczeństwo Polaków! Właśnie zabezpieczyliśmy środki w wysokości 4 mld dolarów, czyli prawie 15 mld zł na jego zakup. Łącznie w ramach amerykańskiego programu Foreign Military Financing pozyskaliśmy już blisko 20… pic.twitter.com/hhzXcE1hoC — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) September 9, 2026 While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington. In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation, including DiNanno, was in Poland this week to discuss potential locations for the base. World.title: “We remember where Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,” says Polish FM

We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s foreign minister has expressed concern over the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party at a time when Germany is rapidly rearming – suggesting that it has echoes of the build-up to World War Two. “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as Europe’s largest economy, to play a strong role in ensuring our common security,” Radosław Sikorski told German newspaper Handelsblatt. “But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead – and that is precisely what the AfD represents,” he added. Polens Außenminister Sikorski: „Wir wollen, dass Deutschland (…) eine starke Rolle bei der Sicherung unserer gemeinsamen Sicherheit spielt. Aber wir erinnern uns nur allzu gut daran, wohin ein wiederbewaffnetes Deutschland in den Händen einer rechtsextremen, prorussischen Partei führen kann (…)“ [image or embed] — Andreas Prause (@andreas-prause.eu) 8 September 2026 at 21:05 Poland was, on 1 September 1939, invaded by Nazi Germany, marking the start of World War Two and over five years of brutal occupation. The attack was launched in cooperation with the Soviet Union, which invaded Poland from the east two weeks later. After Hitler was defeated, Germany had no major far-right party for decades. However, that has changed in recent years. In 2024, the AfD came first in the Thuringian state election, with 33% of the vote. Last Sunday, it won in Saxony-Anhalt, with 44%. The party also came second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition. Opinion polls now show that the AfD is the most popular party nationally, with support of around 28%, well ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), on 21%. The AfD’s growth has been watched with particular concern in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further disquiet in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 In the wake of the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland would celebrate an AfD victory. He claimed there were some such people in Law and Justice (PiS) and Confederation (Konfederacja), the two main right-wing opposition parties. However, PiS’s reaction to AfD’s rise has been mixed. On Tuesday, PiS MP Małgorzata Golińska told Polskie Radio that it represents a “kind of browning” of politics in Germany – a reference to the brown shirts of Hitler’s SA paramilitary forces that helped bring him to power in the 1920s and 1930s. “A return to very dangerous thinking is taking place there and we must observe in which direction it will all develop,” added Golińska. “From Poland’s perspective, we should not overreact with any particular emotion, but we also cannot be naive [in thinking] that nothing is happening there.” By contrast, another PiS MP, Jarosław Sellin, told Onet Radio that PiS and the AfD “say similar things” when it comes to EU climate and migration policies. But he added that “this does not mean we have to like what the AfD says about history, relations with Poland, and Russia”. Polish PM @donaldtusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” right-wing opposition figures who have welcomed the far-right AfD's election victory in Germany However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted https://t.co/goSWlbeGA8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 Responses from Confederation have likewise been mixed. The group is actually made up of two main factions, one of which, a libertarian party called New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja), is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. New Hope’s spokesman, Wojciech Machulski, told the Fakt daily that they are “united [with AfD] in our opposition to EU migration and climate policies” but at the same time “we do not accept the anti-Polish statements”. Krzysztof Mulawa, an MP from the National Movement (RN), which makes up the other half of Confederation, told the newspaper that “several of the AfD’s demands are unacceptable from the Polish perspective”. But he said that there were areas of shared interest, such as abolishing the euro. A number of figures from PiS and Confederation have also expressed hope that the AfD’s rise at the expense of establishment parties can herald a similar development in Poland, which, like Germany, is ruled by a pro-EU coalition ranging from centre-left to centre-right. Europa się budzi, a establishment wpada w panikę. Wynik AfD pokazuje, że ludzie mają dość dyktatu Brukseli, Zielonego Ładu i niszczenia państw narodowych przez nielegalną imigrację. Polityczne trzęsienie ziemi dopiero się zaczyna. Piękna, biała Europa narodów wkrótce powróci. — Włodzimierz Skalik (@Wlodek_Skalik) September 7, 2026 One party that has been unambiguously positive in its response to AfD’s victory is the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian group that broke away from Confederation last year and is currently polling support of around 9% “Europe is waking up, and the establishment is falling into panic,” wrote KKP’s deputy leader, Włodzimierz Skalik, on social media. “A beautiful, white Europe of nations will soon return.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: EU Moves to Curb Airbnb-Style Rentals to Boost Long-Term Housing
World.content:
The EU has introduced a framework to support long-term rentals in tourist-heavy cities. Airbnb warns it creates regulatory uncertainty without improving long-term housing outcomes.

The EU has announced an affordable housing plan aimed at encouraging long-term rentals and making housing more accessible for Europeans.

Unveiled on Wednesday, the plan aims to create clarity and predictability in how rules are applied by local authorities, particularly in neighbourhoods popular with tourists where short-term rentals have displaced residents.



“Lack of affordable housing is a matter of concern for so many of our European citizens,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press statement. “Essential workers and students cannot afford to live where they serve and study. But most importantly, it is about fairness. Today, we are delivering for all Europeans.”

“The new rules are designed to help competent authorities identify ‘areas under housing stress’ using a common methodology,” a Commission press release explains.

Housing in Europe is getting worse

The latest data on access to accommodation across Europe are worrying, and have pushed the Commission to intervene.

Recent Eurobarometer data shows that 50 per cent of European city dwellers think that housing is an urgent problem they experience. House prices have skyrocketed faster than local incomes across most European capitals, rising 64.9% between 2015 and 2025 and rents 21.8%, according to EU data.

Even people who cannot afford to buy are facing rising rents, which consume 40% of household income, and middle-class families are also increasingly facing a reality where they can’t afford to buy or rent, but also aren’t eligible for social housing.

Many residents in cities like Lisbon, Barcelona and Prague complain that short-term rental platforms like Airbnb have removed homes from the market and pushed prices up, often forcing them to move.

Short-term rentals represent only 1.2% of the EU’s total housing stock, but they can account for up to 20% in some tourism hotspots. With too few homes being built where demand is strongest, Brussels estimates it needs more than 2 million new homes every year to fix the problem.

Airbnb, the largest worldwide platform for short-term rentals, has criticised the plan as not sufficiently clear.

“Airbnb shares the Commission’s ambition to make housing more affordable. But as drafted, the Affordable Housing Act will not add a single home to the long term rental market, while adding regulatory uncertainty for hosts across European cities,” the company wrote in a press statement after the Commission’s announcement.

The plan must now be negotiated by the EU co-legislators before being approved.

World.title: Prague’s Industrial Palace to Reopen to the Public for Guided Tours
World.content:
After a major renovation costing more than CZK 3 billion, Prague’s Industrial Palace at the Výstaviště exhibition grounds will open its doors to the public in two weeks.

From September 25 to October 11, visitors will be able to explore the history and architecture of the landmark and see how it has been transformed during the renovation on guided tours organised by Výstaviště Praha and Prague City Tourism.



According to Výstaviště Praha, the palace will not remain open to the public on a regular basis after the tours. Instead, it will serve as a venue for exhibitions, trade fairs and other scheduled events.

The renovation of the Industrial Palace, including the reconstruction of its fire-damaged left wing, began in February 2022, more than 13 years after the wing was destroyed by a fire in October 2008.

The approximately one-hour guided tour costs CZK 91. Organisers say the symbolic price refers to 1891, the year the Industrial Palace first opened. Tickets are available through the Prague City Tourism website. Places are limited, and some tour dates have already sold out.

The first major event scheduled at the renovated palace will be the Designblok festival in early October.

Built in Just Ten Months

The Industrial Palace was built for the 1891 Jubilee Provincial Exhibition based on designs by architect Bedřich Münzberger. It is considered an important example of both artistic and technical heritage. The building was the first in the Czech lands to feature an architectural design based on a prefabricated iron structure.

Contemporary records show that 450 workers completed the building in just ten months, despite flooding and severe frosts affecting the exhibition grounds during construction.

From the beginning, the palace served as a venue for exhibitions and cultural events, although it was originally intended as a temporary structure.

Between 1952 and 1954, the communist government decided to repurpose the building, ordering its main hall to be converted into a social and dance hall. The building was also renamed the Congress Palace and became part of the Julius Fučík Cultural and Recreation Park, which operated at the site at the time.

One Wing of the Palace Was Destroyed by Fire

On October 16, 2008, a fire destroyed the left wing of the Industrial Palace after items left on an electric hot plate caught fire. The person responsible was never identified.

The renovation did not begin until early 2022. Under the original plans, the work was supposed to be completed last year.

However, once the foundations, floors and suspended ceilings of the right wing were uncovered, it became clear that the condition of the historic building was worse than expected, leading to additional work and delays.

World.title: New York Inspired New Residential Project in Prague’s Smíchov
World.content:
A new seven-story residential building planned for Prague’s Smíchov district has moved closer to construction after securing a zoning decision.

The project, known as Smíchovská Žehlička, is being developed by BPD Partners and Top Estates and is expected to be completed in 2029.

The building will contain 66 apartments as well as eight commercial units for shops, services and restaurants. It will also include shared coworking and community spaces. The total gross floor area is expected to be close to 8,000 square meters.

The project is planned for a wedge-shaped site between Kováků and Na Zatlance streets, directly below Mrázovka Park. The unusual shape of the plot and the significant difference in elevation between the two streets have made the site particularly difficult to develop.

The project has been in preparation for more than a decade. BPD Partners, the investment group owned by Czech businessmen Vasil Bobel, Petr Pudil and Jan Dobrovský, began working with architect Patrik Hoffman on the scheme in 2010.

Inspired by New York’s Flatiron Building

The shape of Smíchovská Žehlička is largely determined by the site’s narrow, wedge-shaped plot and surrounding streets. The design also takes inspiration from New York’s Flatiron Building, whose distinctive triangular form became a response to an equally unusual urban site.

The Prague project aims to use the constraints of its location in a similar way. Rather than attempting to conceal the site’s difficult geometry, the design makes it a defining feature of the building.

The residential units and commercial premises will all be offered for sale. The development will also provide shared areas intended for coworking and community activities.

If permitting and construction follow the current schedule, Smíchovská Žehlička could be completed by the end of 2029.

World.title: Award-Winning Holocaust Documentary to Premiere in Prague
World.content:
Award-winning Holocaust documentary UnBroken will have its Czech premiere at Prague’s Edison Filmhub on Friday, September 25.

The screening will take place alongside the opening of the new “Rescuers of Children” exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum.

Director, producer and writer Beth Lane will attend the Prague screening.



The documentary tells the story of Lane’s mother, Ginger Lane, and her six siblings, who survived the Holocaust after being hidden for two years by German farmers Paula and Arthur Schmidt.

The seven Jewish children were sheltered on the couple’s farm in Brandenburg, about 60 kilometers east of Berlin. They survived the war and emigrated together to the United States in 1946.

They are believed to be the only known family of seven Jewish siblings to have survived the Holocaust and later emigrated together as a family. Ginger Lane, now 86, is one of two surviving members of the family.

Paula and Arthur Schmidt were later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations, an honor given to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews during the Holocaust.

Their story is also featured in “Rescuers of Children,” the new exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum. The exhibition examines the experiences of children and other vulnerable people during the Holocaust and presents stories of individuals who risked their lives to help those facing persecution.

The Prague screening follows the documentary’s German premiere in Dachau on July 17, where UnBroken received the inaugural Lichtbrücke Prize for Human Rights in Film.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by UnBroken (@unbrokenthefilm)

The film premiered in 2023 at the Heartland International Film Festival, where it won Best Documentary Feature Premiere. It has since been screened in more than 50 cities, including at the United Nations in New York and Vienna, the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York and the Pilecki Institute in Warsaw.

UnBroken was released on Netflix in the United States in April 2025 and has since surpassed 1.5 million streams there.

The Czech premiere will take place at Edison Filmhub in Prague on September 25, 2026.

World.title: GALLERY: One of Europe’s Largest Aquariums Set to Open in Czechia in 2028
World.content:
A new public aquarium costing around CZK 700 million is planned for the Brno Exhibition Centre, with construction expected to begin in 2027 and the first visitors arriving in the second half of 2028.

The project, called Green Planet: National Aquarium, will occupy Pavilion C at the Brno Exhibition Centre. It is expected to contain around 100 aquariums and water tanks holding more than four million liters of water.



The facility will be home to about 400,000 animals representing roughly 500 species, including rare species. Developers say the project will rank among the largest aquarium complexes in Europe.

Brno Mayor Markéta Vaňková said the aquarium could attract around 500,000 visitors during its first year of operation, including people from across the South Moravian Region and neighboring countries.

The main attraction will be a 2.5 million-liter ocean tank featuring a 55-meter underwater tunnel.

Visitors will be able to walk through the tunnel while observing marine life around and above them. The aquarium will also feature hundreds of other aquatic species across its various tanks.

The developers say the number of animals will put the complex among Europe’s largest aquariums. They estimate that it will contain around 36 times as many animals as the Barcelona Aquarium.

The project is also designed around reducing water consumption.

According to the plans, recirculation systems will clean and treat water before returning it to the tanks. The developers say efficient water management will be one of the project’s priorities.

Czech and international specialists are involved in preparing the aquarium, which is expected to include both educational and visitor-focused elements.

World.title: Prague to Host Central Europe’s First Climate Week
World.content:
Prague will host the first international climate week in Central Europe from September 14 to 20, with more than 50 conferences, seminars, workshops and other events planned across the city.

Climate Week Prague will bring together representatives from climate research, finance, government, business and other sectors to discuss how cities and economies can respond to climate change.

The official opening will take place at the Prague Planetarium on Monday, September 14, at 2:30 p.m.



Speakers will include former European Commissioner for Climate Action Connie Hedegaard, Deputy Director-General for Climate Policy at the European Commission and a former Czech environment minister Jan Dusík, and Prague Mayor Bohuslav Svoboda of the ODS party, who is supporting the event.

The program will cover a broad range of issues, including how cities can adapt to rising temperatures, water management, energy, construction, agriculture and transport.

Finance will be a major part of the agenda. The CEE Sustainable Finance Summit, running from September 14 to 16, will examine the impact of geopolitics and artificial intelligence on Europe’s economic competitiveness.

Climate Week Prague has been organized by a coalition of independent organizations led by the International Sustainable Finance Centre. The group also includes research institutions, the Climate Facts think tank, banks, investors and trade unions representing workers in the construction and energy sectors.

The organizers say the increasing effects of climate change, including more frequent heat waves, were among the main reasons for launching the event.

Data cited by Fakta o klimatu illustrates the change in Prague’s summer temperatures.

Between 1961 and 1990, the city recorded seven tropical nights, when temperatures remained at or above 20 degrees Celsius throughout the night. Over the following 35 years, that number increased to 165, according to data from the Czech Academy of Sciences’ Institute for Global Change Research.

Average summer minimum temperatures in Prague also increased during the period, rising from 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, according to Fakta o klimatu.

The local figures come as international assessments warn of further warming. Reuters reported earlier in September, citing the United Nations Environment Programme, that global temperatures are expected to exceed the key 1.5-degree-Celsius threshold above pre-industrial levels within the next few years.

Further warming is expected to contribute to more extreme weather and increase pressure on ecosystems, glaciers and low-lying coastal cities.

World.title: Prague’s Petřín Funicular to Return to Service on September 22
World.content:
Prague’s Petřín funicular will resume passenger service on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, following a two-year reconstruction of the railway and its infrastructure, the Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has announced.

Service will begin at 7 a.m., with the new fourth-generation cars departing from both Újezd and Petřín stations.

Trains will then run according to the regular timetable, with departures every 10 minutes until 10:15 p.m.



The reopening comes almost exactly two years after the previous funicular was taken out of service. The third-generation cars made their final journey on September 13, 2024, after prolonged heavy rainfall destabilized and eroded sections of the hillside.

New cars increase capacity

The two new cars were designed by Czech designer Anna Marešová and built by Swiss manufacturer CWA Constructions SA. The vehicles cost a combined CZK 137.7 million and were delivered to Prague in April.

Each car can carry up to 120 passengers, compared with a capacity of 100 on the previous vehicles. The design also introduces glass roofs, giving passengers a clearer view of Petřín Hill during the journey.

Air conditioning, however, will not be installed. Because of technical limitations, the cars will instead use forced-air ventilation. The decision has already drawn criticism from some Prague residents, who have questioned how comfortable the cars will be during hot summer days, particularly given their large glass roofs.

The two-year reconstruction involved more than replacing the vehicles. Workers strengthened the foundations beneath the track, installed new rails and upgraded the funicular’s traction system.

How much will the new funicular cost?

A single journey will cost CZK 100 when purchased on site. Passengers using the PID Lítačka mobile application will pay CZK 90.

Passengers with valid long-term Prague public transport passes covering one month to one year will continue to ride without paying an additional fare.

The same applies to holders of 24-hour and 72-hour passes, children under 15 and passengers aged over 65.

World.title: Prague Botanical Garden to Host Grape Harvest Festival
World.content:
The Prague Botanical Garden will host its traditional grape harvest festival at St. Clare’s Vineyard on September 12 and 13, bringing two days of wine, fresh burčák, live music and activities for visitors.

The festival, known as Vinobraní na Vinici sv. Kláry, will feature wines from producers across the Czech Republic, Moravia and other countries.

Visitors will also have the chance to taste white and red burčák made from grapes harvested this year at St. Clare’s Vineyard.



The first grapes for the festival have already been picked by hand. Workers harvested 2,700 kilograms of table grapes and the Modrý Portugal variety. The grapes are now being used to produce this year’s burčák, a young wine that is still undergoing fermentation and is traditionally associated with the Czech grape harvest season.

Alongside wines from the St. Clare’s winery, the festival will present a selection of wines from other producers from the Czech Republic, Moravia and abroad.

Two days of live music

Music will be a major part of the weekend program. Saturday’s main stage lineup includes Jordan Haj and Emma Smetana, YES BROTHERS and 20 MINUTES.

On Sunday, visitors can see the Děda Mládek Illegal Band, BRASS AVENUE, MOVEBREAKERS and OFF BEAT ORCHESTRA. A second music stage will also operate near the St. Clare’s wine shop.

The festival program includes more than music and wine. Visitors can join guided tours of the vineyard, take part in workshops and creative activities, or attend the Vínohrátky educational program. The guided tours are included in the admission price.

The event will run from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both September 12 and 13. Activities will take place at St. Clare’s Vineyard and in the Ornamental Garden of the Prague Botanical Garden.

Tickets bought at the venue cost CZK 280 for adults and CZK 180 for children and young people aged 3 to 17.

Online tickets purchased by September 11 are CZK 250 for adults and CZK 150 for children and young people. Children under three can enter free of charge.

World.title: A new must-see in Budapest: rediscover the Citadella – photos
World.content:
If you live in Budapest, you already know the silhouette. High above the city on Gellért Hill, the Citadella and the Liberty Statue have been part of Budapest’s skyline for generations. Locals have even given the statue an affectionate nickname: the “bottle opener”, inspired by its unmistakable shape.

The Hungarian Bastille

Following a comprehensive renewal, the Citadella has reopened as a modern cultural and community destination, bringing together history, architecture, green spaces and some of the most spectacular views in Budapest. But behind the panorama lies one of the most fascinating historical locations in the city.

Source: Várkapitányság

Gellért Hill itself takes its name from Bishop Gellért, who, according to tradition, was martyred here nearly a thousand years ago. Centuries later, following the defeat of the 1848–49 Hungarian Revolution and War of Independence, the Habsburg authorities built the Citadella above the city, a fortress that came to be seen as a kind of “Hungarian Bastille” and a powerful symbol of oppression.

Its walls still bear traces of the Second World War, while the Liberty Statue above the fortress has witnessed another dramatic chapter of Hungarian history. The monument became associated with Soviet rule, and during the 1956 Revolution the symbols of communist power surrounding it were torn down. Yet the central figure survived, was later reinterpreted, and today remains one of the defining symbols of Budapest.

Source: Várkapitányság

Few places tell the complex story of the city quite so vividly.

To understand Hungary, start at the Citadella in Budapest

At the heart of the renewed Citadella, the Bastion of Liberty offers an immersive introduction to thirteen centuries of Hungarian history in more than 1,700 square metres. In around half an hour, visitors can gain an insight into the events that shaped Hungary, making it an ideal starting point for anyone who lives, studies, works or does business here.

Source: Várkapitányság

Interactive installations, cinematic storytelling and audiovisual experiences bring the past closer, while an audio guide available in 10 languages makes the exhibition easily accessible to Budapest’s international community.

The experience is also an ideal addition to a business programme in Budapest. International colleagues, clients and partners can discover the country behind the destination and gain valuable cultural and historical context in a compact, engaging format.

Tailor-made programmes are available for corporate and professional groups, contact us to request an individual offer. For an entirely different experience, discover the Citadella during one of our sunset walks. Watch Budapest change as the sun sets over the city and experience the renewed fortress and its panoramic terraces in a unique atmosphere.

Source: Várkapitányság

From fortress to public space

For much of its history, the Citadella was designed to keep people out. Today, the opposite is true. The renewal has opened the former military fortress to the city. New passages connect the two sides of Gellért Hill, while a distinctive V-shaped opening breaks through the once-enclosed fortress walls.

At its centre, a new public park of more than 6,000 square metres is surrounded by renewed green spaces, walkways and panoramic terraces, transforming the Citadella into a place to meet, walk, relax and experience Budapest from above.

Source: Várkapitányság

If you missed – Gellért Hill: Budapest’s iconic landmark of history, liberty and breathtaking views

See Budapest differently

Walk through Citadella Park, explore the renewed fortress walls and take in the city from the Round Bastion Terrace and Roof Garden 360.

Bring friends who have just moved to Budapest. Visit with family, introduce international colleagues and business partners to Hungary, or simply rediscover one of the city’s most familiar landmarks for yourself.

Because living like a local is about more than knowing the city. It is about understanding the stories behind it. The Citadella has watched over Budapest for generations. Now it is Budapest’s turn to rediscover it.

Live like a local. Discover the history. See Budapest differently.

Citadella reopening: Budapest landmark with one of the city’s best panoramas welcomes visitors again

World.title: Inside the Karpacz Economic Forum 2026: Poland’s rise, political divides and the future of the V4
World.content:
Three days, more than 6,500 participants, hundreds of panel discussions, politicians, businesspeople, local government leaders and experts – the Karpacz Economic Forum 2026 was an impressive event by its sheer scale alone. Yet what was even more interesting on the ground was seeing how the economic and political figures of one of Europe’s most dynamically developing countries view their own situation. And also how differently the very same economic figures can be interpreted.

All this took place not in Warsaw, Kraków or another major Polish city, but in Karpacz, a mountain resort near the Czech border.

A small town that becomes one of Poland’s centres for three days

At first glance, the choice of venue may seem surprising. Karpacz is hardly a conventional conference city, yet the Hotel Gołębiewski and the surrounding infrastructure have enough capacity to host an event attended by several thousand people without major disruption.

According to the official summary by Forum Ekonomiczne, more than 6,500 participants attended the 35th Economic Forum, held between 8 and 10 September, with more than 500 debates, panels and other events taking place. The programme covered eight major thematic areas, ranging from the economy and international politics to digitalisation, artificial intelligence and healthcare.

The true scale of the event could best be appreciated on site. Conference rooms were spread across several floors of the hotel and in pavilions erected in front of the building, while gala events and banquets were held on a separate floor. According to the organisers’ official information, even the logistics centre itself was located 3.5 kilometres from the main conference venue.

According to an on-site report by wroclaw.pl, around 500 media representatives, 1,200 local government officials and 900 foreign delegates arrived in Karpacz. Although a significant part of the programme was held in Polish and focused primarily on Polish issues, interpretation was available for the more important panels, making much of the conference accessible to international participants as well.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026: a strong economy facing serious dilemmas

One of the most interesting lessons of the three days for me was just how differently the same economic data can be interpreted.

Poland is recording particularly strong growth by European standards. The European Commission’s May forecast projected GDP growth of 3.5 percent for 2026, while unemployment remains exceptionally low. At the same time, the picture is far from problem-free: the Commission expected a budget deficit of 6.5 percent and a further increase in public debt.

The OECD’s June forecast was somewhat more cautious, projecting growth of 3 percent in 2026 and specifically highlighting risks related to energy prices, global demand and the geopolitical situation in the region.

In Karpacz, therefore, the same economic performance was presented in one discussion as proof of a successful convergence model, and in another as the starting point for examining the challenges facing a country entering a new stage of development.

Perhaps this was precisely what made the forum so interesting: within just a few conference rooms of one another, it was possible to hear entirely different conclusions drawn from the same economic reality.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Both government and opposition figures turned out in Karpacz

Numerous prominent figures from Polish political life also attended the forum. The organisers highlighted the participation of, among others, Defence Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski, Development Minister Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, Science Minister Marcin Kulasek, Deputy Speaker of the Sejm Krzysztof Bosak and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki, while numerous state secretaries were also present.

The presence of right-wing and opposition politicians was particularly conspicuous. Morawiecki received a standing ovation, while Krzysztof Bosak’s appearance also prompted a strong reaction from the audience. According to the report, former Prime Minister Beata Szydło and former Defence Minister Mariusz Błaszczak also spoke at the event. Andrzej Duda, Poland’s president between 2015 and 2025, likewise appeared at several events.

The gala dinners were among the forum’s most spectacular occasions. This was where awards recognising outstanding achievements in the economy, business and public life were presented. Perhaps the most important of these, the 2026 Person of the Year award, went to Infrastructure Minister Dariusz Klimczak.

In case you missed it – Looking beyond price per square metre: how the new-build housing markets of Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest differ

Morawiecki: the V4 must continue even when countries are led by different political camps

Mateusz Morawiecki’s appearance was particularly interesting to me because I also had the opportunity to put a question directly to the former Polish prime minister at the forum.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

I asked whether, if he were to return to government following Poland’s 2027 election, he would continue Visegrád Group cooperation even if Hungary’s prime minister were Péter Magyar rather than Viktor Orbán.

Morawiecki gave an unequivocal yes.

According to the former Polish prime minister, the V4 must be maintained at all costs, and it must not be allowed to fall apart or lose its significance again simply because the countries concerned are governed by political forces with differing views.

The essence of his answer was that regional cooperation must survive party-political differences. Poland, Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia share numerous economic, infrastructural and geopolitical interests that remain regardless of which political camp happens to be in power.

The message is particularly noteworthy because the V4 has been on hold in recent years precisely because of foreign-policy and political differences among its member states.

Polish–Hungarian rail links: Budapest to Warsaw took ten hours 20 years ago – and still does today

A much more critical assessment of the state of Polish–Hungarian relations was heard during another panel.

Balázs Szabó, president of the Polish Nationality Self-Government of Dunakeszi and the Association of Modern Polish Thought, said that in his view the previous Hungarian government had not done enough over its 16 years in office to develop Polish–Hungarian relations in practical terms, with transport providing one of the clearest examples.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Szabó pointed out that around 20 years ago it took roughly ten hours to travel by train from Budapest to Warsaw, and that journey times have not decreased substantially since then.

He considered this particularly problematic given that Hungary undertook a major international railway investment in another direction: the Budapest–Belgrade railway line was upgraded, while no project of comparable scale was launched towards Poland.

According to Szabó, a modern Budapest–Warsaw connection would go far beyond tourism.

A north–south railway connection could also be of strategic importance for logistics, freight transport and closer links between the countries of the region. While new north–south logistics corridors and high-speed rail connections are being developed across Europe, Hungary is not yet a major player in these networks.

Szabó said, however, that some change may already be perceptible. He noted that Dávid Vitézy, transport and investment minister in Hungary’s new government, has already spoken about developing rail connections towards Poland. This does not yet amount to a concrete investment project, but he believes it is an important indication that the issue could once again make its way onto Hungary’s transport policy agenda.

Vitézy is indeed preparing a large-scale railway development programme: according to a 11 September report by 24.hu, the minister spoke about a comprehensive HUF 3.5 trillion – approximately EUR 9.6 billion – rail and transport development framework.

More than fifty Hungarians attended the forum

The composition of the participants was also interesting from a Hungarian perspective. More than fifty people from Hungary registered for the event, several of whom also spoke in panel discussions.

In previous years, the Hungarian delegation regularly included ministers from the Orbán government as well as political and public figures close to the former governing party. This year, several Fidesz politicians or participants linked to the previous period of government could again be seen at the event, while high-level representation from the new government led by Péter Magyar was much less noticeable.

Among those present was former Speaker of the Hungarian National Assembly László Kövér, who had originally been scheduled for two events but ultimately took part in one panel discussion. Péter Márki-Zay, mayor of Hódmezővásárhely, also travelled to Karpacz and attended several events. Their encounter even made it into the Hungarian press: 24.hu reported that, according to Márki-Zay, László Kövér declined to shake his outstretched hand.

The composition of the Hungarian participants was also interesting in light of the fundamental change in Hungary’s political situation a few months earlier. The personal and institutional network built up over recent years was still clearly visible at the forum, while relations between Hungary’s new government and the Karpacz Economic Forum are evidently still at the beginning of a new era.

I was invited to one of Central Europe’s largest economic forums, as the owner of DNH MEDIA GROUP Ltd., by the Warsaw Enterprise Institute Foundation to attend both the event and the press trip that followed.

Karpacz Economic Forum: much more than just an economic conference

By the end of the Karpacz Economic Forum 2026, this was perhaps my strongest impression: although it is called an economic forum, for three days it effectively becomes a Central European meeting place where economics, politics, geopolitics, infrastructure, technology and business are almost inseparable.

Karpacz Economic Forum 2026. Photo by Daily News Hungary

Conversations in the corridors and over dinner were at least as important as those taking place on stage. And across the hundreds of panels, it was sometimes possible to hear completely different answers to the same question depending on whether one was listening to a minister, an opposition politician, a businessperson or an economist.

By many indicators, Poland has every reason to look to the coming years with optimism. At the same time, Karpacz also showed that rapid economic growth does not in itself eliminate dilemmas. On the contrary: the greater the country’s economic and political weight becomes, the more important the question of how it chooses to use that strength.

From a Hungarian perspective, one of the most important lessons may have been something that emerged in two very different discussions: Polish–Hungarian relations cannot be built solely on the political friendship of whichever parties happen to be in government. Whether the issue is the V4 or a modern railway connecting Budapest and Warsaw, long-term cooperation requires relationships and infrastructure capable of surviving changes of government.

As we wrote after the election, Polish–Hungarian friendship could gain new momentum. Magyar and Tusk discussed exactly this in Warsaw.

World.title: Former PM Orbán reveals why he nominated man for high state honour later convicted for sexual abuse of many children
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has revealed why he nominated the paedophile director of the children’s home in Bicske for a high state honour.

Péter Magyar, Hungary’s prime minister, today published a document proving that the director was nominated for the award in a submission bearing Orbán’s signature. Proceedings had already been brought against him in 2011, yet the nomination went ahead on the recommendation of Zoltán Balog, then minister for human resources.

Orbán brushes off question

Asked today in Kötcse why he had nominated the director of the Bicske children’s home in 2016 – he has since been convicted of paedophile offences – Orbán replied that someone had put his name forward and that the press should ask the person responsible.

Péter Magyar speaking in the Hungarian Parliament. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Anita

Magyar had earlier published the nomination document, which bears the name of Orbán, who was prime minister at the time, as the signatory. It said the director deserved the honour for his work educating disadvantaged children and preparing them for independent lives.

If you missed – Sexual abuse, starvation, squalor and accident hazards: Orbán’s government concealed the reality of Hungary’s children’s homes

The scandal surrounding János Vásárhelyi erupted in 2016, after a former resident of the Bicske children’s home took his own life, having grown tired of nobody believing him. Vásárhelyi was convicted in 2019, but the first official complaint and police investigation against him dated back to 2011, after two employees of the home reported that several children had accused him of sexually abusing them. Police closed the investigation in 2012, citing a lack of evidence.

Nomination came from Zoltán Balog

“It was the same Zoltán Balog who recommended the paedophile director of the Bicske children’s home for a state honour to Viktor Orbán, and who later secured a presidential pardon from Katalin Novák for Endre Kónya, an accomplice in the paedophile abuse,” Magyar wrote on Facebook on Saturday.
