World.title: Tallinn has 50 kilometers of walkable underground pipes
World.content:
Tallinna Vesi development manager Marti Vaksmann says that there are 3,000 kilometers of pipelines beneath Tallinn, including 50 kilometers of large pipes where a person can walk. He notes that being inside a wastewater collector is not the most pleasant experience, but it is part of the job.

Construction has been underway all summer at the Hipodroom intersection in Tallinn, and the reason for the repairs lies underground.

"We're going about four meters deep here, but in Tallinn some places reach depths of up to 30 meters," said Vaksmann, development manager for water and sewerage assets at Tallinna Vesi. "We've measured that Tallinn has 3,000 kilometers of pipelines, and about 50 kilometers of those are large enough for us to walk through."

The existing pipes were installed nearly a century ago, when Tallinn still used a combined sewer system, with stormwater and wastewater flowing through the same pipe. "Today we're building a separate stormwater pipeline right under the Hipodroom intersection. We're planning for the next 50 years, assuming rainfall may become more intense, so we won't need to rebuild this pipe again. If it seems to passersby that not much construction is happening at Hipodroom site, that's because most of it is underground," Vaksmann said.

Vaksmann said he likes pipes and doesn't feel afraid walking inside them. "Many people don't like tight spaces, but that's our job. Right now we're in a stormwater collector, but there are also wastewater collectors, and walking in those is not the most pleasant — but someone has to do it."

"In addition to the large pipelines, there's also a water pipe here, a sewer pipe, heating pipelines, and various cables under the sidewalks. Whenever possible, we shift pipelines under the sidewalk," Vaksmann explained. "There are no buildings directly above us."

World.title: Mari Roosvalt and Jaan Elken's joint exhibition sums up 25 years of work
World.content:
On 12 September, the Pärnu Museum of New Art will open "Dialoog" (Dialogue), a joint exhibition by painters Mari Roosvalt and Jaan Elken. The retrospective brings together works created by the two artists over the past 25 years.

"Perhaps some of our principles are similar. Elken has worked in acrylic, while I've mostly stayed with oil and built my approach around that. We share a certain common attitude toward this dialogue. Many of our themes overlap — ecological and political subjects. We follow the art field closely and pay attention to what's happening around us," said painter Mari Roosvalt.

"We have so many overlaps and so many opportunities for dialogue, and we're connected through technique. We're both painting innovators, and here we present a more forceful, robust kind of painting, full of life in the brushstrokes, palette‑knife marks, collaged elements, flags and slogans that make up the works. It's essentially a painting hybrid with echoes of early pop art. There were an incredible number of connections, so I truly enjoyed putting this exhibition together. I thank Mari for her trust," said painter Jaan Elken.

The exhibition at the Pärnu Museum of New Art (MONA) will remain open until 18 October.

World.title: Packaging rules for small businesses 'a problem we must tackle together', EU official says
World.content:
New EU packaging rules could saddle micro‑businesses with heavy costs and bureaucracy when selling across borders, prompting the European Commission to signal it may allow flexibility for the smaller firms, a senior official said during a visit to Estonia.

New extended producer‑responsibility requirements may make selling into another member state too costly and bureaucratic for very small companies, said Patrick Child, deputy director‑general of the European Commission's environment directorate.

The main goal of the EU packaging regulation is to reduce excessive packaging and packaging waste, promote reusable packaging and recycling, and harmonize standards across member states so the packaging sector can function more effectively at EU level. The aim is also to reduce the climate and environmental impact of packaging, support the single market and lessen Europe's dependence on imported raw materials. The agreed rules will take effect gradually.

In August, the provisions concerning hazardous substances in food‑contact packaging materials entered into force. Most requirements will apply starting in 2030.

The exact content of several rules — such as the ban on plastic packaging for fruit and vegetables under 1.5 kg — will be clarified through implementing acts now being drafted by the European Commission, taking into account input from member states, businesses and other stakeholders. "We must ensure the regulation does not hinder the functioning of the internal market; on the contrary, our aim is for rules to be more uniform across Europe," Child said.

Child visited Estonia this week to discuss two topics with authorities and stakeholders: EU circular‑economy proposals and implementation of the Nature Restoration Regulation. In the context of the packaging regulation, one question raised was how the new rules will affect small and medium‑sized enterprises operating across borders — specifically how companies will contribute to waste‑management costs in the future.

Some provisions have prompted concerns that they impose excessive administrative burdens and costs on companies. "We are discussing this with the aim of reaching a result that stimulates economic activity in EU countries and creates more jobs," Child said.

System needs more flexibility

Asked what changes companies should prepare for, Child said the new regulation followed extensive preparation and consultations with businesses. He stressed that the agreed requirements will not take effect overnight — the goal is a smooth, controlled transition.

"We already see that companies investing in new technologies and more sustainable packaging solutions, or developing them, are anticipating market developments and creating business opportunities for the future," he said.

Still, Child acknowledged that the system needs more flexibility so that micro‑ and small enterprises exporting to other member states — for example via online platforms — do not face excessive costs or administrative burdens. "This is a problem we must tackle together," he noted.

A year ago, the Commission proposed suspending the obligation to appoint and pay for an extended producer‑responsibility representative in another member state. "I understand that for micro‑enterprises this can be too expensive," Child said. He explained that the system should be based on mutual recognition between member states or exempt small companies from certain requirements. The proposal is currently under discussion among member states.

In Estonia, media attention has focused on the country's intention to introduce some requirements stricter than those in the EU regulation. "Generally, as long as national rules remain within what the legislation allows, higher environmental‑protection standards are acceptable to us," Child said.

Higher environmental standards welcomed

He added that each case must be assessed individually and Estonian laws reviewed. "But in principle, we welcome it when a member state has a higher level of environmental protection," Child said.

Regarding the packaging of unprocessed fresh fruit and vegetables and pre‑packed fresh produce under 1.5 kg, plastic packaging will be restricted starting 1 January 2030. This does not mean, for example, that cucumbers cannot be sold in packaging at all — the ban applies to certain types of single‑use plastic packaging.

Member states may grant exemptions if there is proven need — for example to prevent water loss, wilting, microbiological risks, physical damage or oxidation, or when mixing organic and conventional products cannot be avoided otherwise. The procedure for applying exemptions will be clarified.

"With fresh food and vegetables, we must be extremely careful with anything that could reduce product quality or pose risks to consumers," Child said.

World.title: Tallinn Half Marathon sees fastest times ever recorded
World.content:
Kenyan runners dominated the Tallinn Marathon half‑marathon on Saturday, winning both the men's and women's races and setting new event records.

More than 5,000 participants started the 21.1‑kilometer race at 9 a.m. on Saturday from Falgi tee at the foot of Pikk Hermann tower. The top four finishers were all from Kenya, and for the first time ever in Estonia, the half‑marathon distance was completed in under one hour.

Vincent Kiptoo won with a high‑class course record of 59 minutes and 48 seconds. Johana Erot finished second (1:00:51), Enos Kipruto Saat third (1:01:22), and Edwin Kiprop Kiptoo fourth (1:01:49). The fastest Estonian was Leonid Latsepov, who placed fifth in 1:04:20.

Kenyan runners also took the top two spots in the women's race. Regina Wambui Ndungu, who finished seventh overall, won with a standout Tallinn half‑marathon record of 1:07:35. Winsam Jerono placed second (1:10:29), and Morocco's Soukaina Atanane finished third (1:11:24).

Ronja Hofstetter of Switzerland was fourth (1:14:36), followed by Norway's Lene Nylund (1:22:51). The fastest Estonian woman was Pille Hinn, who finished sixth in 1:23:02.

Estonia's largest mass‑sport event continues with the 10‑kilometer Tallinn Autumn Run at 14:00 and concludes Sunday morning at 9:00 with the marathon distance.

World.title: Iraq closes three Iran crossings as hunt begins for Saudi pipeline attackers
World.content:
Baghdad – Iraq closed three border crossings with Iran on Saturday, officials told AFP, after a drone attack on a Saudi Arabian pipeline that both Riyadh and Baghdad said was launched from Iraq.

Soon after the attack, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed the military commander in Missan province, bordering Iran, after authorities determined that the drones had been launched from there.

No group has claimed responsibility, and an alliance of powerful Tehran-backed Iraqi armed groups said they hadn’t struck the pipeline, but Riyadh has previously accused these groups of targeting its oil infrastructure.

An Iraqi security source and a government official told *AFP *that authorities ordered the closing of three border crossings with Iran.

The security source said that the decision is “part of an intelligence effort to track down the perpetrators and prevent their escape… and to hinder the smuggling of drones through these crossings”.

Both sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not allowed to speak to the media, could not specify when the crossings would reopen.

The closed crossings are Shalamsheh in Basra province and al-Shib in Missan, as well as al-Mandali in the central province of Diyala.

– Other border crossings with Iran are still open –

The government’s security media cell said that authorities “have started administrative and security reorganisation operations at several border crossings”.

It added that they have stepped up “intelligence activities” to determine “the breaches and violations that took place at these crossings”, without specifying which border posts.

It later announced that passengers stranded for hours at two crossings were permitted to pass.

In July, the United States and Saudi Arabia said they had struck Iran-backed militants in Iraq in response to attacks on US forces and Saudi oil facilities.

Pro-Iran armed groups have supported Tehran during the Middle East war, claiming hundreds of attacks on US bases in Iraq and across the region.

On Saturday, those groups, operating under the umbrella of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, said they had not struck the pipeline.

“Accusations against the Iraqi resistance regarding the targeting of vital Saudi installations on Friday are an honour that we do not claim,” they said in a statement.

Under mounting US pressure, Zaidi has pledged to ensure that armed factions surrender their weapons to the state.

The issue has fuelled tensions in recent weeks, with several groups refusing to disarm.

World.title: Anthropic boss calls for slowing pace of AI development
World.content:
New York – Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday called on artificial intelligence (AI) firms to slow down the development of the powerful technology, amid mounting worries over the risks of “superintelligent” computer systems.

His comments came a few days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of “gambling with our lives” in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in a post on his personal website.

“AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious.”

“Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way,” said Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela in 2021.

“But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence.”

Amodei’s statement echoes another call by Anthropic in early June to slow or suspend development.

Then in late July, Sam Altman, the boss of Anthropic rival OpenAI, said developers might need to voluntarily pump the brakes on their rapid advances to give society a chance to catch up.

At roughly the same time, more than 1,000 employees at cutting-edge AI companies including Amodei signed a petition calling on the US government to help “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”

OpenAI had revealed that during testing, the AI models broke out of their confined environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site developers use to store and share code.

Earlier this week, Coxon, 27, sounded the alarm after spending the past three years pretraining AI models — first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach.

Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data.

“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said Tuesday.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he said in a post on X.

Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI’s capabilities exceed human intelligence.

World.title: Hull hold Chelsea, Liverpool fail to beat Fulham in Premier League
World.content:
London – Hull held free-scoring Chelsea 2-2 at Stamford Bridge to go third in the Premier League as Liverpool failed to find a way past struggling Fulham in a 0-0 draw on Saturday.

It was a familiar tale for Chelsea as the front three of Morgan Rogers, Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer dazzled, but the Blues were undone by an inability to defend.

In five games against top-flight opposition since Xabi Alonso took charge, Chelsea have scored 16 times and conceded 12.

Hull were the last side in the Premier League to concede, but after three clean sheets they were finally breached when Rogers drilled in at the near post on seven minutes.

Mohamed Belloumi took advantage of Chelsea’s slackness at the back to blast home on the volley after Jorrel Hato got caught under a cross to the back post.

The Algerian winger then put Hull in front with a deflected strike after Emi Martinez failed to deal with a corner.

Pedro drilled a Palmer cross into the top corner to bring Chelsea level just after the hour mark.

But the home side could not find a winner as Hull’s honeymoon back in the Premier League goes on with only defending champions Arsenal and Manchester City above them in the table.

“We have to be happy,” said Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic. “It’s a huge result for us.”

– Fulham fight for Arbeloa –

Liverpool remain unbeaten under Andoni Iraola but there were boos at Anfield after Fulham picked up their first point under Alvaro Arbeloa.

Former Liverpool defender Arbeloa was reportedly fighting for his job after losing his first three league matches since arriving in west London from Real Madrid.

Yet a Liverpool forward line featuring three £100 million ($135 million) players in Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak failed to click against the Cottagers’ leaky defence.

“When you draw, especially at home, you can’t be happy,” said Iraola, who blamed fatigue after his side’s Champions League exertions against Atletico Madrid on Wednesday.

“Today we lacked a bit of freshness and we did not do enough offensively to make the difference.”

It was Fulham who had the better chances to take all three points as Gonzalo Garcia missed a glorious opportunity in the first half and Alisson Becker produced a brilliant save to deny Josh King the winner.

Liverpool climb to sixth but could find themselves already six points off the top should Arsenal win at Sunderland later on Saturday.

Aston Villa are rooted in the relegation zone after Nottingham Forest exacted revenge with a 2-1 win at Villa Park.

Villa beat their Midlands rivals in the Europa League semi-finals last season on their way to lifting a first trophy for 30 years.

Eyebrows were raised at the club record reported £45 million Forest paid Chelsea for Liam Delap after failing to make the grade at Stamford Bridge.

But Delap proved his worth with a long-range strike into the bottom corner to open the scoring.

Alysson levelled with Villa’s first league goal of the season, but Igor Jesus secured Oliver Glasner’s first win as Forest boss.

Glasner’s old club Crystal Palace’s poor start to the campaign continued with a 3-2 home defeat to Ipswich.

The visitors were aided by Axel Disasi’s first half red card as Zian Flemming’s first goal for the Tractor Boys snatched all three points in stoppage time.

Brentford remain unbeaten thanks to Kevin Schade’s double in a 2-2 draw at Bournemouth.

The Cherries, by contrast, are yet to win in the Premier League under Marco Rose despite leading in all four games.

Tottenham are aiming to kickstart their league season with a first goal and win at home to Everton later.

Manchester United host local rivals City in the pick of Sunday’s action.

World.title: Ukraine’s economy hobbled by Russian strikes
World.content:
Kyiv – Ukraine’s economy is being crippled by intensifying Russian strikes hitting key sectors and its GDP could slump by 1.5 points in 2026, Kyiv officials said Saturday, warning of a “very difficult” winter ahead.

Russia, which devastated Ukraine’s energy sector during the course of 4.5 years of war, has since this summer stepped up a campaign of missiles and drones that Kyiv is struggling to intercept.

These have severely restricted grain exports in the Black Sea — a crucial source of Kyiv’s revenue.

The strikes have also targeted steel companies, another key sector, as well as supply chains — notably in the rail sector — and major warehouses.

“The economy is in the most difficult situation,” Ukraine’s Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said during the annual Yalta European Strategy forum in Kyiv.

He said the intensity of the strikes and the level of destruction have increased.

“We anticipate a very difficult winter in terms of both critical infrastructure, which is being destroyed every day by Russian attacks, but also in terms of overall economic conditions in the country,” said Ukraine’s economy minister, Oleksandr Kravchenko.

Kyiv estimates that “the total destruction of infrastructure and assets are likely to be close to $10 billion” this year.

This destruction and the blockage of seaports are likely to reduce national GDP by 1.5 points, he added, with some Western experts calling the situation “catastrophic.”

– Rising war costs –

Roksolana Pidlasa, the head of the budget committee in Ukraine’s parliament, described a bleak outlook.

“It can get worse, but it’s already bad now,” she told the same forum.

“Russia specifically targets revenue-generating industries by attacking grain corridors, by attacking seaports and metallurgical plants,” she said at the same forum.

“It is not something that you could reconstruct quickly.”

Ukraine’s largest steelworks, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rig, said Saturday that a Russian missile strike killed two of its workers and damaged facilities.

Kyiv has also upped its retaliatory strikes on Russia, targeting oil facilities, factories and warehouses.

President Volodymyr Zelensky hopes his US counterpart Donald Trump will pressure Russia to ensure Black Sea ports reopen and for a mutual suspension of strikes on energy sites.

He warned of the risk of food crises in African and Asian countries, saying Moscow was also unable to export its grain through the Black Sea. Both countries are key global suppliers of grain.

– Food and energy truce –

“At the very least, again, if peace is impossible from today… we can at least resolve the issue of an energy truce, a food truce, food security; such decisions can be made,” he told the Kyiv forum this weekend.

He called on resolving these “now” and “not in winter”.

At the same time, Kyiv’s military spending is rising.

Pidlasa said that in 2024 “one day of war costs 140 million US dollars per day, this year it costs 190 million dollars a day.”

Kyiv, she said, has had to start using international aid this year to even pay its soldiers’ wages.

The release of nearly $30 billion in international aid intended to finance this year’s budget deficit is conditional upon parliament passing draft laws demanded by Western countries, Koretsky said.

These include anti-corruption measures after Ukraine was hit by several large-scale graft scandals during the war with Russia.

But parliament is struggling to approve suggested laws, which include unpopular measures such as imposing duties on parcels from abroad, intended to boost revenues.

World.title: Antonelli fastest again in crash-hit final practice
World.content:
Madrid – Championship leader Kimi Antonelli stayed on top for Mercedes ahead of Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc in Saturday’s extended crash-hit third and final practice ahead of qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old Italian clocked a best lap in one minute and 32.797 seconds to outpace the Monegasque by 0.166 seconds ahead of both McLarens in a session that saw seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton slam into the barriers in the second Ferrari.

Hamilton’s crash led to a red flag stoppage that lasted 54 minutes and rendered an extra quarter of an hour added, as the drivers’ continued to explore the limits of the new high-risk Madring circuit, dubbed a ‘car-killer’ in many quarters.

In the end, Antonelli’s pure talent took him clear again with Leclerc second ahead of Oscar Piastri and world champion Lando Norris with four-time champion Max Verstappen taking fifth for Red Bull in the final minutes.

George Russell was sixth in the second Mercedes, seven-tenths off his team-mate’s pace, ahead of Liam Lawson in the second Red Bull, Nico Hulkenberg of Audi, Hamilton and Gabriel Bortoleto in the second Audi.

After a crash-free opening hour on Friday, the second produced one crash – for Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad, who returned to take 14th place, and the third delivered two as Oliver Bearman also hit the barriers in his Haas in the final minute.

After a slow start, Ferrari had joined the fray on softs and clocked immediate fastest laps before a hasty Hamilton slammed into the barriers.

The 41-year-old Briton locked up at the final corner after 24 minutes, breaking his front wing which was stuck under the car as he reversed successfully and began to return to the pits. The session was red-flagged.

Race engineer Carlo Santi realised and asked him to “stop in the safest place possible” but Hamilton was not keen to obey. He replied, saying “if I can make it back, I will. If not, I will do it safely”.

Told he had a right front puncture and told again to stop, he finally pulled up, knowing he had ignored orders, driven in an unsafe condition and probably faced a penalty. It was, he knew, a bad incident for him.

With 15 minutes remaining, Race Control stopped the timer to allow a final quarter of an hour action once repairs were completed.

This was a rare occurrence as F1 does not usually allow for additional time, except for qualifying sessions, but it guaranteed a frantic finale for a sell-out crowd basking in the sun with the young Italian jousting with Leclerc.

World.title: Iraq PM dismisses Maysan Police Chief over drone strikes on Saudi pipelines
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi, ordered the dismissal of Maysan Governorate’s police chief on Saturday, September 12, 2026, mounting an aggressive command-level purge following cross-border drone strikes that struck critical Saudi oil pipeline infrastructure.

The swift disciplinary directives were disclosed by the Military Spokesperson for the Commander-in-Chief, Major General Sabah Al-Noman, who confirmed that Al-Zaidi additionally mandated the immediate transfer of all provincial security agency directors to headquarters reserve pending exhaustive internal investigations into severe operational lapses within the southern governorate.

The sweeping shakeup in Maysan’s security hierarchy follows an official announcement from Riyadh confirming that the kingdom’s strategic East–West crude pipeline sustained drone attacks across segments located within the Riyadh and Medina regions.

Saudi authorities verified that the unmanned aerial systems originated from Iraqi territory, leaving multiple human casualties and physical damage along the energy network. Riyadh stated that it opted against immediate military retaliation at this stage in response to an explicit personal appeal by Prime Minister Al-Zaidi, who requested that Baghdad be granted the diplomatic space and operational window needed to execute decisive accountability measures on the ground, even as Saudi Arabia affirmed its full sovereign right to defend its territory, national security, and strategic facilities.

Al-Zaidi’s decision to remove the provincial police leadership deepens an ongoing institutional overhaul across Maysan, coming shortly after the Prime Minister dismissed the Commander of Maysan Operations and convened a military board of inquiry against the entire operational command.

The unprecedented sanctions were triggered by conclusive technical and intelligence findings confirming that the drones targeting the Saudi pipeline infrastructure were launched directly from launch sites situated within Maysan Governorate, compelling Baghdad to take assertive steps to preserve regional stability and enforce state command over its southern territorial boundaries.

World.title: Acting Minister lays foundation stone for British University in Baghdad
World.content:
Bagdhdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Acting Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research, Abdul Hussein Al-Mousawi, laid the foundation stone on Saturday for the British University in Baghdad, marking a major milestone in the country’s ongoing academic modernization.

The ground-breaking ceremony was held in Al-Jawahiri Residential City, situated in the Abu Ghraib district west of the capital, officially launching construction on a campus designed entirely around United Kingdom higher education benchmarks and curricula.

The institution is set to house four anchor colleges covering vital technical disciplines: the College of Pharmacy, the College of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, the College of Engineering, and the College of Education, directly targeting emerging labor market deficits across both public and private sectors.

The inception of the British University arrives amid a broader, dynamic renaissance across Baghdad’s private education landscape, where demand for accredited foreign schooling has surged exponentially in recent years.

The capital has evolved into an active hub for premium international curricula, already hosting five fully accredited institutions delivering International Baccalaureate, American, and British tracks, including Baghdad British International School (BBIS), English International School Baghdad (EISB), and Cadmus International School.

This momentum is poised to accelerate further with major greenfield expansions on the horizon, most notably plans by the SABIS educational network to introduce an International School of Choueifat campus within the burgeoning Abu Ghraib corridor.

At the tertiary level, the British University project builds upon a proven institutional precedent established six years earlier with the founding of the American University of Iraq – Baghdad (AUIB). Since opening its doors in 2020, AUIB has earned widespread acclaim and deep institutional trust among Baghdad households, proving that local demand for rigorous, globally accredited campus environments is both robust and sustained.

By bringing a dedicated British collegiate model to the capital’s western growth zone, the initiative not only broadens academic diversity but also reflects a concerted national strategy to integrate world-class schooling infrastructure into Iraq’s next generation of master-planned residential cities.

World.title: Iraq PM Al Zaidi to meet Macron in Paris for energy and security talks
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi is set to meet French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris on Sunday for high-level bilateral talks, marking his first official European tour aimed at forging expanded strategic partnerships.

The summit comes against the backdrop of heightened regional volatility affecting international shipping routes and energy supplies, alongside ongoing preparations regarding the bilateral security framework as the international coalition against ISIS approaches anticipated operational transitions.

According to a statement issued by the Élysée Palace, the bilateral agenda centers on critical economic sectors, prioritizing joint collaboration in energy, transport, municipal water networks, infrastructure, and healthcare, alongside deepened security and defense coordination.

Both leaders are expected to formalize their discussions by signing a series of undisclosed bilateral agreements and commercial contracts, signaling a mutual push to involve French corporations in Iraq’s domestic reconstruction and infrastructure pipeline.

On the security front, the French presidency underscored that both leaders will reaffirm their shared resolve to combat terrorism relentlessly and prevent ISIS from regaining operational capabilities, all within a framework that guarantees full respect for Iraqi sovereignty during the upcoming shifts in the coalition’s mandate.

Paris reiterated that sustaining defense and intelligence coordination with Baghdad remains a central cornerstone for preserving wider Middle Eastern stability.

Economic fallout from regional unrest will equally dominate the Elysee discussions, particularly regarding maritime commercial corridors and the uninterrupted flow of Iraqi crude exports to global markets.

In light of recurring shipping bottlenecks and transit pressures, Macron and Al-Zaidi aim to coordinate mechanisms to safeguard and steadily resume these export flows, a move designed to alleviate broader pressures across global energy markets, bolster Iraq’s petroleum-dependent fiscal revenue, and sustainably protect consumer purchasing power within importing nations, including France.

World.title: BRICS hammers out joint declaration after India bridges Iran-UAE chasm
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In a dramatic repeat of the 2023 G20 Declaration under Indiaâs presidency, BRICS member-states reached a consensus for a joint declaration following intensive, late-night negotiations that lasted till 4 am on Saturday.

The talks had been strained by sharp differences between the UAE and Iran over the West Asia conflict and an earlier meeting of the BRICS foreign ministers under Indiaâs presidency had ended without a consensual statement.

Also Read |

The 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration announced by

was solidified by a rare leader-level Iran-UAE meeting - between Iran President Masour Pezeshkian and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan â in the middle of the war that started on February 28.

In a delicately worded compromise, the declaration addressed the interests of both sides by expressing serious concerns over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and also peaceful nuclear facilities under full safeguards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), in violation of international law and relevant resolutions of the IAEA. This implicit criticism of US-Israeli action against Iran was crucial in getting Iran to sign off on the declaration.





âWe in BRICS must fight against the normalization of attacks on civilian, vital infrastructure. The same applies to peaceful nuclear infrastructure," said Pezeshkian at the summitâââ.

Nuclear safeguards, safety, and security must always be upheld, including in armed conflicts, to protect people and the environment from harm, said the declaration.

Significantly, the joint statement did not name any country or explicitly condemn attacks, prioritising instead dialogue and diplomacy, UN Charter, civilian lives and infrastructure and respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity of all States, while also expressing deep concern over continued escalations and calling for maximum restraint.

Also Read |

In the declaration, the leaders recalled their respective national positions on West Asia and stressed the need to work together to maintain smooth flow of global trade, supply chains and energy, in accordance with applicable international law.

Official sources said India led prolonged negotiations at multiple levels to reconcile sharp differences between the 2 sides and forge consensus with support from other member-states who were keen that the summit didnât end without a joint statement.

The BRICS consensus is reminiscent of the last-minute G20 2023 Delhi declaration that was achieved in the middle of the escalating Russia-Ukraine war with a carefully nuanced formulation that called upon all States to refrain from use of force for territorial acquisition but without naming Russia.

The BRICS declaration also came days before Iranâs meeting with GCC countries on the Strait of Hormuz situation. In Pezeshkianâs meeting with the crown prince, the leaders underscored the importance of supporting efforts to ease tensions, promote de-escalation and strengthen regional stability.

Indian officials had on Friday expressed confidence about a constructive outcome from the negotiations, following Modiâs meeting with Pezeshkian in which he expressed solidarity with Tehran, seeking a long-term and win-win partnership with Iran.

On other issues, like in Rio last year, China and Russia, as permanent members of the UN Security Council, reiterated their support to the aspirations of Brazil and India to play a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.

Importantly for India, the declaration expressed strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as âcriminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committedâ and strongly reiterated condemnation of the Pahalgam terrorist attack.

âWe reaffirm our commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens,â said the declaration.

On the Palestine issue, BRICS countries, including India, expressed deep concern on the continued violence in Gaza despite the ceasefire agreement of October 2025. âWe call for halting any policies aimed at forced displacement of Palestinians from Gaza Strip and express concern regarding arrangements that may prejudice the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people and legitimize or prolong occupation,â said the declaration.

There was no mention of the Ukraine war in the declaration this year. The declaration backed comprehensive reform of the UN, including the Security Council, with a view to making it more âdemocratic, representative, effective and efficientâ and to increase the representation of developing countries in the Council's memberships.

World.title: SIA searches Poonch, Udhampur in radicalisation probe
World.content:

JAMMU: Five locations in Poonch and Udhampur districts were searched by Jammu & Kashmir State Investigation Agency (SIA) Saturday as part of an investigation into the alleged spread of secessionist narratives and radicalisation through online and offline channels, including social media platforms allegedly operated from across the border.An SIA spokesperson said investigators found that some individuals were allegedly in contact with suspicious persons across the Line of Control (LoC) and the border. World.title: Brics resolve for joint mechanism to extradite fugitives
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In a unified resolve to combat money laundering and corruption, the Brics member nations on Saturday reiterated their commitment to âeffectively identify, detect and disrupt money laundering schemesâ and strengthen digital financial security, including prevention of fraud in cross-border payment systems.

The grouping for the first time emphasised on putting a mechanism to extradite fugitives from each otherâs country and initiate steps towards asset recovery from such criminals.

âWe welcome the establishment of Brics Expert Network on Asset Recovery to enhance cooperation among focal points and the BRICS repository on informal cooperation for tracing fugitive offenders sought for corruption and supporting extradition,â the joint declaration stated.

There is an ongoing discussion on developing a network of law enforcement agencies for enhancing cooperation on actions against fugitive offenders.

The member nations also pledged to âpromote cooperation in the prevention and combating of corruption and to the continued implementation of relevant international agreements, in particular the UN Convention against Corruption.â

World.title: Modi-Xi-Putin bonhomie, car diplomacy, gala dinner, Pahalgam condemnation and New Delhi Declaration: Brics Summit key takeaways
World.content:
NEW DELHI: India hosted the 18th

in New Delhi on September 12-13, bringing together leaders of the expanded 11-member grouping for discussions on global conflicts,

, trade, energy, technology, climate change and reform of international institutions.

India used its 2026 chairship to push a people-centric agenda centred on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability.

The summit was marked by high-level bilateral meetings, visible displays of bonhomie among leaders and efforts to bridge differences over the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region. PM Modi held separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, while leaders also participated in the Brics Business Forum and other summit engagements.

From PM Modi and Putin travelling together by car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex to PM Modi and Xi sharing warm moments and the leaders participating in a gala dinner and cultural engagements, the summit combined diplomacy with symbols of Brics unity.

Also read -

The summit adopted the New Delhi Declaration, a 45-page document containing 140 points that brings together the grouping's positions on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance and development.





PM Modi-Xi bilateral: Boundary question and reset in ties

PM Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit, with both sides stressing the importance of viewing India-China relations from a strategic and long-term perspective.

The two leaders committed to seeking a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable solution to the boundary question. PM Modi stressed that differences should not become disputes and highlighted the importance of mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest.

The discussions also covered peace and tranquillity along the border, economic relations, trade imbalances, supply chains and people-to-people exchanges. The meeting came as New Delhi and Beijing seek to stabilise bilateral ties while continuing to manage differences over the boundary.

The Modi-Xi meeting was one of the summit's most closely watched engagements, given the strategic importance of India-China relations and their simultaneous participation in an expanded Brics framework.

PM Modi-Putin meeting: Ukraine, West Asia and $100 billion trade target

PM Modi held an over 45-minute bilateral meeting with Putin on the eve of the summit, reviewing the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussing regional and global developments.

The two leaders discussed the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the West Asia crisis on maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers. PM Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remained the way forward in resolving conflicts and said India was ready to contribute to peace efforts.

Five Indian seafarers have died in the Black Sea amid the Russia-Ukraine hostilities, making maritime safety an important concern for New Delhi.

The two sides also discussed defence, energy, critical minerals, civil nuclear cooperation, fertilisers, infrastructure, technology and industrial cooperation. India and Russia agreed to work towards taking bilateral trade to $100 billion by 2030.

Putin also invited PM Modi to Russia for the 24th India-Russia Annual Summit.

The dates will be finalised through diplomatic channels.

Car diplomacy: PM Modi and Putin travel together

After their bilateral meeting, PM Modi and Putin travelled together in the same car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex before attending the Brics Business Forum.

The unusual visual quickly became one of the defining moments of the summit, highlighting the close nature of the India-Russia relationship amid continuing geopolitical pressure on Moscow and India's effort to maintain strategic autonomy.

PM Modi later highlighted the growing India-Russia economic relationship, including the participation of companies from both countries at the INNOPROM industrial exhibition held at Bharat Mandapam.

Thirukkural gift: PM Modi presents Putin Russian translation

PM Modi presented Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the classical Tamil work attributed to poet-saint Thiruvalluvar.

"Two thousand years ago, Thiruvalluvar wrote the Thirukkural. It includes the entire gamut of human life.

It has been translated into the Russian language. I am confident that the people-to-people contact will increase with the translation of the Thirukkural into Russian, which will play a big role in strengthening our relations," Modi told Putin.

The gift was presented as a cultural bridge between India and Russia and reflected the emphasis placed by India on people-to-people links during its Brics chairship.

PM Modi-Pezeshkian talks: West Asia and regional peace

PM Modi met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the summit, with the two leaders discussing India-Iran relations, Brics cooperation and the conflict in West Asia.

PM Modi reiterated India's position that disputes must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy and stressed the need for lasting peace and stability in the region.

The discussions also covered freedom of navigation and commerce and the safety and well-being of seafarers, issues that have acquired greater importance amid disruption to shipping routes in the region.

The meeting followed the leaders' earlier interaction on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek.

India also stressed the importance of expanding bilateral trade channels and pursuing a long-term and mutually beneficial relationship with Iran.

PM Modi, Xi, Putin and leaders showcase Brics unity

The summit was accompanied by a series of high-profile visuals showing leaders of the expanded grouping interacting informally.

PM Modi was seen greeting Putin and Xi together, holding their hands and sharing smiles. In another visual, Modi walked alongside Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian.

Also read -

PM Modi was also seen holding hands and walking alongside Pezeshkian and other leaders during the Brics Business Forum. The images were widely seen as a demonstration of the grouping's effort to project unity despite differences among members on major geopolitical issues.

The presence of leaders from Russia, China, Iran, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, South Africa and other member states underscored the diversity of interests represented within the expanded grouping.

Gala dinner: Leaders gather for cultural evening

The Brics leaders also attended a gala dinner hosted during the summit, providing an informal setting for interactions between heads of government and state.

Also read -

The cultural programme and dinner formed part of India's effort to showcase its heritage alongside the formal diplomatic agenda. The event brought together leaders who had spent the summit discussing contentious issues ranging from wars and terrorism to trade and global governance.

The informal interactions added a softer dimension to a summit otherwise dominated by difficult geopolitical negotiations.

Banyan tree plantation: Symbol of Brics unity

A symbolic tree plantation ceremony was also organised during the summit, with Brics leaders participating in the planting of a Banyan tree.

The Banyan tree, known for its extensive roots and interconnected branches, was presented as a symbol of continuity, resilience and interconnectedness.

The gesture complemented India's 2026 Brics theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability".

Also read -

The plantation also reflected India's attempt to connect the summit's diplomatic agenda with sustainability and environmental cooperation.

Brics Business Forum: Trade, investment and technology

The Brics Business Forum brought together heads of state, ministers and business leaders to discuss trade, investment, finance, technology and development.

PM Modi highlighted the economic weight of the expanded grouping, saying:

"Today, BRICS nations represent 50 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of its GDP, and over 25 per cent of global trade. Moreover, while global GDP has grown approximately two-and-a-half-fold over these years, the combined GDP of BRICS nations has expanded nearly four-and-a-half-fold. In other words, the economic strength of BRICS has grown at nearly twice the pace of the rest of the world."

"The growing scale, speed, and optimism of BRICS are clearly evident among us. This forum, hosted in India, is the largest BRICS Business Forum to date," the Prime Minister added.

Also read -

Pezeshkian called for Brics to convert its economic potential into practical cooperation through trade, investment and joint financing.

"We believe that the true strength of BRICS is not confined merely to the size of its members' economies; rather, it becomes more apparent when these capacities are transformed into a network of trade, investment and joint financing â a transition from potential cooperation to operational one," he said.

Putin stressed the importance of business-to-business relations and economic partnerships, arguing that they could help create more resilient international economic relations.

Putin attacks trade restrictions, backs new growth platform

At the Business Forum, Putin criticised what he described as attempts by Western competitors to regain their former economic leadership.

"We have always been told that competition is a sacred cow, something that must not be touched," Putin told a BRICS business forum event.

"Yet, unfortunately, âtoday your Western competitors are trying by any means necessary to regain their former leadership."

"This â competition is âsometimes assuming unsightly forms," he said. "They even include direct âphysical attacks or the âdestruction of industrial and logistical facilities, pipelines, and so forth."

Putin also criticised restrictions on international transport corridors, shipping and trade and called for Brics to contribute to building "a new, sustainable platform for global growth".

India-Russia economic partnership gets push

The summit also provided an opportunity for India and Russia to discuss expanding economic cooperation amid Western sanctions and geopolitical uncertainty.

The two countries discussed the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030 and cooperation in infrastructure, energy, technology, defence, critical minerals and civil nuclear energy.

The sides also explored industrial cooperation in railways and tunnelling, the steel value chain and greater access to the Russian market for Indian exporters.

India continues to maintain strong energy ties with Russia, while seeking to expand trade beyond traditional sectors.

Brics pushes practical cooperation across sectors

India's 2026 chairship focused heavily on converting Brics into a platform for practical cooperation rather than limiting it to political declarations.

More than 350 meetings and high-level engagements were organised across approximately 30 cities during India's chairship. These covered political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.

PM Modi said: "It gives me immense pleasure to welcome and greet you all to India. Indiaâs BRICS chairmanship is based on a people-centric and humanity-first approach. Resilience, innovation, cooperation, and sustainability have been our priorities."

"Alongside these priorities, we have placed special emphasis on connecting BRICS cooperation with the common people. With this vision in mind, more than 350 meetings were organised.

We had the opportunity to welcome your teams to approximately 30 cities..."

Agriculture: Digital farming and climate resilience

Brics countries agreed on new mechanisms to strengthen agricultural cooperation.

These include Centres of Excellence on agro-ecology for research and knowledge sharing on natural, organic and regenerative farming, a Brics Network on Digital Agriculture using artificial intelligence, geospatial intelligence, IoT-enabled monitoring and advanced data analytics, and BRICS AGRIN, a voluntary framework covering agricultural inputs, seeds and genetic resources.

The initiatives seek to promote climate-resilient farming and greater technology-driven cooperation among member countries.

Health: Lifestyle, traditional medicine and mental health

The Brics Mission for Healthy Lifestyle was launched along with a roadmap for joint cooperation for 2026-2029, focusing on preventive approaches to obesity and other non-communicable diseases.

Members also agreed to establish an Expert Working Group on Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine, covering research, evidence generation, academic exchange, quality standards and protection of traditional knowledge.

Mental health cooperation was also strengthened through the Brics Training Hub Network and Network of Centres of Excellence, with NIMHANS India as the coordinating centre.

Energy: Smart grids and storage

Brics adopted guiding principles on energy storage and smart grids and launched a Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage.

The initiative will provide a platform for knowledge sharing, capacity building, policy and regulatory cooperation and pilot projects among member countries.

The summit also placed emphasis on energy security, diversified energy sources and equitable energy transitions.

MSMEs and startups: New platforms for businesses

India pushed stronger cooperation for micro, small and medium enterprises and startups.

The Brics MSME Cooperation Portal will connect MSMEs, technology centres, trade associations, financial institutions and policymakers across member countries.

A Brics Incubator Network will connect startups with incubators in other member countries, while the Brics Startup Innovation Fund is intended to support early and growth-stage startups.

Logistics and global supply chains

Brics members agreed on a Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework aimed at improving resilience, sustainability and connectivity.

The grouping also advanced cooperation on global value chains through the GVC Action Plan 2026-2030, including a Technical Council and joint study.

The initiatives are intended to reduce vulnerabilities caused by fragmented supply chains, improve connectivity and promote economic diversification.

Urban mobility and climate-resilient infrastructure

The summit also advanced cooperation on sustainable urban development.

A Brics Urban Mobility Hub was established as a platform for technical cooperation and knowledge sharing. Members also adopted voluntary principles on climate-resilient urban infrastructure.

An Urban Research and Knowledge Network was established to facilitate cross-border research, peer learning and institutional cooperation.

Skilling, youth and sports technology

India also advanced cooperation on skills and employment through BRICS CONNECT, a voluntary network covering capacity building, social security, women's workforce participation, employability and digital public infrastructure.

The Brics Youth Cooperation Framework 2026 was adopted to provide greater continuity and structure to youth cooperation.

Sports technology cooperation was institutionalised through a working group focusing on technical information, research, institutional experience and best practices.

Science and research cooperation

The Brics Science and Research Repository was welcomed as a structured platform for sharing scientific knowledge among member countries.

The initiative is intended to strengthen research collaboration and facilitate greater exchange of scientific information across the expanded grouping.

Brics 2026: A wider and more diverse grouping

Brics currently comprises 11 countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE.

The expansion has significantly widened the grouping's geographical reach across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America.

It has also brought together countries with different political systems, economic priorities and positions on major international conflicts.

India's chairship therefore focused not only on expanding cooperation but also on finding consensus among members with competing interests.

New Delhi Declaration: Key outcomes

The summit concluded with the adoption of the New Delhi Declaration 2026, following intensive negotiations among members. The 45-page declaration contains 140 points and represents India's central diplomatic outcome from its 2026 chairship.

The declaration addresses terrorism, conflicts, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance, development and the interests of the Global South.

Terrorism: Pahalgam attack explicitly condemned

The declaration strongly condemns terrorism in all its forms and manifestations and calls for "zero tolerance for terrorism".

It specifically condemns the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terrorist attack, in which 26 people were killed. The declaration also condemns cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.

Brics reaffirmed that terrorism cannot be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and called for those involved in terrorist activities and their support to be held accountable.

The grouping also called for progress towards the adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism under the UN framework.

West Asia: Ceasefire, diplomacy and two-state solution

The declaration expresses deep concern over the continuing escalation in West Asia and calls on all parties to exercise maximum restraint.

It stresses dialogue, consultation and diplomacy as the means to address conflicts and calls for the protection of civilians and humanitarian assistance.

On Gaza, Brics called for the upholding of a ceasefire, unhindered humanitarian aid and an end to forced displacement of Palestinians. It reaffirmed support for a two-state solution based on the internationally recognised 1967 borders.

Unilateral war condemned

The declaration condemns unilateral military action without naming any country.

The language assumes significance because Brics includes members with differing positions on the major conflicts in West Asia and the wider international system.

The consensus was reached after negotiations continued into the early hours of Saturday, with India working to bridge differences between members and produce a common position.

UN reform and greater Global South representation

Brics reaffirmed its support for comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including the Security Council.

The grouping called for greater representation of developing countries in global decision-making and a more democratic, representative and inclusive international system.

China and Russia reiterated support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.

Trade: Opposition to tariffs and protectionism

The declaration expresses concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures that distort international trade and create uncertainty for businesses and supply chains.

Brics reaffirmed support for a rules-based multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization.

The grouping also called for the restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.

Sanctions: Brics rejects unilateral coercive measures

Brics voiced opposition to unilateral coercive measures that it considers inconsistent with international law and the principles of the UN Charter.

The declaration calls for such measures to be eliminated and highlights their impact on international economic relations.

The position reflects a longstanding Brics push for a more balanced international economic and political order.

Local currencies and cross-border payments

The declaration supports greater use of local currencies in cross-border payments and trade settlements among Brics countries.

Members acknowledged ongoing work on interoperability between payment and messaging systems and efforts to facilitate trade settlements and investment in local currencies.

The initiative forms part of the wider Brics effort to strengthen financial resilience and cooperation.

Energy security and transition

The declaration calls for stronger energy security through diversified energy sources, resilient infrastructure and stable markets.

It also supports just, orderly, equitable and inclusive energy transitions while recognising the differing circumstances and priorities of member countries.

Brics backed cooperation involving renewables, nuclear energy, hydropower, hydrogen, fossil fuels and other low-carbon technologies.

Women and inclusive development

The declaration recognises women as leaders, decision-makers and drivers of economic growth and social transformation.

It highlights women's participation in governance, entrepreneurship, employment and peacebuilding and calls for greater financial and digital inclusion.

The grouping also emphasised skills development and access to productive and social services.

Tackling organised crime and illicit financial flows

Brics expressed concern over illicit financial flows linked to drug trafficking, firearms trafficking, terrorism financing, human trafficking and organised crime.

The grouping called for stronger cooperation between member countries to trace and disrupt criminal proceeds and tackle transnational criminal networks.

The larger message from New Delhi

The New Delhi Declaration combines a strong political message on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia and global governance with a broad economic and development agenda.

For India, the outcome represents an effort to demonstrate that the expanded Brics can reach consensus despite major geopolitical differences.

The declaration also places India's priorities of resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability at the centre of a wider agenda covering trade, technology, energy, health, agriculture, finance and development.

The summit therefore ended with two parallel messages: Brics wants a stronger collective voice in global affairs, while India wants that voice translated into practical cooperation that reaches businesses, communities and ordinary people.

World.title: Chhattisgarh BJP Minister's brother Guru Dhaldas Saheb joins Congress
World.content:
Guru Dhaldas Saheb, a leader from the numerically significant Satnami community and the older brother of Chhattisgarh Minister, and BJP leader Guru Khushwant Saheb, has joined the Opposition Congress in the State.

Comprising around 13% of Chhattisgarh's population, the Satnami community represents the largest Scheduled Castes group in the State. Mr. Dhaldas’ family belongs to the lineage of Baba Guru Ghasidas who founded the Satnam Panth in the 19th century.

Mr. Khushwant Saheb and their father Guru Baldas Saheb had joined the BJP after leaving the Congress in 2023 ahead of the State Assembly elections, with the former winning on a BJP ticket from the Arang Assembly constituency.

Mr. Dhaldas joined the Opposition party in the presence of former Chief Minister Bhupesh Baghel at the latter's official residence on Friday (September 11, 2026). "The beginning has been made. Together, we will remove the BJP,” Mr. Baghel wrote on X.

On Saturday (September 12, 2026), State Congress president Deepak Baij said Mr. Dhaldas’ entry was just the trailer and there were more more BJP leaders – whom he called naraz phuphas (or grumpy uncles a term used by PM Narendra Modi to target his critics) – preparing to join the Congress.

On his reasons to switch over, Mr. Dhaldas told journalists that the BJP was not acting according to the principles of Guru Baba Ghasidas. He also added that he had discussed the issue with his family and there were no political differences between them despite him breaking ranks.

He expressed interest in contesting the 2028 Assembly polls if his new party gave him a chance. "If I don't contest elections, how will I serve the people? If the party gives me an opportunity, I will certainly contest,” he said, adding that Mungeli, a Scheduled Caste-reserved constituency, would be his preferred seat in the event of contesting.

On Arang, the seat currently represented by his younger brother in the State Assembly, he said that he would contest from there if his brother is not fielded [by the BJP]

World.title: Yemen govt. forces say hit Houthis in Red Sea city
World.content:
Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces said on Saturday (September 12, 2026) that they had struck Iran-allied Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha, as the number of civilians forced to flee the renewed fighting soared.

U.S. news site Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman had twice called U.S. President Donald Trump to request American strikes on the Houthis last week but the request was rejected.

The ongoing clashes follow a week-long Houthi offensive that culminated in the group capturing the remainder of Yemen's Red Sea coast and several strategic islands, and cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the sea's southern entrance.

The waterway has become an important artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports after Iran largely cut off shipments through the Gulf with its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the war in West Asia. The Houthis have recently declared their own maritime blockade of Riyadh's Red Sea ports.

The government news agency Saba reported on Saturday (September 12, 2026) that Yemeni "forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia" near the port of Mocha, and quoted a spokesman for the forces as saying they had also struck Houthi targets just outside the city.

The Houthis, meanwhile, said on Saturday evening (September 12, 2026) that over the past 48 hours, "Saudi enemy aircraft conducted 129 airstrikes" on areas under their control.

Yemen's civil war, which began in 2014 with the Houthi capture of the capital Sanaa, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022 but roared back to life in July.

Saudi Arabia first entered the war on the side of Yemen's internationally recognised government in 2015 and continues to support the Aden-based administration.

On Saturday night (September 12, 2026), Saudi authorities said a Houthi projectile fell in an area near the border, hours after issuing alerts warning of the risk of possible attacks. The civil defence directorate said the incident resulted "in two injuries and material damage to a mosque, several buildings, and vehicles".

'Not even a shelter'

The Yemeni civil war uprooted millions of people, and the latest fighting has led even more to flee their homes.

The fall of Mocha to the Houthis on Thursday (September 10, 2026) drove many residents to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.

One of the displaced, Abdulali al-Rajihi, said the Houthis "told us: 'Leave, scatter, you have half an hour'". "We fled wearing the clothes on our backs. And we took our children, as much as we could manage."

Saddam Ali escaped from Al-Waziyah with his 11 children and a few possessions crammed into a small pick-up truck. He said he hadn't found a single free house in the city, "not even a shelter".

The UN's migration agency said on Saturday (September 12, 2026) that, since July, 76,000 people had fled the fighting, a figure that had quadrupled since last week. It said it was providing support but warned that "needs are far outpacing what we can deliver".

"The situation is deteriorating by the day," it added.

The renewed fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.

World.title: Jamia hostel protest over mess food escalates; varsity denies assault charges
World.content:
The All India Students’ Association (AISA) on Saturday (September 12, 2026) accused an Assistant Proctor of assaulting students amid an ongoing protest over poor food quality at Jamia Millia Islamia’s Jammu and Kashmir Girls’ Hostel. The university denied the allegation and instead said the students had manhandled security personnel. The authorities also said most of the students’ demands had already been accepted.

The protest broke out on Thursday (September 10, 2026) after students complained about the poor quality of food served in the mess, alleging that insects and foreign objects were regularly found in their meals. The students have been demanding an immediate change of the mess vendor, recruitment of female staff, and a written assurance from the administration that no disciplinary action will be taken against those participating in the agitation.

In a statement issued on Saturday (September 12, 2026), AISA accused the university administration of using force against the demonstrating students. The student body claimed that the assistant proctor Maqsood Ahmad Malik manhandled and assaulted a student near the Dean of Students’ Welfare office around 1 a.m. on Friday (September 11, 2026), after the electricity was switched off. It also alleged that several students suffered minor injuries during the commotion.

The students, AISA said, continued their sit-in through the night near Centenary Gate despite the power outage. It also alleged that Gate No. 13 was closed and barricaded with three layers, which it described as an attempt to isolate the protesters.

Rejecting the allegations, university officials said most demands were accepted on day one and accused the students of escalating the situation.

A Jamia Millia Islamia spokesperson said, “Students broke two gates of the girls’ hostel, putting everyone’s security at risk, and manhandled members of the proctorial team.” The university also added that the protesters were not demonstrating at the designated protest site near Gate No. 18.

The university also clarified that lights in parts of the campus are routinely turned off to save energy and the move was unrelated to the protest.

(With PTI inputs)

World.title: The Houthis vs Saudi Arabia | The new lords of the Red Sea
World.content:
On July 13, an Iranian civilian aircraft carrying a high-level Houthi delegation was heading towards Sana’a, Yemen’s capital. Under an unwritten understanding between the Houthis (or Ansar Allah), who control northern and northwestern Yemen, including Sana’a, and the country’s Saudi-backed government, planes seeking to land in Houthi-held territory were required to obtain prior approval. The Houthi delegation had left Yemen on July 3 on another Iranian aircraft to attend the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran’s Supreme Leader who was assassinated by the U.S. and Israel on February 28 when they launched their war against Tehran.

Yemen’s Saudi-backed government had protested the Iranian plane transporting Houthi leaders, arguing it was a violation of Yemen’s sovereignty. It also opposed the delegation taking an Iranian plane back home, and instead offered to facilitate their return on a non-Iranian airline. The government’s main concern was that the flight could also be used to transport personnel of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and military equipment to Yemen. The Houthis, nevertheless, chose to return on a Mahan Air flight. To prevent the aircraft from landing, Saudi-backed forces bombed the runway of Sana’a airport, forcing the plane to land in Hodeidah. This was the trigger.

The Houthis, who took control of Sana’a in 2014, said the strike was a violation of a 2022 ceasefire. They responded by bombing Saudi energy infrastructure and launching an offensive in Hodeidah and Taiz governorates. They also imposed a naval blockade on Saudi vessels in the Red Sea. Within two months, the Houthis made dramatic territorial gains, seizing the entire Red Sea coastline of Yemen and taking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow chokepoint connecting the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, under their control.

A revivalist movement

The roots of the Houthi movement can be traced to ‘Believing Youth’ (Muntada al-Shahab Al-Mu’min), a Zaydi revivalist group founded in Northern Yemen in the early 1990s. Hussein al-Houthi and his father, Badr al-Din al-Houthi, influential Zaydi clerics in northern Yemen, became the movement’s leading figures. Inspired by the Iranian revolution of 1979 and the rise of Hezbollah in southern Lebanon in the 1980s, Badr al-Din and his sons started building vast social and religious networks among the Zaydi Shias of Yemen, who make up roughly one-third of the Sunni-majority country’s population. While the Zaydis are seen as part of the Shia branch of Islam, both in terms of theology and practice, they are different from the ‘Twelver’ Shias of Iran, Iraq and Lebanon.

In 2004, Ali Abdullah Saleh’s government, upset with the growing popularity and rebellion of the Houthis, issued an arrest warrant against Hussein. He resisted the arrest, starting an insurgency. In September, government troops attacked the rebels and killed Hussein. But the movement he founded would only grow, forcing Saleh to step down in 2012 and capturing Sana’a from government forces in 2014.

Alarmed by the rise of an Iran-aligned Shia militia across its southern border, Saudi Arabia formed a coalition and declared war against the Houthis in 2015. An intense bombing campaign followed, but the Saudi-led coalition failed to dislodge the rebels, who built a parallel state in northern Yemen. In 2022, amid a broader rapprochement between Iran and Saudi Arabia, the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces agreed to a ceasefire.

The Saudis also struggled to build a credible counterweight to the Houthis inside Yemen. The top leadership of the government was based in Saudi Arabia, while in the south, the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council broke with the government and pursued its own separatist agenda, further weakening the anti-Houthi camp. Broader tensions between Saudi Arabia and the UAE also complicated their war efforts in Yemen. But the Saudis still maintained an air and naval blockade on Houthi-held territory.

The ceasefire allowed the Houthis to consolidate their position in the north and northwest, despite economic woes. The parallel state, an ideologically committed base, years of warfare and sustained Iranian support enabled the group to transform itself into a formidable territorial army. Their access to the Red Sea, a key shipping route, raised their profile as a naval force. When Israel launched a devastating war on Palestinians in Gaza following Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack, Houthis “declared war” against Israel “in solidarity with the Palestinians”. They also carried out attacks on Israel-linked ships in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. In March 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump announced a major air and naval operation against the Houthis, threatening to destroy the group. Despite the enormous firepower brought against them, the Houthis continued launching missiles and drones at U.S. naval forces. Seven weeks later, Mr. Trump announced an end to the U.S. strikes following an Oman-mediated ceasefire.

After the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28, the Houthis, to the surprise of many, stayed out of the conflict. Iran retaliated by attacking American bases in the Persian Gulf and shutting down the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis understood that Iran’s closure of the strait strengthened their strategic position: they had the capacity to disrupt maritime traffic through the Red Sea. They also wanted the Saudi blockade of their air space and ports lifted. In the first week of July, as a second round of bombings between Iran and the U.S. was unfolding, the Houthis decided to test Saudi Arabia’s resolve by sending a delegation to Iran on an Iranian plane. Saudi Arabia responded by bombing the runway at Sana’a airport as the delegation was returning, effectively breaking the ceasefire. Then the Houthis moved rapidly up the escalation ladder.

Renewed conflict brings Saudi Arabia under enormous pressure. After traffic through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted by Iran, Riyadh increasingly relied on its Red Sea terminals to export crude oil. Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, connecting its oil fields in the east with the ports on the Red Sea, allowed the Kingdom to skirt the impact of the disruptions in Hormuz to a certain extent. But the Houthis, after the ceasefire broke down, directly targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, apparently in coordination with Iran-aligned Shia militants in Iraq. On September 11, Saudi Arabia announced that the pipeline was shut, following drone attacks from Iraq. In Yemen, in a lightning offensive launched in early September, the Houthis captured the port cities of Mokha and Dhubab and the Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb, extending their control along the coast and into the strait.

Two chokepoints

More than 20% of the world’s seaborne oil trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. The Red Sea, which connects Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal in the north and Bab el-Mandeb in the south, typically carries roughly 12-15% of global trade. This means that Iran and Ansar Allah now have the ability to exert pressure on two of the world’s critical maritime chokepoints. The Houthi capture of more territories along the Red Sea, as government forces collapsed within days, has also given them a clear upper hand in the civil war and allowed them to consolidate their position inside Yemen.

On February 27, before the war, both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait were open, and Iran was prepared to make concessions on its nuclear programme. On June 17, when the U.S. and Iran signed an MoU, committing Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in return for sanctions relief from the U.S. and a regional ceasefire involving Lebanon, the Bab el-Mandeb was still fully open. Today, maritime traffic through both the chokepoints is disrupted, any regional ceasefire will have to include Yemen, and any final settlement will have to address the Houthis’ demands, while Iran’s nuclear programme has been pushed to the back burner.

World.title: Dipke visits families in M.P.’s Balaghat, puts lens on tribal children’s deaths
World.content:
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke on Saturday (September 12, 2026) visited the tribal villages in Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat district, where several children of the Baiga tribe died due to monsoon-related illnesses and lack of access to healthcare facilities, and met the families of the victims.

Mr. Dipke, who visited several villages, said the children could have been saved had they received timely treatment. The CJP blamed the government’s negligence for the deaths.

In a post on X, Mr. Dipke said, “I am still in Balaghat, meeting the families of the KIDS who have died. What I am hearing from locals is deeply disturbing. They say the actual number of deaths is much higher than what is being officially reported (36). 86 children have been hospitalised recently after the tribals’ protest.”

“I have also been told that children are being cremated without conducting post-mortems, and in some cases, even in the absence of parents. Sub Divisional Magistrate is the one who is behind all this. These children could’ve been saved had they received treatment on time,” he added.

Earlier, speaking to reporters, he said he had come to Balaghat to fix accountability in the matter. “We completely sympathise with families who have lost their children and will definitely come forward to ensure justice for them. We have come only to fix responsibility and accountability,” he said before meeting the families.

More than 30 children have died in several villages of Balaghat’s Birsa block over the past two and a half months due to a number of infectious diseases such as measles, malaria, respiratory illness, malnutrition, anaemia, and dehydration.

Balaghat Collector Kumar Satyam told The Hindu that even though Chief Minister Mohan Yadav had sanctioned financial assistance to the families of these children, the deaths cannot be attributed to any single disease.

He said more than 450 children received treatment at government hospitals in the last few months, and that health screenings have been conducted across 40 villages of Birsa block.

Gaining trust

“It’s not just children who have been impacted by these seasonal diseases. Adults have fallen ill too. But because the children in the region have poor immunity, they have been affected the worst,” Mr. Satyam said, adding that the administration’s outreach has been able to gain the trust of locals, who have long been cut off from modern medical infrastructure and relied on faith healing practices. “The situation is now improving and the frequency of cases is reducing.
