World.title: Tokayev, U.S. Special Envoy Sergio Gor discuss Kazakhstan-U.S. strategic partnership
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 12. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with U.S. Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit.

This was reported by the press service of the President of Kazakhstan.

Kassym-Jomart Tokayev noted the dynamic development of the expanded Kazakh-American strategic partnership and emphasized the importance of further strengthening cooperation.

“I am currently preparing to participate in the G20 Summit in Miami. I think this will also be a good opportunity to discuss issues on the bilateral agenda. We prefer not beautiful words, but concrete action and practical steps to advance our mutual cooperation,” the President of Kazakhstan said.

In turn, Sergio Gor noted that, thanks to close and trusting contacts between the leaders of Kazakhstan and the United States, bilateral relations have reached an unprecedentedly high level.

“Today, trade and economic ties and cooperation between our countries are developing actively. Our President attaches great importance to strengthening the partnership with Kazakhstan and Central Asia,” the Special Envoy said.

The meeting also addressed important areas of joint work, particularly artificial intelligence and digitalization.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the sides reaffirmed their commitment to further expanding their multifaceted partnership and giving additional impetus to mutually beneficial cooperation.

The official website of the President of Kazakhstan had previously also reported on Tokayev’s meetings with Sergio Gor and the development of the expanded Kazakh-American strategic partnership.

World.title: Construction of Zar village in Kalbajar nears completion - Special Representative of President
World.content:
KALBAJAR, Azerbaijan, September 12. Construction work in the village of Zar in the Kalbajar district is nearing completion, and resettlement to the village is expected to begin soon, Trend correspondent reports.

Special Representative of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the Kalbajar district Bashir Hajiyev told journalists about this on the second day of the visit of representatives of the diplomatic corps accredited in Azerbaijan to Karabakh and East Zangezur.

He said that 547 individual houses have already been built in the village.

“Construction work in the village of Zar is already nearing completion. In addition to 547 individual houses, a 100-seat kindergarten and a school for 528 students have been built here. Once construction work is completed, resettlement to the village will also begin soon,” B. Hajiyev said.

The Special Representative noted that following the resettlement, the native residents of Zar village will return to their ancestral lands and live and work there.

World.title: Weekly review of prices of Azeri Light, Dated Brent, and Urals
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 12. Average prices for Azeri Light (CIF), Azeri Light (FOB Ceyhan), Dated Brent, and Urals rose this week (from September 7 through 11).

According to Trend’s calculations based on data from oil market participants, the average price of Azeri Light (CIF) crude, produced at the “Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli” field in Azerbaijan, increased by $11.48, or 11.23%, compared to the previous week, reaching $113.67.

Based on the data, the highest price for this grade of crude oil during the week was $120.02 per barrel, and the lowest was $107.31.

The average FOB price of Azeri Light crude at the Turkish port of Ceyhan was $109.84 per barrel, which is $10.54, or 10.61%, higher than the previous week’s figure. Over the week, the highest price reached $115.55 per barrel, while the lowest was $104.23.

The price of Urals crude rose by $10.31, or 13.59%, compared to the previous week, reaching $86.19 per barrel. Over the week, the highest price was $91.27, and the lowest was $81.60.

Dated Brent crude averaged $113.66 per barrel, up $14.91, or 15.1%, from the previous week. Over the course of the week, the price per barrel ranged from a high of $120.31 to a low of $106.51.

World.title: Veterans call for greater royal commission transparency across 'broken system'
World.content:
It has been two years since the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide handed down its final report, but veterans and advocates say greater transparency and action is needed on the 122 recommendations.

"Momentum has drifted a little bit," veteran and Flinders University professor Ben Wadham told ABC News.

A new campaign has been launched by the university's Open Door Initiative, with the intention of putting the spotlight back on the recommendations.

If you or anyone you know needs help: Lifeline on 13 11 14

Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467

Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636

Headspace on 1800 650 890

ReachOut at au.reachout.com

Professor Wadham is a member of the Defence and Veterans' Service Commission (DVSC), which was established following the royal commission's recommendation 122, to establish a new statutory entity to oversee system reform across defence.

"Government is telling us one thing, but if you try to find the actual information on that, it's very difficult," Professor Wadham said.

"We need a public record by a public department, preferably one with some independents like the DVSC to provide that tracker so that veterans and families know that something is happening, who's responsible for it, what stage it's up to, when it'll be complete and whether it's having the right effects for their experiences."

Professor Ben Wadham, director of Open Door Initiative, said momentum has drifted two years after the the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide. (Supplied: Flinders University)

As part of the campaign, Open Door released a 10-minute documentary on the impact of veteran suicide.

Loss of brother, son life-changing

Among those featured is Navy veteran John Armfield, who served for 20 years as a Royal Australian Navy clearance diver, where he had five operational deployments.

He said he "loved" his career, but shared the painful loss of his brother Andrew, who died by suicide after serving in the air force.

Mr Armfield said he raised the alarm after his brother made an attempt on his life in 2011.

Navy veteran John Armfield implores the government to work through the recommendations. (Supplied: Flinders University)

"Throughout the recovery process I identified failures in his treatment which I raised through the correct and appropriate commands and no-one paid attention to a junior sailor trying to save his brother," he told ABC News.

Mr Armfield said he only learned about an inquiry into the death of his brother 10 years after he died.

His mental health suffered and by 2023 he was medically discharged.

"The system is broken," he said.

"In my case, the chain of command weaponised the military justice system.

"No-one has ever been held accountable. No-one has ever been reprimanded. They've actually been either promoted or put into these positions where they will now investigate cases like mine."

Open Door Initiative researcher Karen Bird was also part of the documentary.

Open Door Initiative researcher Karen Bird lost her veteran son to suicide in June 2017. (Supplied: Flinders University)

Her son Jesse Bird served in Afghanistan and died as a result of suicide in June 2017.

"I want to know where all the recommendations are up to other than 'underway' or 'in progress' because what does that mean?" she said.

Government says progress is being made

Minister for Veterans' Affairs and Defence Personnel Matt Keogh told ABC News that "a quarter of the recommendations" had been implemented by the end of last year.

"We're on track to implement two thirds of them by the end of this year," he said.

Mr Keogh referenced the establishment of the new Veteran and Family Wellbeing Agency on July 1 and the December 2025 announcement of an independent inquiry into military sexual violence within the Australian Defence Force.

"Just this week, on the second anniversary of the royal commission's final report, we've announced that we've upgraded our response to 15 of the recommendations … agreeing to do even more work than was in our initial response," he said.

"I think we've provided regular updates on where we're going and the things that we've been implementing as well as, of course, working with the Defence and Veterans' Service Commission on its inquiry so that its report provides that overall scrutiny and transparency."

Federal Veterans Affairs and Defence Personnel Minister Matt Keogh said two thirds of recommendations will be implemented by the end of this year. (ABC News)

In July, RSL Australia called on government to scrap the veterans' allied healthcare 'cap'.

From July next year, there will be a $5,000 threshold for allied healthcare spending for veterans, with treatment above that amount to require demonstrated clinical need.

"A cap should not be the solution," Mr Armfield said.

"Why is this problem happening in the first place? Please Minister, you're responsible for the service personnel. Stop them becoming medically retired veterans."

World.title: Crime lessons Sydney could learn from former murder capital of Europe
World.content:
Young people contracted by gangs to commit crimes "shouldn't be punished" for being "exploited", a justice reform advocate says.

It comes after the Minns government on Monday announced young people could face adult penalties if convicted of organised crime violence.

Boosted powers to target Sydney's gangsters, but police face a new problem They are the extraordinary powers the premier has promised to expand in a bid to combat gangland violence, but they face a major test in this era of organised crime.

The raft of proposed measures includes a maximum sentence of life imprisonment under new aggravated offences for conspiracy and attempted murder.

NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said at the time some children were being contracted by underworld figures on the dark web "for a very small amount of money" and had a disregard for the consequences of their actions.

Last week university student Marco Tapia and 40-year-old Joshua Macdonald were shot in what NSW Police suspect to be "mistaken identity" shootings.

Joshua Macdonald (left) and Marco Tapia were both killed in separate shootings last week. (Supplied)

At a press conference last week, NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley described this "new model" as a case of "whack-a-mole".

"Every time somebody is removed from the streets another person is there, a vulnerable person is there, a young person is there," she said.

Within the last 12 months, Taskforce Falcon, which was set up to combat organised crime violence, had arrested more than 800 perpetrators, including young people.

'Prison itself causes harm'

Ms Sotiri says gangs contracting young people to commit crimes should be considered a form of "child abuse". (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

Justice Reform Initiative (JRI) executive director Mindy Sotiri said "we shouldn't be punishing children because adults are exploiting them".

"If children are being exploited by adult gang members, that's child abuse, that's child exploitation," she said.

"The way to respond to children's involvement in this sort of activity is not by further criminalising children or further pushing them deeper into a system which is absolutely only going to lead to them engaging in more serious reoffending.

"We cannot hold children to the same standards that we hold [as] adults because they are not able to be criminally responsible in the same ways."

She said "prison itself causes harm" by exacerbating common disadvantage among children, which increases reoffending chances.

"The current situation in Australia is that 85 per cent of children who go to prison return within 12 months," Ms Sotiri said.

The justice reform advocate says sending youths to prison does not address why they may have offended. (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

She said there were approximately 208 children in NSW prisons, of which "the majority are not sentenced" and "haven't actually been found guilty of anything".

"Most people are released without any sort of order," Ms Sotiri said.

She said the reasons why young people turned to crime needed to be addressed.

Youth Justice NSW executive director Kelly-Anne Stewart said while it was important there were consequences for actions, the service recognised some of the "most vulnerable" young people can be involved.

"School disengagement and educational exclusion; out-of-home care, homelessness and housing instability; disability, mental health, drug and alcohol issues, family dysfunction, poverty and intergenerational trauma all figure large in the lives of young people with Youth Justice," Ms Stewart said.

"In Youth Justice we work with a commitment to do everything we can to support the young people we are engaging with reach their full potential without further offending, which in turn makes our communities safer."

International success stories

In June, the JRI brought international experts to Australia who oversaw "absolutely transformative shifts" in youth justice in their respective countries.

They gave evidence of successful approaches to the NSW Parliamentary Select Committee on Youth Justice, and a Federal Senate Inquiry into Australia's youth justice and incarceration system.

Scotland, UK Read more Read more Scotland's Glasgow was formerly known as the murder capital of Europe, with significant youth crime and gang issues. Ms Sotiri said there were now no children in Scottish prisons since 2024. She said the country's legislation described predatory adults using children for criminal activities as "child abuse". Community Justice Scotland chief executive, Karyn McCluskey, told the NSW select committee the youth crime turnaround was "a product of decades of layered, interconnected policy and cross-party support". She said investment in a child's early life, a national child wellbeing framework and a welfare-based children's hearing system rather than traditional court helped address the situation. Scotland also implemented secure care facilities, which are different to prisons. Children up to 18 years of age who present a risk to themselves or others are housed in a safe environment where they can continue schooling and receive support. They are often referred to one of the four independent charities by the Children's Hearings System or the Criminal Justice System. Ms Sotiri said the country adopted a public health approach. Spain, EU Read more Read more In Spain, non-government organisation Fundación Diagrama, which began in 1991, runs about 70 per cent of the country's youth justice facilities. The 35 custodial centres accept people aged 14 to 23 who are remanded or sentenced to custody. Ms Sotiri said it had reduced recidivism rates to around 15 per cent, compared to around 85 per cent historically. Professionals including psychologists, psychiatrists, social workers, occupational therapists and reintegration workers support the youths. The team's main goal is to promote and develop resources aimed at prevention treatment and integration. "We don't run prisons; we run re-educational centres, and it's fundamentally very different from what you would be experiencing in Australia," Fundación Diagrama CEO David McGuire told the NSW select committee. Hawaii, US Read more Read more Ms Sotiri said Hawaii had embraced an Indigenous-led trauma-informed diversion remodel and closed 80 per cent of their detention centres. She said as of 2022, there were 82 per cent fewer children in prison, with no girls incarcerated. That was for the first time since 1961, with overall crime rates reducing by 86 per cent. Kawailoa Youth and Family Wellness Centre youth facility administrator, Matelina Aulava, told the select committee that over decades, the country had implemented legislative and administrative changes. They were aimed at reducing "reliance on youth detention and improving outcomes for young people". "These reforms included expanding diversion options, strengthening community-based services, and introducing trauma-informed and family-centred approaches," she said. New York, US Read more Read more The founder of Youth Correctional Leaders for Justice, an association of 75 juvenile justice correctional leaders in the US, told the NSW select committee the country had "made a lot of mistakes" along the way to reducing youth crime rates. Vincent Schiraldi said during the 80s and especially the 90s, there was appetite to "lock kids up", with some 'adult crime, adult time' laws being implemented. To combat large numbers of incarcerated youths, studies were conducted with kids who engaged in crime and programs were developed to address underlying issues. The Close To Home Act placed emphasis on best practice, prioritising investment in neighbourhood resources where young people live. "Since the year 2000, there's been a 75 per cent reduction nationwide in the number of young people in juvenile facilities," Mr Schiraldi said.

Proactive approaches in NSW

The JRI submitted more than 50 examples of Australian intervention and early prevention programs to the NSW select committee.

But Ms Sotiri said some were not funded enough to cause systemic reductions in crime and imprisonment.

Ms Stewart said the government had committed $146.3 million in the last budget towards early intervention and diversion programs like Youth on Track and NSW's Safe Aboriginal Youth Program, to help guide young people at risk away from crime.

"Many of these intervention initiatives are being co-designed with local communities to ensure they meet local needs, because we understand that there is no one-size-fits-all solution," she said.

"Youth Justice continues to monitor and share information with other youth justice jurisdictions, both in Australia and internationally and we work closely with them to implement new initiatives and programs which may be suitable."

Ms Catley says police are "pulling its weight". (ABC News)

Ms Catley said last Thursday NSW Police was "pulling its weight" working with young people to keep them out of the justice system and recognised the Police Youth Command's involvement in south-west Sydney.

She also mentioned POLEN, where police work with Polynesian communities and involve influential elders to talk about respect and the "path of destruction" crime can cause.

"Quite frankly, we need to work together as a community to really identify when these kids are starting to go off the rails and also then having an opportunity for them to have some mentors, to have some opportunity," she said.

World.title: Wallaroos scare England but fail 'mission impossible'
World.content:
Australia's rugby women have given England's world champions a run for their money by leading sensationally at half-time, but the Wallaroos' dream of downing the Red Roses crumbled as they ended up losing 48-15 in Salford.

The English were stunned in the first 40 minutes of their WXV Global Series opener on Saturday (Sunday AEST) as the Australians went in to the break with a 10-5 lead but any hopes of handing the hosts their first defeat after 38 straight victories was buried after the break.

The John Mitchell-coached world champs, initially rusty in their first outing since being crowned European grand slam champions in May and struggling to adapt to the new smaller size 4.5 ball being trialled, ran in eight tries in total as their set-piece finally began to tick over to their normal high efficiency.

But Australia could be proud of their efforts, deserving their half-time lead as they controlled the breakdown and defended stoically even after being reduced to 14 for 10 minutes in the first period when halfback Samantha Wood was sin-binned for a deliberate knock-on.

Still, they went in to the break with the lead thanks to barnstorming prop Faliki Pohiva rumbling her way over for a try after Michaela Leonard's stolen lineout on England's five-metre line, but the world champions were hardly inconvenienced, despite their initial rustiness.

"It is an absolute joke if you are worried about being down 10-5," said Mitchell afterwards and the response of his team demonstrated they were surely never really concerned.

"More important is how we worked our way back into it."

In front of a crowd of 9,251, England did indeed begin to turn it on, with May Campbell, captain Meg Jones, Bryony Field, Mia Venner and Sadia Kabeya all crossing for tries in a 20-minute spell to add to player-of-the-match Abi Burton's first-half score.

Lucy Packer and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald also then went over, with Asoiva Karpani scoring a second for the Wallaroos late on in a show of defiance amid the hammering.

Loading Instagram content

Wallaroos skipper Siokapesi Palu Sekona was proud of her "super-stoked" side's efforts.

"Unfortunately, I don't think that score is a reflection of the game we produced," she said.

"I know that we didn't finish the way we wanted to but we're going to take a lot of positives.

"That's the first time England have trailed at half-time since 2019, I believe, and so we'll take a lot of confidence.

"Against a world-class team like that we can actually give it, so for us it's about stringing it for a full 80-minute game now."

The Wallaroos travel to Marseille for their next assignment against France next weekend.

Flanker Lily Bone failed a HIA midway through the first half while Palu Sekona (knee) and debutant Amelia Whitaker will both be monitored after suffering knocks.

Meanwhile, Scotland were swept aside 64-26 in Edinburgh as Canada warmed up in style for their World Cup final rematch against England in Exeter next weekend.

AAP

World.title: No smooth ride for Labor to a fourth term in Victoria
World.content:
When Ben Carroll publicly guaranteed he would not overthrow Jacinta Allan at an ill-fated press conference, one Labor figure solemnly told him he would become the next Josh Frydenberg.

Carroll would lose his formerly safe seat because of an unpopular leader, they warned.

Back in 2022, Frydenberg, having remained loyal to then-prime minister Scott Morrison while his popularity tanked, went on to lose his prized federal seat as deputy Liberal leader.

Carroll ultimately didn't leave it to chance.

The former deputy premier rolled his leader in July and declared repeatedly this was a new government with a new direction.

Instead, it was the state One Nation leader Warren Pickering's redemption arc that this week took the state into new territory ahead of the state election in November.

Loading...

Pickering admitted past drug use and repeated drink driving charges.

Victorian politics, though, has the disposition of a merry-go-round and the same problems are still coming around for the new premier: crime is bad (this week, insurance data shows it).

Potholes are bad (the auditor-general's report this week shows that).

Former VicRoads staff blame privatisation for state's crumbling roads The Victorian Auditor-General's Office has labelled almost half the state's roads "poor or very poor". Ahead of the Victorian election, parties have made major roadworks pledges to win voters.

The government is subject to the whims of the upper house, which this week sunk Labor's promised right for Victorians to work from home.

And if it didn't, the state of Victoria was likely to have found itself before the High Court again.

Even with a royal commission and strengthened anti-corruption watchdog, integrity standards can always get worse (as with the revelations Labor had in 2025 introduced a clandestine tax on public transport fares, now due to be abolished).

After 12 years, the government is carrying the weight of repeated scandals — alleged corruption on taxpayer-funded construction projects, in particular — and a worsening debt position.

A human story

This week, former Liberal and now crossbench MP Moira Deeming reappeared.

Moira Deeming will run as a Family First candidate in the coming state election. (ABC News: Leanne Wong)

She was removed as the Liberal Party candidate for the Western Metro Region in July, having refused to apologise to her party room colleague Matthew Guy after accusing him of putting her in a headlock at a community function.

Mrs Deeming wants to go around again with Family First after being excommunicated by the Liberals.

"Nice for Moira," Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said on Thursday.

Can the Liberals topple Victoria's government? There are fewer than 100 days until the Victorian state election. How might the opposition win power?

This week, though, Victorian politics was treated to a rare thing: a human story.

One Nation leader Warren Pickering, who is gunning for Labor's seat of Pakenham on Melbourne's outer-southeastern fringe, broadly confirmed reporting in The Australian that he had used drugs (speed, ecstasy and marijuana) in his 20s.

This was a day after federal leader Pauline Hanson had declared the claims were false.

In Melbourne, Pickering's remarkable press conference sparked another seasonal question for MPs door-stopped at parliament: "Have you ever tried drugs?"

The answers from Victorian pollies were much the same as the last time as the last time the press pack asked.

"I did smoke pot a couple of times in my younger years" was intermixed with "no, I'm very boring".

Loading...

Only the state's two Legalise Cannabis MPs were notable exceptions.

The contrast with Pickering was clear.

MPs were unwittingly playing into One Nation's successful spinning of the former soldier's colourful backstory: that the major parties are made up of dull and inauthentic career politicians.

"One Nation do not grow our candidates in Petri dishes like Labor and the Liberal Party," said One Nation's recently anointed national director, James Ashby.

Minutes earlier, Hanson's right-hand man had ejected ABC and Guardian journalists from the press conference.

Loading

Pickering agreed he'd repeatedly lost his licence for drink driving.

But he rejected claims he had abused ice in the family home back in the day, as alleged by his estranged former partner.

"She's got a vendetta against Warren and has for many years," Pickering's stepson told reporters.

Effectively, a woman was trying to tear the man down. It played perfectly to One Nation's base.

Premier avoids personal attacks

Under the old rules, political careers were killed off for much less.

Now, Labor insiders figure their best approach is not to give Pickering's comeback story any more oxygen.

They doubt he could parlay this into building broader appeal at the state election in two months, with consistent polls tipping One Nation to be big disruptors.

The premier's own seat of Niddrie, which Carroll holds with a 6.7 per cent margin, is still at risk.

Rather than focus on the personal, Carroll was keen to emphasise he was more worried about Pickering's policies and One Nation's language on multiculturalism and migration.

"I'm always someone that's believed in second chances," Carroll said.

But, he added: "Let's look at their policies."

Labor believes it maybe, kind of, has a pathway to another go on the carousel for a fourth ride on November 28.

This week suggests it won't be a smooth ride to get there.

World.title: NDIS slashes Brisbane woman's physical therapy hours, citing 'value for money'
World.content:
April Coulson went to bed one night as an active, independent teenager and woke up unable to move from the armpits down.

A bleed on her spinal cord had left her paralysed.

"It was pretty terrifying," she says of that day seven years ago. "My strength and my ability to even sit up was completely gone."

April before her life changed forever when she woke up unable to move from the armpits down. (Supplied: April Coulson)

It would take two years before doctors were able to provide some answers into why the bleed occurred.

Scans revealed rare blood vessel malformations in other parts of her body, leading doctors to suspect a similar malformation had bled onto her spinal cord.

April, then 19, spent six months in hospital before returning to her parents' Brisbane home.

April Coulson's mother, Ann-Louise, says she was not sure if her daughter was going to make it. (Supplied: April Coulson)

"I was extremely dependent," she says of those early days after leaving hospital in a wheelchair.

" When I first came home, I was still struggling to get up out of bed. I couldn't transfer. I could barely hold myself up in the chair for more than an hour at a time. "

She had to be strapped into the wheelchair.

Support workers funded through the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) helped her to shower, get dressed, and eat — daily activities she could no longer perform herself.

"I had to get carried in and out of bed, into a shower chair," April says.

April spent six months in hospital. (Supplied: April Coulson)

The NDIS also funded her wheelchair, a ramp into the bottom floor of her family home, and daily intensive therapy sessions, including exercise physiology, physiotherapy, and occupational therapy.

"In the very early stages, it was sometimes twice a day," she says.

"It was amazing. One of the whole reasons that I am where I am today was the support I was receiving."

Pressure sores post-injury

In the first 18 months of being home, April says she developed three pressure sores, requiring her to "lie down on my side for a couple of weeks at a time".

April Coulson's mum Ann-Louise pushing her daughter in her wheelchair at their Brisbane home. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

"Pressure sores are something that can leave someone with a spinal cord injury in a hospital bed for six months," she says.

"Once I got into that rhythm of continuous rehab, I've never had a pressure sore since."

With more therapy, April built her strength to the point she no longer had to be strapped into her wheelchair, and she was able to start driving a modified car.

Eventually, she transitioned into full-time employment and came off the disability support pension.

April Coulson was a healthy and active teenager until 2019 when she suffered a bleed into her spinal cord. Through rehabilitation, she's working full-time. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

She has also reduced her support worker hours to just four hours a week to help with housework.

But acting against expert advice, the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) — the body responsible for the NDIS — has recently slashed her therapy hours by two-thirds, suggesting unqualified support workers and family members can fill the void.

Her physical therapy hours have plummeted from six to two hours a week.

A request for funding to pay for a $5,000 replacement ramp, which has already been rebuilt to allow April to access the house, was also denied.

In a written internal review decision, an NDIA public servant ruled the extra therapy hours, and replacement ramp were not "value for money".

April Coulson using the ramp at her family's home in Brisbane. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

"It is expected the disability support workers have appropriate qualifications and training to complete the role they have been employed to complete and assist you in implement (sic) exercise routine," the delegate wrote.

April says using support workers would be unsafe.

"I'm already extremely injury prone with severe osteoporosis and other complications," she says.

"To put myself in the risk of someone who isn't qualified is just a danger to me."

April says she also does not have the specialised equipment at home required for her rehabilitation sessions.

April Coulson at home with her mum, Ann-Louise. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

She says her therapists frequently use hoists and slings in her treatment, allowing her to get into an upright position.

"They'll have two qualified exercise physiologists on you at all times because there's such a risk for injury," April says.

"To try to replicate that at your home, you would need two support workers with … equipment that costs over $30,000 for a full hoist or sling. It just doesn't make sense.

"The really disheartening thing is I've had doctors, exercise physiologists, occupational therapists, and physiotherapists, all explain and write to the NDIA justifying why it's not safe.

"If they would even just have a conversation or even read the plethora of documents and reports that we provide to them, they would probably take a more reasonable approach."

April says the slashing of her therapy hours this year has meant losing some of the independence she's regained through her rehabilitation post injury.

So much so, she's worried she'll have to give up full-time work.

"I've experienced significant increase in my pain, my tightness, my fatigue, a much greater reliance on my parents, my sister, to help care for me," April says, when asked about the loss of physical therapy hours.

Dr Martin Laverty, one of the original architects of the National Disability Insurance Scheme. (ABC news: Ian Cutmore)

NDIS architect worried about cuts

Dr Martin Laverty, one of the original architects of the NDIS, says he's very concerned by the cuts to participant plans being made against the evidence of health professionals.

"There's something very wrong with the way in which our assessment for people with disabilities is currently operating," he says.

NDIS 'failing' some disabled Australians The National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) last month determined Lucy Muggeridge's one-on-one care at home wasn't "value for money".

"The National Disability Insurance Agency is pulling back on therapeutics, it's pulling back on active overnight support, it's changing the way in which people can access the community.

"If a health professional is providing a recommendation that a therapy is so important to April, and thousands like her, we should be funding those supports under the NDIS because that's why the scheme was set up in the first place."

Dr Laverty, the CEO of disability service provider Aruma, says the federal government plans to introduce a new support needs NDIS assessment tool in the next 18 months.

"The question is how do we ensure that between now and the replacement that's on the way we keep people safe?" he says.

"The system in place today is no longer fit for purpose. It's producing outcomes that mean people like April are missing out on the essential therapy and equipment aids that would help them live a normal, everyday life."

Changes needed to keep scheme 'sustainable'

Dr Laverty has been one of the biggest supporters of the Albanese Government's recent NDIS changes, to ensure the scheme "is sustainable in the years ahead".

"But while ever it continues to put this pressure on April, her family, and thousands like her, it means the NDIS is not working the way we need it to," he says.

The NDIS Amendment (Securing the NDIS for Future Generations) Bill has been criticised as rushed and dangerous. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

In a statement, the NDIA did not comment on April's case.

But it said it reviewed "all submitted evidence, including from allied health professionals, when making decisions on an individuals (sic) funding allocation".

Closure of AEIOU centres impacting children with autism a month on The nationwide closure of specialist centres has put a spotlight on the adequacy of National Disability Insurance Scheme funding for children with "severe, profound, lifelong" autism.

"While every request is considered, some requests may not be approved, as we are required to make decisions as to what is reasonable and necessary," a spokeswoman said.

April's mum Ann-Louise Coulson says she is "incredibly proud" of her daughter's determination in dealing with her disability.

"The first week, we weren't even sure she was going to make it," Ann-Louise says.

"It was a very tough time."

Ann-Louise Coulson says she's proud of her daughter, April, and how she has dealt with her disability. (ABC news: Mark Leonardi)

Ann-Louise says April finished her university degree in hospital and completed her master's after coming home while working hard at her rehabilitation.

She says the family is grateful for the NDIS in helping April return "to be an independent and productive member of society".

But she is worried April is deteriorating with the reduction in therapy hours.

"It's like sitting in an economy class airline seat," Ann-Louise says. That's what it's like all day long and her body just gets so tight."

Without physical therapy, April seizes up, her spasticity gets "a bit out of control," her mother says.

April Coulson, 26, in the backyard of her parents' Brisbane home. (ABC news: Janelle Miles)

"She's just worked so hard. She works full-time and sometimes I think if she quit her job tomorrow and went back on the disability pension a lot more things would open up to her and that doesn't seem fair," she says.

"They're not rewarding her initiative and her discipline."

April is appealing the cuts to her plan at the Administrative Review Tribunal.

World.title: Tropical island needs caretakers to live in barely inhabited 'paradise'
World.content:
Living on a remote island with full responsibility for your own needs instead of relying on society is "beautiful" for Martin Papay, even though it takes him months to produce the coconuts, pineapples and honey he needs to prepare a piña colada.

He has always sought remoteness and found it in a tree house lifestyle on Middle Percy Island 15 years ago.

Visitors to Middle Percy often gather around the famous A-frame. (Supplied: Ralph Ender)

The almost 20-square-kilometre tropical paradise, 125 kilometres south-east of Mackay in North Queensland, has a population of two.

But there is room for numbers to increase five-fold, with the group that manages the island seeking more live-in volunteer caretakers to maintain infrastructure and promote conservation.

Ultimate sea change

Ralph Ender moved to Middle Percy at the beginning of the year, first restoring his new home — a wooden octagonal structure that had been untouched for five years.

On a regular morning he wakes with the sun, then cleans up after the goats that sleep on the washing machine under the house.

He said it was then onto tasks including pumping rainwater, watering the garden, tending to the chooks and bottling honey from the island's bees.

Goats were introduced to the island in the 1870s. (Supplied: Ralph Enders)

During the morning tasks, the visitors usually arrive — in the dry season.

There is no regular transport between Middle Percy and the mainland, but between about May and October it is frequented by yachties for whom the island is a bucket-list destination.

When Mr Ender arrived, Mr Papay was away from the island, so he went about four months without seeing a soul.

When dozens of boats started arriving each day, the conversation with outsiders was welcome.

"You get used to that feeling of being alone, which I like," he said.

"[When the boat season starts] I can't scream when I want or run around naked … it would be to their amusement though.

"[But] human interaction is one of the things I miss the most."

Middle Percy islanders largely survive on things they can grow or catch on the island. (Supplied: Ralph Enders)

Not for the faint of heart

Most of Middle Percy Island is declared national park.

The remaining 316 hectares are separated into the Percy Island Conservation Park, which is looked after by the Percy Island Conservation Group Inc, of which resident volunteers are members.

The sparsely populated island has a rich history. (Supplied: Kate Joy)

Director Cathryn Radclyffe said the group was searching for "suitably skilled" volunteers who can commit to living on the island for at least a year.

"Island residents are essential to maintain island infrastructure, gardens, apiary and grazing animal levels, as well as maintaining the traditions of hospitality for crew of visiting vessels," she said.

Cottage industries on the island include tanning skins and beeswax products sold in the island's produce stand, with revenue going back into maintenance.

Accommodation on the island is free, but volunteers need to be able to support themselves.

Beeswax products are sold to visitors to the island. (Supplied: Ralph Enders)

Mr Papay said it was a lot of work to live self-sufficiently, requiring skills in cooking, carpentry, animal husbandry and horticulture.

"Yesterday was goat hunting," he said.

"I slept in the ute at the top of the island … it was a four-hour process to get three goats.

"You carry them on your back, back to the ute … then it's chopping the goats up, processing them … and putting them in the freezer.

"Tomorrow, is taking off honey from the hives."

Despite the physical nature of the work, Mr Papay said the rewards were worth it.

"It feels like a strength every time you get things like that done which provides for your future needs," he said.

"It's not work, it's love, it's passion, doing the things you need to do to survive."

For a period, Ralph and his dog Amigo lived alone on Middle Percy together. (Supplied: Ralph Ender)

But aside from the physically demanding tasks, living remotely can take an emotional toll.

For Mr Ender, who enjoys an afternoon lounging on the verandah enjoying "million-dollar views" of the Pine Islets after a hearty lunch of goat stew, the island lifestyle is not all hammock lounging and beach walks.

He said he still struggled to talk about the passing of his dog, Amigo, who died in his arms while the pair was alone on the island.

"There's lots of dramas," he said.

"You've got to be capable of dealing with those emotions on your own.

"It's not easy."

World.title: More F1 pain for Piastri after 'pretty shocking' qualifying in Spain
World.content:
Oscar Piastri's increasingly underwhelming Formula 1 season has taken another bad turn in Madrid with a "pretty shocking" qualifying lap at the Spanish Grand Prix.

The Australian's hugely disappointing seventh-place finish in qualifying on the new Madring street circuit came as teammate Lando Norris delivered a pole-grabbing lap hailed by McLaren's team boss as a "masterpiece".

The world champion produced his dazzling lap in the sunshine seemingly from nowhere, clocking a 1 minute 31.82 seconds circuit to edge Mercedes's championship leader Kimi Antonelli by just 0.011 of a second, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen third and Ferrari's ‌Lewis Hamilton fourth.

But while a "shocked" Norris was hailing what he called "probably one of the best laps I've done", it was back to the drawing board for Piastri, who was disappointed to finish in 1:32.294 — remarkably, nearly half a second behind his teammate.

"The first lap wasn't too bad but the second lap was pretty shocking. Disappointing," said the 25-year-old, who could find it difficult to make much headway from seventh on Sunday on an unforgiving, tight circuit where, he admitted, overtaking "will be difficult".

He is keeping up a brave face, though, still talking up how he hopes to earn a victory somewhere this year to set himself up for a realistic crack at the title in 2027.

Piastri has not won a race since the Dutch Grand Prix now over a year ago when he was leading the 2025 championship, but he is adamant his dramatic fall-off was not a factor in his disappointing 2026 campaign.

"Of course, I would love to win a race ‌or two this year, ‌or more if I can. But for me, honestly, the biggest thing, the end goal is to ​try and win championships," he said.

"And if I can't do that this year, then I want to make sure I'm as best prepared as I can for next year."

For the moment, though, that still seems a long way off as his smooth driving style just doesn't seem to be suited to the vast changes to the 2026 F1 cars.

F1 debuts new track with Monumental corner Formula 1 debuts a new circuit to its calendar, and despite no grand prix raced yet, the Madring already boasts a corner that is poised to become an iconic scene in motorsport.

"It's all to do with ‌technically driving the car. There's nothing to do with a hangover from last year … it's very much a technical thing," he explained.

"It's not like I'm slow, feeling sorry for myself or thinking about last year. It's just that a few of the weekends I've had to drive the car in a different way that just hasn't really worked for me.

"The biggest thing this year has been the cars are very different to drive, both from a power unit point of view but also the car itself is fundamentally very ​different and the tyres also.

"You've got to drive it ​very differently and I would say it's not ⁠necessarily in the way that I would choose to drive a race car. So there's just been some struggles getting ​to grips with that."

Meanwhile, though, Norris does seem to be getting to grips with it, producing "one of those laps where everything pretty much worked perfectly".

The champion's 19th career pole and third of the season was hailed by McLaren team boss Andrea Stella as a "masterpiece", which could only have been bettered if he had not made a mistake at the very last corner that possibly cost him 0.3 of a second.

Norris had been only sixth after the first run in the third qualifying session but he diced daringly with the wall during the breathtaking final lap, and declared over the radio at the end: "Oh, what a lap, gorgeous … oh, that might be my best one."

AAP/Reuters

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix from 9pm AEST on Sunday, September 13.

World.title: Anthropic boss calls for AI slowdown, Altman and Musk agree
World.content:
Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei has called on AI firms to slow down the development of the powerful technology, amid mounting worries over the risks of "super-intelligent" computer systems.

His comments came a few days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement.

OpenAI boss Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns xAI, quickly chimed in to say they agreed with Mr Amodei's assessment, as pressure builds for improved oversight.

"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Mr Amodei wrote in a post on his personal website.

"Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.

"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way.

" But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence. "

Mr Amodei's statement echoed another call by Anthropic in early June to slow or suspend development.

Then in late July, Mr Altman said developers might need to voluntarily tap the brakes to give society a chance to catch up.

Sam Altman says OpenAI would commit to one of Mr Amodei's proposals while Elon Musk also expressed support. (Reuters)

More than 1,000 employees at cutting-edge AI companies including Mr Amodei signed a petition calling on the US government to help "deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development".

OpenAI had revealed during testing, AI models broke out of their confined environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site developers use to store and share code.

In that incident and others, the blame was placed on AI agents, which are software programs that can carry out tasks without constant supervision by humans.

"Dario is right," Mr Musk wrote on X, as Mr Altman said: "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier."

'Gambling with our lives'

Earlier this week, Mr Coxon, 27, sounded the alarm after spending the past three years pre-training AI models, first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach.

Anthropic researcher says AI 'could kill us all' A researcher for AI developer Anthropic has quit the company and is one of a growing number of AI experts to call on the industry to slow down.

Pre-training is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data.

"Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Mr Coxon said.

"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."

Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI's capabilities exceed human intelligence.

'Taking over the entire internet'

Mr Amodei cautioned that the Hugging Face incident should not be dismissed as a one-off.

"A swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack and that were unrelated to the task at hand," he said.

" Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in six to 12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet. "

Mr Amodei said his company would grant "employee-like access" to a team of "third-party evaluators" who would verify adherence to safety practices, and he called on all companies to follow his lead.

Mr Altman said he would commit to similar outside oversight, adding he would have "more to share soon".

Mr Amodei also suggested companies work together to establish common safety standards, and said he supported some kind of government cooperation on the issue.

In early August, the US government put in place a voluntary security review process for advanced AI models before their release, but the parameters of that program remain unclear.

Industry observers say they are not sure how effective it would be, as US President Donald Trump's administration has favoured a light-touch, deregulatory approach to most industries, including tech.

AFP

World.title: Warner Bros axed this Looney Tunes movie. But fans refused to accept defeat
World.content:
The story of how Coyote vs Acme came back from the dead is crazier than a Looney Tunes cartoon.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Will Forte could not have been prouder of Coyote vs Acme. The live-action animation hybrid, in which a disgruntled Wile E. Coyote and his lawyer (played by Forte) face off against John Cena in a chaotic courtroom battle, was one of the most entertaining – and heartwarming – projects he’d worked on. His wife, after watching it for the first time, even told him it was hands-down the best thing he’d ever done. So it’s safe to say that its inexplicable axing in 2023 sent Forte into a head-spin. Will Forte (right) couldn’t have loved Coyote vs Acme more. Suffice to say, its cancellation floored him. “This was a movie that I wanted so badly to share with my kids, but [I realised] I was never going to get to. It was confusing, frustrating and heartbreaking. I was just pissed,” said the American actor and comedian, who is known for his stint on Saturday Night Live and, more recently, Tina Fey’s The Four Seasons. Coyote vs Acme, Dave Green’s absurd comedy in the vein of Who Framed Roger Rabbit, was ready to hit screens when it was suddenly shelved by Warner Bros in November 2023. Despite ongoing praise from its producers, overwhelmingly positive test screenings and a $US70 million budget, the studio decided it would be better off as a $US30 million tax write-off. Its fate mirrored that of Batgirl and Scoob! Holiday Haunt, both of which were cancelled by Warner Bros the year prior. Coyote vs Acme has an impressive cast, including John Cena and several iconic Looney Tunes characters. But that didn’t stop it from being axed. “With the relaunch of Warner Bros Pictures Animation in June, the studio has shifted its global strategy to focus on theatrical releases,” a WB Motion Picture Group spokesperson told The Hollywood Reporter in 2023. “With this new direction, we have made the difficult decision not to move forward with Coyote vs Acme. We have tremendous respect for the filmmakers, casts and crew, and are grateful for their contributions to the film.”



Loading The decision was driven by a desire to offset corporate losses, a strategy spearheaded by the studio’s new head, David Zaslav. But for those who worked on the film, as well as the Looney Tunes fans feverishly anticipating its release, it was a punch to the gut. “We heard that Warner Bros was going to shelve it, but they still said we could come see the movie that next Tuesday. So, for the five or six days before that screening, I thought, ‘This is probably going to suck. If they’re going to shelve it, it can’t be good. Maybe these producers are just too deep in it to see that’. Then I showed up [to the screening] and I just loved it with all my heart. I was so proud of it, which was heartbreaking. I got so mad for a long time,” Forte says. Loading The film’s cancellation was especially disappointing given how broad he expected its appeal to be. Based on a 1990 New Yorker article by Ian Frazier, Coyote vs Acme tells Wile E. Coyote’s story. Fed up by the countless Acme products that have malfunctioned – costing him his lifelong dream of capturing the Road Runner – he decides to sue the major corporation with the help of Kevin Avery (Forte), a down-and-out billboard lawyer. This results in the unlikely pair going head-to-head with Acme’s chief executive, Foghorn Leghorn, as well as his ruthless lawyer Buddy Crane (Cena). For Looney Tunes fans, it delivers a healthy dose of nostalgia, reconnecting audiences with “old buddies”. Forte himself says the cartoons helped to form his comedic mind from a young age, subconsciously inspiring him to weave some of its madcap absurdity into his own comedy. That said, you don’t need to be a fan to enjoy this film. It has “a bit of everything”, Forte says, from legal drama to slapstick comedy. Loading



“It’s just this weird thing of: The movie’s testing really well, and it’s your IP [intellectual property]. If you’re not going to take a chance on that, what are you going to take a chance on?” Beyond the upset and disappointment, however, lay a painfully ironic parallel. Coyote vs Acme is largely Wile E. Coyote’s story. It’s an underdog tale, or as Forte puts it, a tale about “the little guy against the big corporation”. Everyone, from the cast and crew to the fans, immediately noticed the connection between Coyote’s journey and the film itself. If anything, it just made the movie even more resonant, Forte says, not only to himself but to every other Looney Tunes lover. Related Article Cartoons ‘That’s not all, folks!’ The voice actor taking Looney Tunes back to its roots As soon as the film was scrapped, fans and industry heads went to battle on social media, launching relentless campaigns in a bid to pressure Warner Bros into selling the project to another studio. “Disappointed, and somewhat mystified by the Coyote vs Acme news,” the film’s composer Steven Price wrote on X. “Dave Green made (and completed) an excellent movie, and a lot of people – not least the brilliant musicians and colleagues who worked with me on the score – poured their hearts into it … that’s (f---) all folks!” Writer-director BenDavid Grabinski, who received an off-screen additional literary credit for the film, lamented Warner Bros’ decision, writing on X that Coyote vs Acme was “the best of its kind” since Who Framed Roger Rabbit. “The leads are super likable. It’s beautifully shot. The animation is great. The ending makes everyone f---ing cry,” he wrote. “I thought the goal of this business was to make hit movies?”



View post on X Looney Tunes fans even released an online petition urging Warner Bros to release Coyote vs Acme, attracting 23,483 supporters. It was in this response that Forte discovered a silver lining. “It was a good lesson in the power of people,” he says. “Fans of the movie did not give up. They had hope when I didn’t.” It was their “constant noise-making”, he says, that eventually caught the attention of another studio: Ketchup Entertainment. In late March 2025, Ketchup – a far smaller studio than Warner Bros, but one that has released hits such as Michael Mann’s Ferrari (2023) – acquired the rights to Coyote vs Acme in a deal reportedly worth about $US50 million. And now, nearly three years since it was axed, it’s finally set to appear on Australian screens on September 17. Wile E. Coyote never gives up. Coyote vs Acme didn’t either. Ketchup has become something of a saving grace for Looney Tunes, having also recently released The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie, another film jettisoned by Warner Bros. This movie, which is entirely animated, managed to gross $US8.2 million in domestic ticket sales after just three weeks in cinemas. In a slightly twisted way, Forte says he’s actually grateful to Warner Bros for cancelling Coyote vs Acme.



“It might have all happened for a reason,” he says. “As much as I think they made a mistake not putting it in theatres themselves, I’m thankful that they let somebody else do it. And look, I understand it’s always a crap-shoot. They’re making a business decision … [but] it might be because of that craziness that we went through – that rollercoaster ride that Warner Bros put us through – that might make more people hear about the movie.” Related Article Cinema Crash to classic: How Practical Magic’s box-office hex marked the spot for Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock It certainly was a tough journey, he says. But neither the fans nor those involved in the film gave up on it – just like Coyote refused to give up on catching the Road Runner. “This is a character who doesn’t know the word ‘quit’. He’s facing insurmountable odds, and he just still goes for it every single time. He fails spectacularly, picks himself back up, gets a little rest, and then goes out again. It’s a good lesson for people – I wouldn’t say use that in your desire to kill birds or people, but you know, just in that attitude towards positive goals.” Wile E. was never Forte’s favourite Looney Tunes character – he preferred Elmer Fudd and Bugs Bunny (aka “the Fonzie of Looney Tunes”) – but the coyote is definitely up there now. Forte developed a deep connection with this wildly resilient character, even before post-production brought him to life and he was just a tennis ball on a stick. Coyote is an underdog who found hope among the madness – just as Forte did with this film. Coyote vs Acme is in cinemas on September 17. World.title: ‘There’s someone on the bridge!’ The new reality series taking viewers behind the scenes of the biggest rescues
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV ‘There’s someone on the bridge!’ The new reality series taking viewers behind the scenes of the biggest rescues Bridget McManus September 13, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Over a year that brought horror and tragedy to Sydney’s iconic shores, a television crew has been quietly capturing the unpredictable work of the water police. From busting drug traffickers, to searching for sunken weapons, shepherding swimmers away from sharks and releasing rehabilitated sea turtles – it’s all in a day’s work for the men and women of the NSW Police Marine Area Command. For the first time, this unit, known as “the MAC”, which patrols Sydney Harbour, its inland waters, and the entire NSW coastline up to 200 nautical miles out to sea, has allowed TV cameras on board, for Ten’s new series Sydney Harbour Cops. Sydney Harbour Cops follows the NSW Police Marine Area Command on patrol. In the absence of Bondi Rescue (the 19th season of which Waverley Council has confirmed is on hold due to ongoing negotiations with production company CJZ), Sydney Harbour Cops offers fascinating insight into what goes on beyond the breakers. “Initially, [being filmed] was a bit foreign,” says Senior Constable Brendan Nix, who has been with the MAC diving unit for 23 years of his 36-year policing career. “Towards the end, it was more comfortable. The producers would give you a bit of a heads-up about what they were going to ask, and if you said something silly, they’d do it again.”



Nix doesn’t watch other police observationals, preferring Air Crash Investigation or the true-crime series presented by retired Victorian homicide detective Ron Iddles. And forget police dramas. “[Dramas] can’t give a true reflection of the tenacity. It could be years and years of investigation.” Related Article Australian TV Wide World of Sports was a ratings hit. But it wasn’t enough to impress Kerry Packer In Sydney Harbour Cops, Nix co-ordinates a hair-raising search in Lismore for a World War II grenade tossed into muddy water by a member of the public. “Obviously, as you touch a grenade, or a firearm or a sharp weapon, you’re very careful how you palpate, or feel it, and you secure it safely and surface with it,” he says. “The varied skills that the Marine Air Command deliver, whether it’s entering the water with the divers, or operating small and large vessels and navigating safely for hundreds of nautical miles out to sea to undertake rescues, that skill base doesn’t come overnight.” Senior Constable Matt Calbert, a former surf lifesaver, was just as reluctant to become a reality TV star. He appears in the first episode, whizzing up the Hawkesbury to the water-access-only suburb of Bar Point, to transport a 92-year-old woman to hospital.



“I definitely don’t want to be famous … But I feel like a lot of people probably don’t know what we do,” he says. “I’m just excited for the community to get a glimpse into our day-to-day life. And if they can take away a rule or a safety practice that they didn’t previously know, that’d be great.” Sydney Harbour Cops producer Naomi Elkin-Jones on the job. Producer Naomi Elkin-Jones, who worked on UK police drama Blue Lights before moving to Sydney and making Ten’s Dogs Behaving (Very) Badly, says the production was tightly controlled by the NSW Police media unit. A filming supervisor was on every shoot, and each final cut had to be approved. “They advise in the moment if a story is going to be OK for us to follow, and we have to go through a formal review process once every episode is made,” she says. Related Article Streaming ‘I don’t have a death wish’: The Aussie chef who swapped restaurants for the wild Elkin-Jones found the experience eye-opening. “Before I worked on this series, the water police were just the police on the harbour. But hopefully this will make them visible.”



She was struck by the composure of the officers during harrowing incidents, such as when a member of the public dangled from the bottom of the Harbour Bridge for more than an hour. “That was very confronting,” she says. “We were doing all our drone shots that beautiful, non-rainy day, and we were about to head back to base for lunch, and then the call came in: ‘There’s someone on the bridge!’ … It’s been an especially challenging year, and for [the MAC], to have us on board at the same time, that could add extra pressure. But they’ve managed it with a lot of grace.” Sydney Harbour Cops premieres at 7.30pm on Tuesday, September 15, on Ten. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: ‘No name is beautiful enough for my child’
World.content:
For many Muslim parents, choosing a child’s name is far more than finding a name that is beautiful or distinctive. A name carries meaning, identity, memory and hope. Parents often believe that a good name can influence a child’s character and serve as a lifelong reminder of the qualities they hope the child will embody. Choosing a Muslim boy’s or girl’s name thus becomes an expression of love, faith and aspiration.

The babies of Muslims are often named after a virtue, the Prophet, or his friends and family. Getty Images

Names can also reflect love and respect for the holy personalities and figures who have shaped Islamic history. Parents may choose names associated with prophets, members of the Prophet Muhammad’s family, revered companions, scholars or other figures whose lives represent courage, compassion, wisdom and devotion.

Muhammad, Ahmed, Musa, Ali, Hassan, Hussain, Hamza, Omer and Osman are common boys’ names connected to prophets or companions. Another common element is “Abdul”, meaning “servant of”, combined with an attribute of God. For example, Abdul Rahman means “servant of the Most Gracious”, while Abdul Karim means “servant of the Most Generous”.

Common girls’ names include Maryam, Fatima, Khadija, Zaineb and Sumaiya, many associated with members of the Prophet’s family or respected companions. Giving a child such a name can quietly keep these stories alive within a family.

World.title: Former Mirvac boss to sell $11m Killara home with tennis court
World.content:
Exclusive PropertyNewsTitle Deeds Former Mirvac boss to sell $11m Killara home with tennis court Kristy Johnson September 13, 2026 — 5:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Mirvac chief executive officer Susan Lloyd-Hurwitz and her husband Stuart Lloyd-Hurwitz have listed their upper north shore Sydney home for $10 million to $11 million, local sources say, after holding it for more than a decade. Records show the couple bought the six-bedroom, four-bathroom house with a tennis court and pool in Killara for $3.55 million in 2013 from Joseph Healy, the co-founder and former chief executive officer of Judo Bank, and his wife Susan. A former property group boss and her husband are offloading their Georgian-style residence in Sydney’s Killara. The couple enlisted Tribe Studio Architects to renovate the two-storey property built around 1923. Situated on 1720 square metres, the residence has timber floorboards, vaulted ceilings, skylights, statement lighting and a neutral palette. Bi-fold doors lead to the pool, tennis court and garden.



Local sources say the price guide for the six-bedroom, four-bathroom home is $10 million to $11 million. Susan Lloyd-Hurwitz has wide experience in the global investment and real estate sectors. In October 2022, Mirvac announced her retirement from Mirvac on 30 June 2023, where she was chief executive officer and managing director for a decade. Susan Lloyd-Hurwitz Renee Nowytarger Now sitting on the board of Macquarie Group Limited, Lloyd-Hurwitz is also a non-executive director of Rio Tinto, and chair of the Australian National Housing Supply and Affordability Council. Her previous roles include managing director of Europe for LaSalle Investment Management, national president for the Property Council of Australia, a director of the Business Council of Australia, and chair of the Green Building Council of Australia.



Stuart Lloyd-Hurwitz is a director of Elp Strategy, a consulting firm for corporate clients. Scott Farquhar and Wendy Wenjing Xu of Sydney Sotheby’s International Realty are selling the home and both declined to comment on any aspect of the listing when contacted. Late artist’s home makes a splash The former home of late Australian artist Charles Blackman in Sydney’s Woollahra, that has been reimagined by its current vendors, is for sale with a buyer’s guide of $10 million, as stated on the listing. The current vendors renovated the former Woollahra home of artist Charles Blackman with a bold palette.



Blackman, who died in 2018 and was a renowned figurative painter best known for his Alice in Wonderland series in the 1950s, sold the property with his ex-wife Barbara Blackman, a celebrated writer and arts advocate, for $1.22 million in 1994. There have been multiple vendors since. Simon Lightbody and Tessa Chirnside, co-founders of Rhodian, an underwriting company that works alongside agencies, brokers and insurer partners, bought the three-level, four-bedroom, four-bathroom abode for $4.3 million in 2020, records show. The home’s decor is anything but white. The buyer’s guide is $10 million. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Millennials to sell one of two Bellevue Hill homes, list it for $37m Approved DA plans lodged with council reveal alterations and additions to the existing dwelling, including a new kitchen, porch, master ensuite, staircase, garage and mud room, with an estimated cost of $736,246.



The couple enlisted Kaiko Design Interiors and Hampton Architecture to transform the facade and interiors into a bold palette of blush, terracotta and sage. Leathered pink travertine, green quartzite, Japanese mosaics and green terrazzo are design details, alongside new skylights and a ribbon spiral staircase with terracotta-hued carpet. A glossy spiral staircase is a focal point of the property. Maclay Longhurst of Sydney Sotheby’s International Realty, who is selling the residence alongside Robert Le, describes it as a “meticulous design with a self-contained apartment”. An auction has been scheduled for October. Long-held home in Byron Bay enclave for sale



A multi-level home in the tightly held Wategos Beach enclave in Byron Bay, is being offered to the market with a buyer’s guide of $17 million. A modern residence with ocean-facing balconies above prized Wategos Beach in Byron Bay has a buyer’s guide of $17 million. Vendors Robert and Helen Lynch, co-founders of Stellar Entertainment, a company that delivers inflight entertainment experiences to airlines around the world, are saying goodbye to the three-bedroom, two-bathroom house that they’ve called home for over 40 years. Records show the Lynch family paid $76,000 for the address in 1980 to architect Rafael Buldrini and his wife Maria. Interiors feature angular ceilings, a neutral palette and expansive glass to capture the coastal views. There is a pool and ocean-facing balconies. The property is perfect for entertaining with its open-plan layout and multiple leisure zones.



The Lynches have enjoyed many milestones at the property from raising their children to watching their grandchildren catch their first waves. Records show the couple also own a unit in Sydney’s Darling Point. The coveted Wategos Beach enclave is home to residents including Rip Curl co-founder Brian Singer, Brisbane developer Adam Flaskas, Afterpay co-founder Anthony Eisen and art dealer Steve Nasteski. It’s not often properties in this prized locale come to market. Homes in the exclusive enclave of Wategos Beach don’t often come to market. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Philanthropist’s Byron Bay home with a zen room has $15m price hopes Robert and Helen Lynch transferred ownership of Stellar Entertainment in August this year after more than 50 years at the helm to chief executive officer Sam Allen, chief financial officer Annie Zhong and chief operating officer Daniel Jacobs.



The company was formed when Robert, who was working at a radio station, and Helen, who had a background in interior design, answered an ad in a Sydney newspaper from Qantas looking for a company to supply boarding music. From there, the company grew. Will Phillips and Nick Gill of Byron Bay Sotheby’s International Realty are selling the home.
