World.title: Are we in World War III, and just don’t know it?
World.content:
Observers are asking if the spot fires that will turn into the next worldwide conflagration are already alight.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When US President Donald Trump accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of “gambling with World War III”, in a furious exchange in the White House in March last year, it was easy, perhaps, to write the statement off as overblown rhetoric.That’s just Trump, trying to strongarm Zelensky into giving up stolen land to Vladimir Putin, in exchange for peace. But in the 18 months since that explosive episode in the Oval Office, the world’s mood has shifted. Mastheads from around the globe – from Japan to the United States and Britain – have begun asking if we are perhaps already in World War III, and just don’t know it. (Or, as The Hill put it on August 11: “World War III is already here, and Trump must rise to the challenge”.) Dialogue, the invite-only social club co-founded by billionaire tech investor Peter Thiel, was reportedly planning to hold a session on “Prepping for WWIII” sometime last month until this year’s conference was cancelled. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump during their heated Oval Office meeting in February. Bloomberg “It’s a fair question, and a number of people are asking it,” says Professor Robert Pape, a University of Chicago political science expert, of whether we’re in third world war now, and just don’t know it. “Because we have two major wars that are impacting big parts of the world happening at the same time [in Iran and Ukraine],” says Pape, whose popular substack, The Escalation Trap, has been monitoring the Iran war. And watchers of history, he says, know how unexpected events can suddenly spark a massive escalation, and unforeseen devastation, within existing wars. We might spy Iran holding the Strait of Hormuz hostage – causing the price of oil, fertiliser and other goods to skyrocket around the world – while the US threatens “D-Day”-like sanctions on Iran and bond markets dive, and think back, worryingly, to earlier times. The impact of hyperinflation on the Weimar Republic in Germany and the rise of the Nazis, for example, or the bloodless, economic warfare that led Japan to bomb an American naval fleet in Pearl Harbour on December 7, 1941.



That event changed the course of World War Two, drawing in the United States, and leading, eventually, to then-president Harry S Truman’s fateful decision to unleash the nuclear bomb. Japan shared no fealty to the Nazi ideology, the motivating force behind Hitler’s reign of terror that saw him direct Germany’s forces to invade country after country across Europe. Rather, Japan decided to bomb Hawaii, only after the US, Britain and the Netherlands had imposed a total oil and raw material embargo on it. The US Battleship Arizona topples into the sea after the Pearl Harbour attack in 1941. AP “So they thought, ‘our survival and our standing as a great power requires going to war with another great power’,” says James Der Derian, director of the University of Sydney’s Centre for International Security Studies. “So, who’s Japan in this instance?” he says, of our current geopolitical climate. “I’d be stressed to say China. But if China feels like its economy is being threatened by failure to have sustained and predictable flow of not just oil and fertiliser, but other things related to oil, and 20 per cent [of that] coming out of the Hormuz Strait, would they become more involved? So far they don’t have that projection of power. But they certainly do have, increasingly, ways of influencing behaviour in this part of the world.” China is riding out the fuel crisis. Bloomberg So far, China seems to have been meeting its energy needs and a notable feature of the economic sanctions announced by Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, last month, was the caution the US exercised towards Chinese interests, declining to target Chinese banks as part of the sanctions regime.



When the war in Iran began in February, Trump declared the conflict would be over in a matter of weeks. That has not come to pass. So we watch, as it drags on, with a new front opening up in the Red Sea, in early August, when the Houthi Rebels, an Iranian ally, began striking oil refineries in Saudi Arabia. This threatens yet another oil export pipeline. In the last few days they took control of a strategic island, giving them control of the sea. All the while, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s persistent refusal to cave to Trump’s demands to withdraw Israeli troops from Gaza and Lebanon, in a bid to broker the peace with Hamas and Hezbollah, further prolongs the conflict. The good news? This does not mean we are in – or on the precipice of – World War III. So says Graham Allison, who served as American president Bill Clinton’s assistant secretary of defence for policy and plans, and was a special adviser to the secretary of defence under then-president Ronald Reagan. The category “world war”, he says, refers to a global conflict with extraordinarily devastating consequences: like the 25 million victims in World War I, and the approximately 60 million dead in World War II. US troops taking part in Normandy landings in June 1944. Reuters “So I reserve ‘World War III’ for the catastrophe that is catastrophic beyond imagination,” says Allison, a Harvard University professor. For many historians, this has meant the dangling fear of another nuclear conflict. Or at the very least, two great powers engaging in battlefield warfare, in which other, smaller nations, are then forced to choose a side. Nevertheless, in 2017 Allison wrote that the world was lurching towards conflict unseen since World War II, culminating in his book Destined For War: Can America and China Escape Thucydides’ Trap?



Does he still feel that we’re lurching towards conflict unseen since World War II? “Yes,” he says, over the phone from Massachusetts. He refers to the ancient Greek historian Thucydides, who argued that when a rising power threatens to displace an established ruling power, the stress and mutual fear this brings often makes violent conflict inevitable. (Thucydides had observed during the Peloponnesian War that “It was the rise of Athens and the fear that this instilled in Sparta that made war inevitable”.) A Chinese sailor aboard a warship in the East China Sea. AP “I think if Thucydides were assessing the situation [now], he would say the two rivals are pretty much right on script,” says Allison, referring to China, the power on the rise, and the US, the established power that is waning. “The rising power is continuing to rise and to feel its oats, and to become more assertive, and continue to complain about the international order ... saying, ‘I need more say and more sway’,” he says, referring to Chinese encroachments in the South-China Sea, and military threats in and around Taiwan, a sovereign territory that Chinese leader Xi Jinping says is an inseparable and integral part of China. “And the colossal ruling power, the US, you can see all of the insecurities that come from them thinking, ‘Wait a minute. What’s happening?’” He refers to Trump’s decision to impose a 145 per cent tariff on China last year, saying: “So, I was quite worried that things could get out of control in an economic confrontation.”



US President Donald Trump displays the signed executive order after his first tariff announcement. Bloomberg Allison’s nerves calmed after Trump backed down on his tariffs. (This, only after Xi responded by cutting the US off from critical minerals, without which the American economy and military industry cannot function.) But he plays out the scenario that could have resulted, had Trump not dropped his tariffs on China. “Well, let’s imagine now, a month later, and the American economy is grinding to a halt,” says Allison. “The fellow that runs Ford Motor Company calls and said, ‘I’m closing the production line for these trucks next week’, if this continues. And the people making Tomahawk missiles and F35s said, ‘We can’t continue producing these’. “So now, what would the US do? … [Likely Trump might think] ‘I’m going to try to cause pain to you’. And as I do that, could one thing lead to another and with a little bit of miscalculation you get to a war? Well, the US and Japan did, in 1941. So that’s one path.” Taiwanese forces conducting an anti-invasion drill on a beach. Getty Given the structural factors at play, he estimates the chance of China and the US becoming embroiled in a full-fledged war at 75 per cent.

World.title: Why One Nation’s rise in Victoria is good for democracy
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictorian election Opinion Why One Nation’s rise in Victoria is good for democracy Neil Mitchell Journalist September 13, 2026 — 5:01am

September 13, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As psephologists gradually realise that a clairvoyant has more chance of predicting the Victorian election, there’s one direct benefit to the political uncertainty: the much mocked, disliked, analysed and confusing beast that is One Nation has improved the contest and given democracy a boost. With all its faults, One Nation has challenged the complacency and arrogance that have defined modern politics, forcing the major parties to think beyond their massaged focus groups and actually listen to the electorate. Photo: Matt Davidson That’s healthy. The question now is whether Ben Carroll and Jess Wilson read the room, show the strength to defy what has become convention, attempt to engage with voters properly, and understand that authenticity is not political poison. Over decades the major players have seen One Nation supporters as thick-headed bogans who want to deport all immigrants and whip graffiti vandals. That no longer stands up. Look at the polls and interstate results. This is a popular and growing movement, and there aren’t that many rednecks in the country.



The party has given genuine and decent disengaged voters hope that at last someone is listening. It may be false hope, but it’s working, and the major parties are starting to understand why. One Nation can’t be entirely driving its own success. It lacks much. Pauline Hanson has been around for decades and achieved little. She is inarticulate and seems bereft of the depth and focus required for high office. One Nation founder Pauline Hanson with the party’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering. Eamon Gallagher The party looks dysfunctional and any serious role in a minority government in Victoria would likely end in tears. If it holds the balance of power in the upper house, as seems probable, whoever is in government will be herding cats. The party leader in Victoria, who says he is running for premier, is Warren Pickering. To date, a serious political role seems beyond him.



That’s without factoring in some nasty but long-past behaviour to which he has now admitted: drug use, drink-driving. (His sexual experimentation is another thing and has nothing to do with anybody else.) However, his handling of that drama: “I’m not a politician, I’m a real person,” may yet skew positive. It snugly fits the One Nation narrative. Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell, the party’s only member in the Victorian parliament, is a contrast. She seems decent and engaging, with friends on both sides. Animal rights activist Georgie Purcell is a mate. She trusts her enough to use her as a babysitter. Apart from personnel challenges, the party has few detailed policies and gets routinely bad press as media fights to expose what some seem to think is an illegitimate threat to their political bubble. But with all these problems the party’s support has surged. Labor and Liberal in Victoria have for months been frightened by it. Now they are terrified. That fear has led to a flurry of people-focused policies like a tougher approach to law and order, improving public transport, and various little bribes to ease cost-of-living pressure.



The opposition will try anything, that’s what oppositions do. But it’s unlikely the scales would have so dramatically fallen from the premier’s eyes if One Nation were not a threat on exactly these issues. Now, in the weeks ahead, will the majors respond with more of the same contrived, artificial, empty politicking. Or do they get real? Related Article Opinion

Celebrity life Hughesy, why so angry? I’m worried your head’s going to explode Kate Halfpenny Regular columnist Ben Carroll is a decent man, respected across politics. That rarely comes through. He speaks in artificial, four-word sentences, think actor Michael Caine. Jess Wilson can be warm, engaging and even funny, with an impish look in her eye. But on duty she mostly seems robotic, earnest and cold.



Neither presents their real self to the voters – instead, the electorate mostly sees the pre-packaged, minder-driven “vote for me” strategy that has failed Victorians for years, alienated voters, and driven them to the One Nation “answer” because the party talks directly to them and sounds real. That’s one reason the comments by magnificently disgruntled comedian Dave Hughes have become so powerful. Unlike the leaders, he’s authentic. People understand what he’s saying. And he nails the frustration. The government was slow to act on crime, bail laws, cost-of-living pressures and corruption. But there’s stark evidence of the orange fear factor and its impact on one more simple issue: potholes. I raised the issue of our crumbling roads more than four years ago, and the radio audience jumped on it. It’s a radio cliche to say callers “jammed the talkback lines”, but they did. They were angry. It touched real people. The campaign was mocked as trivial, although former roads minister Luke Donnellan warned roads were the biggest issue facing the re-elected government. Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell raised potholes 50 times as a new MP.





And this is the problem as nailed by the auditor: “The overall condition of Victoria’s state roads is deteriorating. In 2024, around 48 per cent of the network was in poor or very poor condition, compared to 39 per cent in 2021.” All these years, all these warnings and when the government finally reacts, it produces spin and soft figures. Related Article Opinion

City life There’s a nasty mood festering in this state. Victoria is at war with itself Neil Mitchell Journalist How much pain and money could have been saved, how much danger and frustration avoided, if the government had acted properly four years ago? The inaction on such a basic safety and economic issue was a failure of democracy: the media, politicians, the opposition all took too long to understand the significance of the potholes. The public did not.



Finally, the government heard the clamour, delivering too little too late. But part of the reason the political machine eventually reacted was One Nation and its underlying threat: there is no longer any such thing as a safe seat. Neil Mitchell hosts the podcast Mitchell Unlimited. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Housing with benefits: Why co-housing could be the new Australian dream
World.content:
It was a conversation with their son who put words to something Ross and Paula Wade had always felt: the desire to live a little differently. They wanted to share a garden and were happy to live in a modest home in exchange for community. They just didn’t think realising this dream would come with a $200,000 premium. Members of the Brougham Street Collective in Eltham (from left): Suzanne Hurley, Shaun McLeod, Ann Cox, Pam Wade, Ross Wade, Mae Donaldson and Emily Donaldson. Ruby Alexander The Wades, a couple in their 70s, are part of a group of like-minded prospective home owners who want to live as part of a co-housing development. Recent moves by the federal government to make property more affordable for younger people, such as restricting tax breaks for negative gearing to new builds, has opened the door to thinking about residential property in ways other than an investment. For Australians less concerned about asset price growth and more with building community, the changes signal a new way of living is possible.



Still under construction, the Brougham Street Collective in Eltham in Melbourne’s leafy north-east is already a collection of buildings surrounded by heritage-listed structures of various sizes. It’s planned to have no fences for privacy, no individual driveways and smaller houses. It is set to have 20 homes, of two, three and four bedrooms, a shared garden, babysitting on-site, access to eco-friendly power, communal cooking and good friends of all ages. The Brougham Street Collective is still under construction. Ruby Alexander “It’s magic, staying connected, not only within your own family but with a whole group of people who have become friends,” says Paula. But there is no blueprint for such magic, as the group found out.



Council approval was a sticking point. Brougham Street failed to secure a permit because “planners just don’t have a model for this kind of development”, Ross says. Related Article Housing affordability What was the Great Australian Dream? “It’s just a tick-box process [for the council]. We say we have a common house, they say, well, what’s a common house? I can’t see a box to tick for that.” Brougham Street was forced to go to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to overturn the council’s decision, adding about $200,000 in costs. Ross says while the collective was not thrilled about the cost, the only other option was to abandon the project and sell the land.



“The whole community agreed that it was worth it to secure our dream of living in an intentional community together,” Ross says. The cohousing development in Eltham is set to have 20 homes, of two, three and four bedrooms. Ruby Alexander The co-housing model is more common in Europe, and originated in Denmark in the 1960s. The developments are generally small-scale communities of up to 50 households: resident-governed and -planned, rather than developer-led. Some have communal areas, although each community decides its format. Caitlin McGee, UTS Institute for Sustainable Futures research director, says the motivation for co-housing participation was “largely around social connection”, as family structures change and people seek intergenerational support. “I feel like there’s definitely a connection between the kind of rise in social isolation and this kind of renewed desire for co-housing,” she says. “It’s just this idea that people help each other out a bit more in an informal way and live as a community.”



The number of shared households has risen over recent years. Census data for 2021 shows about 848,000 people lived in group households, with about 19 per cent of these aged 55 and above. Related Article Housing affordability What the Great Australian Dream looks like today The at-cost housing project development in Eltham was spearheaded by Tim Riley, developer and founder of Property Collectives, his tenth project of this type. It is a joint venture where collective members get a vote on the management committee, where decisions are made. “These groups are intentional about creating a certain type of community – every project is different and dependent on the land,” he says. Co-housing remains an anomaly in Australia, where the desire for standalone houses on large blocks dominates the property market.



There are 28 completed co-housing developments around the country, including seven finished in the past three years, according to peak body CoHousing Australia. More than 12 other groups are looking for co-housing opportunities. Teresa Dominik, CoHousing Australia’s planning policy working group convenor and a Brougham Street member, says those numbers aren’t precise. Some co-housing communities have had staged construction, with the new stage a new community group. “Also, increasingly, people are doing more informal types of co-housing – often more like co-living but with many of the elements of co-housing. These aren’t listed but go to people looking at alternative and more affordable housing options.” The myth of the quarter-acre block, says Michael Fotheringham, former managing director of the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute, lives on because “the development industry leans into it, as building detached houses on greenfields is the cheapest model”.



Urban spread, fuelled by a preference for detached housing, means Australia’s suburbs are among the lowest-density in the world. “We still build about six detached houses for every apartment,” Fotheringham says. But not everyone wants to live in a traditional detached home. Vincent Murray, 72, became interested in co-housing after being inspired by communities he had seen in France, where homes surround a village square with shared activities and spaces. He and his partner had long maintained separate residences but wanted another housing option as they aged. Vincent Murray thinks that co-housing provides a transition to life after work. Kate Geraghty “A lot of people have their work community but when you retire you lose all of that, so you need to have something else to put in its place. And so the village concept seems perfect for transitioning to a different sort of life after work,” says Murray, a retired academic.



When a flyer from a group called Agency Cohousing and Community – a development for over-50s in inner Sydney’s Balmain – landed in his mailbox, Murray thought he’d found the perfect solution. “I went along to the meeting and became more involved in it,” he says. He later became president of Agency. Related Article Housing affordability Melissa moved into a share house in her 50s. More people are doing the same “Before COVID a lot of people were very enthusiastic about it. We had these meetings with hundreds of people. And then COVID … Because we couldn’t meet because we’re more at the older end of the age spectrum … people became much more fearful about coming out and meeting people.” Dominik says co-housing had traditionally attracted older people. But recent moves to create more intergenerational communities has piqued the interest of younger people and families as housing affordability plummets and loneliness rises.



“The greatest saving is more that you can actually have a smaller house,” Dominik says, noting there can be communal facilities like guest rooms or shared dining rooms. McGee says “conceptually”, co-housing should deliver affordability benefits. “But in places where we have such a housing crisis and land so expensive, that doesn’t end up as the main driver, the main driver is really about the community-building,” she says. At Brougham Street, to ensure the community is diverse, the older members decided to lower the deposit for younger members. Emily Donaldson and her children will be younger members of the co-housing development. Ruby Alexander



“The collective is definitely age-weighted – it’s a bit of a Boomer paradise currently because of the cost,” says Emily Donaldson, 45, a married mother of three girls. Related Article Exclusive

Housing affordability Where first home buyers have been getting into the market this year The houses, while modest, are not exactly affordable, spanning $875,000 to $1,475,000, with an average cost across the 20 homes of $1.06 million. Setting up co-housing developments in Australia is not simple. Challenges include finding suitable land to build and land costs, as well as getting bank financing. Balmain’s Agency, for example, faced a range of challenges in its attempt to set up its community, and has now wound up after about 10 years.



The high cost of land and development building costs, and inability to borrow via conventional banking mechanisms, were some of the roadblocks. “When you’re in a community group with diverse backgrounds and abilities, some have difficulty, first of all, to visualise what it might look like, and also the financial side of it,” Murray says. Murray outside a site in Sydney’s inner west that was considered by Agency Cohousing and Community as an option for their co-housing development. Kate Geraghty Adam Russell, a partner of creative practice Saltbush Projects, which has worked with prospective co-housing dwellers, says from a legal perspective they can be complicated to set up, with roadblocks including approvals, loans and insurance. “Co-housing is, as a mindset, is establishing a habitat where people live in that sort of way, permanently,” he says.



“And legally it’s also a bit complex because the types of buildings that get customised or custom-designed for co-housing don’t have a very clear pathway or definition under planning codes.” Related Article Exclusive

Construction How Zac Efron is turning an Aussie bush block into his forever home Brougham Street faced this and other complications. The upfront costs were nothing to sneeze at. As their co-housing model operates in the private market, groups only have access to commercial debt funding and their own capital. The group also met resistance from locals. But it was the council’s reluctance to issue a building permit for a development they had not seen before that was the major issue.



Riley expected this, and factored VCAT costs into the project. However, the spend went beyond what he’d imagined. “We spent about $200,000 on additional architectural fees to alter our design to make it VCAT-proof, on lawyer fees and expert witnesses – we called traffic, planning and urban design witnesses. There were also the construction cost escalations,” Riley says. This masthead contacted Nillumbik Shire Council but did not receive a reply. VCAT took only 1½ weeks to rule in favour of the collective. It said this was the type of project that “could and should have been supported and fast-tracked”, an “exemplar of an innovative approach” to addressing the housing crisis. Ann Cox at Brougham Street, which is still under development. Ruby Alexander



The Victorian government has introduced a new planning pathway for apartments and townhouses that demonstrate great design. The Great Design Fast Track is available for apartment and townhouse proposals two to eight storeys in height, with eight or more homes. Related Article Housing affordability Cassandra grew up in a large family home. Then she found something better Projects are assessed against the design principles of being neighbourly, welcoming, landscaped, sustainable, healthy, adaptable and good value. “If you get a permit through the process, there is no chance of going to VCAT,” Riley says. In New South Wales, the NSW Housing Pattern Book and fast-track assessment pathways are not designed specifically for co-living developments, but may be applicable depending on the type of proposal.



“In NSW, co-living development proposals are assessed through existing planning approval pathways, depending on the type of housing proposed and the planning controls that apply to the site,” says a spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure. At Brougham Street as of June, all 20 homes on the about-7000-square-metre block have been purchased and are expected to be completed at the end of the year. Brougham Street members at the site of what will be their new homes. Ruby Alexander “We first heard about the collective over coffee at a cafe, and came to an information day,” says Shaun McLeod. He and his wife Suzanne are future residents of the Eltham development. “We were a little unsure at first but the more we read about it, the more we became convinced it was a great idea.”



For Murray, while Agency has closed down, the experience remains valuable. He has made new friends, some of whom are considering buying into a new development in Rozelle. Murray and his partner have purchased side-by-side units off the plan there. Those who still want to continue to meet up. The group also provides assistance to former Agency members in need. “There’s a group of us that meet once a month for dinner and we rotate it around people’s houses … So we’re still continuing on, in a more informal basis.”

World.title: Warner Bros axed this Looney Tunes movie. But fans refused to accept defeat
World.content:
The story of how Coyote vs Acme came back from the dead is crazier than a Looney Tunes cartoon.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Will Forte could not have been prouder of Coyote vs Acme. The live-action animation hybrid, in which a disgruntled Wile E. Coyote and his lawyer (played by Forte) face off against John Cena in a chaotic courtroom battle, was one of the most entertaining – and heartwarming – projects he’d worked on. His wife, after watching it for the first time, even told him it was hands-down the best thing he’d ever done. So it’s safe to say that its inexplicable axing in 2023 sent Forte into a head-spin. Will Forte (right) couldn’t have loved Coyote vs Acme more. Suffice to say, its cancellation floored him. “This was a movie that I wanted so badly to share with my kids, but [I realised] I was never going to get to. It was confusing, frustrating and heartbreaking. I was just pissed,” said the American actor and comedian, who is known for his stint on Saturday Night Live and, more recently, Tina Fey’s The Four Seasons. Coyote vs Acme, Dave Green’s absurd comedy in the vein of Who Framed Roger Rabbit, was ready to hit screens when it was suddenly shelved by Warner Bros in November 2023. Despite ongoing praise from its producers, overwhelmingly positive test screenings and a $US70 million budget, the studio decided it would be better off as a $US30 million tax write-off. Its fate mirrored that of Batgirl and Scoob! Holiday Haunt, both of which were cancelled by Warner Bros the year prior. Coyote vs Acme has an impressive cast, including John Cena and several iconic Looney Tunes characters. But that didn’t stop it from being axed. “With the relaunch of Warner Bros Pictures Animation in June, the studio has shifted its global strategy to focus on theatrical releases,” a WB Motion Picture Group spokesperson told The Hollywood Reporter in 2023. “With this new direction, we have made the difficult decision not to move forward with Coyote vs Acme. We have tremendous respect for the filmmakers, casts and crew, and are grateful for their contributions to the film.”



Loading The decision was driven by a desire to offset corporate losses, a strategy spearheaded by the studio’s new head, David Zaslav. But for those who worked on the film, as well as the Looney Tunes fans feverishly anticipating its release, it was a punch to the gut. “We heard that Warner Bros was going to shelve it, but they still said we could come see the movie that next Tuesday. So, for the five or six days before that screening, I thought, ‘This is probably going to suck. If they’re going to shelve it, it can’t be good. Maybe these producers are just too deep in it to see that’. Then I showed up [to the screening] and I just loved it with all my heart. I was so proud of it, which was heartbreaking. I got so mad for a long time,” Forte says. Loading The film’s cancellation was especially disappointing given how broad he expected its appeal to be. Based on a 1990 New Yorker article by Ian Frazier, Coyote vs Acme tells Wile E. Coyote’s story. Fed up by the countless Acme products that have malfunctioned – costing him his lifelong dream of capturing the Road Runner – he decides to sue the major corporation with the help of Kevin Avery (Forte), a down-and-out billboard lawyer. This results in the unlikely pair going head-to-head with Acme’s chief executive, Foghorn Leghorn, as well as his ruthless lawyer Buddy Crane (Cena). For Looney Tunes fans, it delivers a healthy dose of nostalgia, reconnecting audiences with “old buddies”. Forte himself says the cartoons helped to form his comedic mind from a young age, subconsciously inspiring him to weave some of its madcap absurdity into his own comedy. That said, you don’t need to be a fan to enjoy this film. It has “a bit of everything”, Forte says, from legal drama to slapstick comedy. Loading



“It’s just this weird thing of: The movie’s testing really well, and it’s your IP [intellectual property]. If you’re not going to take a chance on that, what are you going to take a chance on?” Beyond the upset and disappointment, however, lay a painfully ironic parallel. Coyote vs Acme is largely Wile E. Coyote’s story. It’s an underdog tale, or as Forte puts it, a tale about “the little guy against the big corporation”. Everyone, from the cast and crew to the fans, immediately noticed the connection between Coyote’s journey and the film itself. If anything, it just made the movie even more resonant, Forte says, not only to himself but to every other Looney Tunes lover. Related Article Cartoons ‘That’s not all, folks!’ The voice actor taking Looney Tunes back to its roots As soon as the film was scrapped, fans and industry heads went to battle on social media, launching relentless campaigns in a bid to pressure Warner Bros into selling the project to another studio. “Disappointed, and somewhat mystified by the Coyote vs Acme news,” the film’s composer Steven Price wrote on X. “Dave Green made (and completed) an excellent movie, and a lot of people – not least the brilliant musicians and colleagues who worked with me on the score – poured their hearts into it … that’s (f---) all folks!” Writer-director BenDavid Grabinski, who received an off-screen additional literary credit for the film, lamented Warner Bros’ decision, writing on X that Coyote vs Acme was “the best of its kind” since Who Framed Roger Rabbit. “The leads are super likable. It’s beautifully shot. The animation is great. The ending makes everyone f---ing cry,” he wrote. “I thought the goal of this business was to make hit movies?”



View post on X Looney Tunes fans even released an online petition urging Warner Bros to release Coyote vs Acme, attracting 23,483 supporters. It was in this response that Forte discovered a silver lining. “It was a good lesson in the power of people,” he says. “Fans of the movie did not give up. They had hope when I didn’t.” It was their “constant noise-making”, he says, that eventually caught the attention of another studio: Ketchup Entertainment. In late March 2025, Ketchup – a far smaller studio than Warner Bros, but one that has released hits such as Michael Mann’s Ferrari (2023) – acquired the rights to Coyote vs Acme in a deal reportedly worth about $US50 million. And now, nearly three years since it was axed, it’s finally set to appear on Australian screens on September 17. Wile E. Coyote never gives up. Coyote vs Acme didn’t either. Ketchup has become something of a saving grace for Looney Tunes, having also recently released The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie, another film jettisoned by Warner Bros. This movie, which is entirely animated, managed to gross $US8.2 million in domestic ticket sales after just three weeks in cinemas. In a slightly twisted way, Forte says he’s actually grateful to Warner Bros for cancelling Coyote vs Acme.



“It might have all happened for a reason,” he says. “As much as I think they made a mistake not putting it in theatres themselves, I’m thankful that they let somebody else do it. And look, I understand it’s always a crap-shoot. They’re making a business decision … [but] it might be because of that craziness that we went through – that rollercoaster ride that Warner Bros put us through – that might make more people hear about the movie.” Related Article Cinema Crash to classic: How Practical Magic’s box-office hex marked the spot for Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock It certainly was a tough journey, he says. But neither the fans nor those involved in the film gave up on it – just like Coyote refused to give up on catching the Road Runner. “This is a character who doesn’t know the word ‘quit’. He’s facing insurmountable odds, and he just still goes for it every single time. He fails spectacularly, picks himself back up, gets a little rest, and then goes out again. It’s a good lesson for people – I wouldn’t say use that in your desire to kill birds or people, but you know, just in that attitude towards positive goals.” Wile E. was never Forte’s favourite Looney Tunes character – he preferred Elmer Fudd and Bugs Bunny (aka “the Fonzie of Looney Tunes”) – but the coyote is definitely up there now. Forte developed a deep connection with this wildly resilient character, even before post-production brought him to life and he was just a tennis ball on a stick. Coyote is an underdog who found hope among the madness – just as Forte did with this film. Coyote vs Acme is in cinemas on September 17. World.title: ‘There’s someone on the bridge!’ The new reality series taking viewers behind the scenes of the biggest rescues
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV ‘There’s someone on the bridge!’ The new reality series taking viewers behind the scenes of the biggest rescues Bridget McManus September 13, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Over a year that brought horror and tragedy to Sydney’s iconic shores, a television crew has been quietly capturing the unpredictable work of the water police. From busting drug traffickers, to searching for sunken weapons, shepherding swimmers away from sharks and releasing rehabilitated sea turtles – it’s all in a day’s work for the men and women of the NSW Police Marine Area Command. For the first time, this unit, known as “the MAC”, which patrols Sydney Harbour, its inland waters, and the entire NSW coastline up to 200 nautical miles out to sea, has allowed TV cameras on board, for Ten’s new series Sydney Harbour Cops. Sydney Harbour Cops follows the NSW Police Marine Area Command on patrol. In the absence of Bondi Rescue (the 19th season of which Waverley Council has confirmed is on hold due to ongoing negotiations with production company CJZ), Sydney Harbour Cops offers fascinating insight into what goes on beyond the breakers. “Initially, [being filmed] was a bit foreign,” says Senior Constable Brendan Nix, who has been with the MAC diving unit for 23 years of his 36-year policing career. “Towards the end, it was more comfortable. The producers would give you a bit of a heads-up about what they were going to ask, and if you said something silly, they’d do it again.”



Nix doesn’t watch other police observationals, preferring Air Crash Investigation or the true-crime series presented by retired Victorian homicide detective Ron Iddles. And forget police dramas. “[Dramas] can’t give a true reflection of the tenacity. It could be years and years of investigation.” Related Article Australian TV Wide World of Sports was a ratings hit. But it wasn’t enough to impress Kerry Packer In Sydney Harbour Cops, Nix co-ordinates a hair-raising search in Lismore for a World War II grenade tossed into muddy water by a member of the public. “Obviously, as you touch a grenade, or a firearm or a sharp weapon, you’re very careful how you palpate, or feel it, and you secure it safely and surface with it,” he says. “The varied skills that the Marine Air Command deliver, whether it’s entering the water with the divers, or operating small and large vessels and navigating safely for hundreds of nautical miles out to sea to undertake rescues, that skill base doesn’t come overnight.” Senior Constable Matt Calbert, a former surf lifesaver, was just as reluctant to become a reality TV star. He appears in the first episode, whizzing up the Hawkesbury to the water-access-only suburb of Bar Point, to transport a 92-year-old woman to hospital.



“I definitely don’t want to be famous … But I feel like a lot of people probably don’t know what we do,” he says. “I’m just excited for the community to get a glimpse into our day-to-day life. And if they can take away a rule or a safety practice that they didn’t previously know, that’d be great.” Sydney Harbour Cops producer Naomi Elkin-Jones on the job. Producer Naomi Elkin-Jones, who worked on UK police drama Blue Lights before moving to Sydney and making Ten’s Dogs Behaving (Very) Badly, says the production was tightly controlled by the NSW Police media unit. A filming supervisor was on every shoot, and each final cut had to be approved. “They advise in the moment if a story is going to be OK for us to follow, and we have to go through a formal review process once every episode is made,” she says. Related Article Streaming ‘I don’t have a death wish’: The Aussie chef who swapped restaurants for the wild Elkin-Jones found the experience eye-opening. “Before I worked on this series, the water police were just the police on the harbour. But hopefully this will make them visible.”



She was struck by the composure of the officers during harrowing incidents, such as when a member of the public dangled from the bottom of the Harbour Bridge for more than an hour. “That was very confronting,” she says. “We were doing all our drone shots that beautiful, non-rainy day, and we were about to head back to base for lunch, and then the call came in: ‘There’s someone on the bridge!’ … It’s been an especially challenging year, and for [the MAC], to have us on board at the same time, that could add extra pressure. But they’ve managed it with a lot of grace.” Sydney Harbour Cops premieres at 7.30pm on Tuesday, September 15, on Ten. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: ‘No name is beautiful enough for my child’
World.content:
For many Muslim parents, choosing a child’s name is far more than finding a name that is beautiful or distinctive. A name carries meaning, identity, memory and hope. Parents often believe that a good name can influence a child’s character and serve as a lifelong reminder of the qualities they hope the child will embody. Choosing a Muslim boy’s or girl’s name thus becomes an expression of love, faith and aspiration.

The babies of Muslims are often named after a virtue, the Prophet, or his friends and family. Getty Images

Names can also reflect love and respect for the holy personalities and figures who have shaped Islamic history. Parents may choose names associated with prophets, members of the Prophet Muhammad’s family, revered companions, scholars or other figures whose lives represent courage, compassion, wisdom and devotion.

Muhammad, Ahmed, Musa, Ali, Hassan, Hussain, Hamza, Omer and Osman are common boys’ names connected to prophets or companions. Another common element is “Abdul”, meaning “servant of”, combined with an attribute of God. For example, Abdul Rahman means “servant of the Most Gracious”, while Abdul Karim means “servant of the Most Generous”.

Common girls’ names include Maryam, Fatima, Khadija, Zaineb and Sumaiya, many associated with members of the Prophet’s family or respected companions. Giving a child such a name can quietly keep these stories alive within a family.

Former Mirvac chief executive officer Susan Lloyd-Hurwitz and her husband Stuart Lloyd-Hurwitz have listed their upper north shore Sydney home for $10 million to $11 million, local sources say, after holding it for more than a decade. Susan Lloyd-Hurwitz Renee Nowytarger Now sitting on the board of Macquarie Group Limited, Lloyd-Hurwitz is also a non-executive director of Rio Tinto, and chair of the Australian National Housing Supply and Affordability Council. Her previous roles include managing director of Europe for LaSalle Investment Management, national president for the Property Council of Australia, a director of the Business Council of Australia, and chair of the Green Building Council of Australia.



Stuart Lloyd-Hurwitz is a director of Elp Strategy, a consulting firm for corporate clients. The Lynches have enjoyed many milestones at the property from raising their children to watching their grandchildren catch their first waves. World.title: Are we in World War III, and just don’t know it?
World.content:
Observers are asking if the spot fires that will turn into the next worldwide conflagration are already alight.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When US President Donald Trump accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of “gambling with World War III”, in a furious exchange in the White House in March last year, it was easy, perhaps, to write the statement off as overblown rhetoric.That’s just Trump, trying to strongarm Zelensky into giving up stolen land to Vladimir Putin, in exchange for peace. But in the 18 months since that explosive episode in the Oval Office, the world’s mood has shifted. Mastheads from around the globe – from Japan to the United States and Britain – have begun asking if we are perhaps already in World War III, and just don’t know it. (Or, as The Hill put it on August 11: “World War III is already here, and Trump must rise to the challenge”.) Dialogue, the invite-only social club co-founded by billionaire tech investor Peter Thiel, was reportedly planning to hold a session on “Prepping for WWIII” sometime last month until this year’s conference was cancelled. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump during their heated Oval Office meeting in February. Bloomberg “It’s a fair question, and a number of people are asking it,” says Professor Robert Pape, a University of Chicago political science expert, of whether we’re in third world war now, and just don’t know it. “Because we have two major wars that are impacting big parts of the world happening at the same time [in Iran and Ukraine],” says Pape, whose popular substack, The Escalation Trap, has been monitoring the Iran war. And watchers of history, he says, know how unexpected events can suddenly spark a massive escalation, and unforeseen devastation, within existing wars. We might spy Iran holding the Strait of Hormuz hostage – causing the price of oil, fertiliser and other goods to skyrocket around the world – while the US threatens “D-Day”-like sanctions on Iran and bond markets dive, and think back, worryingly, to earlier times. The impact of hyperinflation on the Weimar Republic in Germany and the rise of the Nazis, for example, or the bloodless, economic warfare that led Japan to bomb an American naval fleet in Pearl Harbour on December 7, 1941.



That event changed the course of World War Two, drawing in the United States, and leading, eventually, to then-president Harry S Truman’s fateful decision to unleash the nuclear bomb. Japan shared no fealty to the Nazi ideology, the motivating force behind Hitler’s reign of terror that saw him direct Germany’s forces to invade country after country across Europe. Rather, Japan decided to bomb Hawaii, only after the US, Britain and the Netherlands had imposed a total oil and raw material embargo on it. The US Battleship Arizona topples into the sea after the Pearl Harbour attack in 1941. AP “So they thought, ‘our survival and our standing as a great power requires going to war with another great power’,” says James Der Derian, director of the University of Sydney’s Centre for International Security Studies. “So, who’s Japan in this instance?” he says, of our current geopolitical climate. “I’d be stressed to say China. But if China feels like its economy is being threatened by failure to have sustained and predictable flow of not just oil and fertiliser, but other things related to oil, and 20 per cent [of that] coming out of the Hormuz Strait, would they become more involved? So far they don’t have that projection of power. But they certainly do have, increasingly, ways of influencing behaviour in this part of the world.” China is riding out the fuel crisis. Bloomberg So far, China seems to have been meeting its energy needs and a notable feature of the economic sanctions announced by Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, last month, was the caution the US exercised towards Chinese interests, declining to target Chinese banks as part of the sanctions regime.



When the war in Iran began in February, Trump declared the conflict would be over in a matter of weeks. That has not come to pass. So we watch, as it drags on, with a new front opening up in the Red Sea, in early August, when the Houthi Rebels, an Iranian ally, began striking oil refineries in Saudi Arabia. This threatens yet another oil export pipeline. In the last few days they took control of a strategic island, giving them control of the sea. All the while, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s persistent refusal to cave to Trump’s demands to withdraw Israeli troops from Gaza and Lebanon, in a bid to broker the peace with Hamas and Hezbollah, further prolongs the conflict. The good news? This does not mean we are in – or on the precipice of – World War III. So says Graham Allison, who served as American president Bill Clinton’s assistant secretary of defence for policy and plans, and was a special adviser to the secretary of defence under then-president Ronald Reagan. The category “world war”, he says, refers to a global conflict with extraordinarily devastating consequences: like the 25 million victims in World War I, and the approximately 60 million dead in World War II. US troops taking part in Normandy landings in June 1944. Reuters “So I reserve ‘World War III’ for the catastrophe that is catastrophic beyond imagination,” says Allison, a Harvard University professor. For many historians, this has meant the dangling fear of another nuclear conflict. Or at the very least, two great powers engaging in battlefield warfare, in which other, smaller nations, are then forced to choose a side. Nevertheless, in 2017 Allison wrote that the world was lurching towards conflict unseen since World War II, culminating in his book Destined For War: Can America and China Escape Thucydides’ Trap?



Does he still feel that we’re lurching towards conflict unseen since World War II? “Yes,” he says, over the phone from Massachusetts. He refers to the ancient Greek historian Thucydides, who argued that when a rising power threatens to displace an established ruling power, the stress and mutual fear this brings often makes violent conflict inevitable. (Thucydides had observed during the Peloponnesian War that “It was the rise of Athens and the fear that this instilled in Sparta that made war inevitable”.) A Chinese sailor aboard a warship in the East China Sea. AP “I think if Thucydides were assessing the situation [now], he would say the two rivals are pretty much right on script,” says Allison, referring to China, the power on the rise, and the US, the established power that is waning. “The rising power is continuing to rise and to feel its oats, and to become more assertive, and continue to complain about the international order ... saying, ‘I need more say and more sway’,” he says, referring to Chinese encroachments in the South-China Sea, and military threats in and around Taiwan, a sovereign territory that Chinese leader Xi Jinping says is an inseparable and integral part of China. “And the colossal ruling power, the US, you can see all of the insecurities that come from them thinking, ‘Wait a minute. What’s happening?’” He refers to Trump’s decision to impose a 145 per cent tariff on China last year, saying: “So, I was quite worried that things could get out of control in an economic confrontation.”



US President Donald Trump displays the signed executive order after his first tariff announcement. Bloomberg Allison’s nerves calmed after Trump backed down on his tariffs. (This, only after Xi responded by cutting the US off from critical minerals, without which the American economy and military industry cannot function.) But he plays out the scenario that could have resulted, had Trump not dropped his tariffs on China. “Well, let’s imagine now, a month later, and the American economy is grinding to a halt,” says Allison. “The fellow that runs Ford Motor Company calls and said, ‘I’m closing the production line for these trucks next week’, if this continues. And the people making Tomahawk missiles and F35s said, ‘We can’t continue producing these’. “So now, what would the US do? … [Likely Trump might think] ‘I’m going to try to cause pain to you’. And as I do that, could one thing lead to another and with a little bit of miscalculation you get to a war? Well, the US and Japan did, in 1941. So that’s one path.” Taiwanese forces conducting an anti-invasion drill on a beach. Getty Given the structural factors at play, he estimates the chance of China and the US becoming embroiled in a full-fledged war at 75 per cent.

World.title: Why One Nation’s rise in Victoria is good for democracy
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictorian election Opinion Why One Nation’s rise in Victoria is good for democracy Neil Mitchell Journalist September 13, 2026 — 5:01am

September 13, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As psephologists gradually realise that a clairvoyant has more chance of predicting the Victorian election, there’s one direct benefit to the political uncertainty: the much mocked, disliked, analysed and confusing beast that is One Nation has improved the contest and given democracy a boost. With all its faults, One Nation has challenged the complacency and arrogance that have defined modern politics, forcing the major parties to think beyond their massaged focus groups and actually listen to the electorate. Photo: Matt Davidson That’s healthy. The question now is whether Ben Carroll and Jess Wilson read the room, show the strength to defy what has become convention, attempt to engage with voters properly, and understand that authenticity is not political poison. Over decades the major players have seen One Nation supporters as thick-headed bogans who want to deport all immigrants and whip graffiti vandals. That no longer stands up. Look at the polls and interstate results. This is a popular and growing movement, and there aren’t that many rednecks in the country.



The party has given genuine and decent disengaged voters hope that at last someone is listening. It may be false hope, but it’s working, and the major parties are starting to understand why. One Nation can’t be entirely driving its own success. It lacks much. Pauline Hanson has been around for decades and achieved little. She is inarticulate and seems bereft of the depth and focus required for high office. One Nation founder Pauline Hanson with the party’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering. Eamon Gallagher The party looks dysfunctional and any serious role in a minority government in Victoria would likely end in tears. If it holds the balance of power in the upper house, as seems probable, whoever is in government will be herding cats. The party leader in Victoria, who says he is running for premier, is Warren Pickering. To date, a serious political role seems beyond him.



That’s without factoring in some nasty but long-past behaviour to which he has now admitted: drug use, drink-driving. (His sexual experimentation is another thing and has nothing to do with anybody else.) However, his handling of that drama: “I’m not a politician, I’m a real person,” may yet skew positive. It snugly fits the One Nation narrative. Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell, the party’s only member in the Victorian parliament, is a contrast. She seems decent and engaging, with friends on both sides. Animal rights activist Georgie Purcell is a mate. She trusts her enough to use her as a babysitter. Apart from personnel challenges, the party has few detailed policies and gets routinely bad press as media fights to expose what some seem to think is an illegitimate threat to their political bubble. But with all these problems the party’s support has surged. Labor and Liberal in Victoria have for months been frightened by it. Now they are terrified. That fear has led to a flurry of people-focused policies like a tougher approach to law and order, improving public transport, and various little bribes to ease cost-of-living pressure.



The opposition will try anything, that’s what oppositions do. But it’s unlikely the scales would have so dramatically fallen from the premier’s eyes if One Nation were not a threat on exactly these issues. Now, in the weeks ahead, will the majors respond with more of the same contrived, artificial, empty politicking. Or do they get real? Related Article Opinion

Celebrity life Hughesy, why so angry? I’m worried your head’s going to explode Kate Halfpenny Regular columnist Ben Carroll is a decent man, respected across politics. That rarely comes through. He speaks in artificial, four-word sentences, think actor Michael Caine. Jess Wilson can be warm, engaging and even funny, with an impish look in her eye. But on duty she mostly seems robotic, earnest and cold.



Neither presents their real self to the voters – instead, the electorate mostly sees the pre-packaged, minder-driven “vote for me” strategy that has failed Victorians for years, alienated voters, and driven them to the One Nation “answer” because the party talks directly to them and sounds real. That’s one reason the comments by magnificently disgruntled comedian Dave Hughes have become so powerful. Unlike the leaders, he’s authentic. People understand what he’s saying. And he nails the frustration. The government was slow to act on crime, bail laws, cost-of-living pressures and corruption. But there’s stark evidence of the orange fear factor and its impact on one more simple issue: potholes. I raised the issue of our crumbling roads more than four years ago, and the radio audience jumped on it. It’s a radio cliche to say callers “jammed the talkback lines”, but they did. They were angry. It touched real people. The campaign was mocked as trivial, although former roads minister Luke Donnellan warned roads were the biggest issue facing the re-elected government. Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell raised potholes 50 times as a new MP.





And this is the problem as nailed by the auditor: “The overall condition of Victoria’s state roads is deteriorating. In 2024, around 48 per cent of the network was in poor or very poor condition, compared to 39 per cent in 2021.” All these years, all these warnings and when the government finally reacts, it produces spin and soft figures. Related Article Opinion

City life There’s a nasty mood festering in this state. Victoria is at war with itself Neil Mitchell Journalist How much pain and money could have been saved, how much danger and frustration avoided, if the government had acted properly four years ago? The inaction on such a basic safety and economic issue was a failure of democracy: the media, politicians, the opposition all took too long to understand the significance of the potholes. The public did not.



Finally, the government heard the clamour, delivering too little too late. But part of the reason the political machine eventually reacted was One Nation and its underlying threat: there is no longer any such thing as a safe seat. Neil Mitchell hosts the podcast Mitchell Unlimited. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Housing with benefits: Why co-housing could be the new Australian dream
World.content:
It was a conversation with their son who put words to something Ross and Paula Wade had always felt: the desire to live a little differently. They wanted to share a garden and were happy to live in a modest home in exchange for community. They just didn’t think realising this dream would come with a $200,000 premium. Members of the Brougham Street Collective in Eltham (from left): Suzanne Hurley, Shaun McLeod, Ann Cox, Pam Wade, Ross Wade, Mae Donaldson and Emily Donaldson. Ruby Alexander The Wades, a couple in their 70s, are part of a group of like-minded prospective home owners who want to live as part of a co-housing development. Recent moves by the federal government to make property more affordable for younger people, such as restricting tax breaks for negative gearing to new builds, has opened the door to thinking about residential property in ways other than an investment. For Australians less concerned about asset price growth and more with building community, the changes signal a new way of living is possible.



Still under construction, the Brougham Street Collective in Eltham in Melbourne’s leafy north-east is already a collection of buildings surrounded by heritage-listed structures of various sizes. It’s planned to have no fences for privacy, no individual driveways and smaller houses. It is set to have 20 homes, of two, three and four bedrooms, a shared garden, babysitting on-site, access to eco-friendly power, communal cooking and good friends of all ages. The Brougham Street Collective is still under construction. Ruby Alexander “It’s magic, staying connected, not only within your own family but with a whole group of people who have become friends,” says Paula. But there is no blueprint for such magic, as the group found out.



Council approval was a sticking point. Brougham Street failed to secure a permit because “planners just don’t have a model for this kind of development”, Ross says. Related Article Housing affordability What was the Great Australian Dream? “It’s just a tick-box process [for the council]. We say we have a common house, they say, well, what’s a common house? I can’t see a box to tick for that.” Brougham Street was forced to go to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) to overturn the council’s decision, adding about $200,000 in costs. Ross says while the collective was not thrilled about the cost, the only other option was to abandon the project and sell the land.



“The whole community agreed that it was worth it to secure our dream of living in an intentional community together,” Ross says. The cohousing development in Eltham is set to have 20 homes, of two, three and four bedrooms. Ruby Alexander The co-housing model is more common in Europe, and originated in Denmark in the 1960s. The developments are generally small-scale communities of up to 50 households: resident-governed and -planned, rather than developer-led. Some have communal areas, although each community decides its format. Caitlin McGee, UTS Institute for Sustainable Futures research director, says the motivation for co-housing participation was “largely around social connection”, as family structures change and people seek intergenerational support. “I feel like there’s definitely a connection between the kind of rise in social isolation and this kind of renewed desire for co-housing,” she says. “It’s just this idea that people help each other out a bit more in an informal way and live as a community.”



The number of shared households has risen over recent years. Census data for 2021 shows about 848,000 people lived in group households, with about 19 per cent of these aged 55 and above. Related Article Housing affordability What the Great Australian Dream looks like today The at-cost housing project development in Eltham was spearheaded by Tim Riley, developer and founder of Property Collectives, his tenth project of this type. It is a joint venture where collective members get a vote on the management committee, where decisions are made. “These groups are intentional about creating a certain type of community – every project is different and dependent on the land,” he says. Co-housing remains an anomaly in Australia, where the desire for standalone houses on large blocks dominates the property market.



There are 28 completed co-housing developments around the country, including seven finished in the past three years, according to peak body CoHousing Australia. More than 12 other groups are looking for co-housing opportunities. Teresa Dominik, CoHousing Australia’s planning policy working group convenor and a Brougham Street member, says those numbers aren’t precise. Some co-housing communities have had staged construction, with the new stage a new community group. “Also, increasingly, people are doing more informal types of co-housing – often more like co-living but with many of the elements of co-housing. These aren’t listed but go to people looking at alternative and more affordable housing options.” The myth of the quarter-acre block, says Michael Fotheringham, former managing director of the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute, lives on because “the development industry leans into it, as building detached houses on greenfields is the cheapest model”.



Urban spread, fuelled by a preference for detached housing, means Australia’s suburbs are among the lowest-density in the world. “We still build about six detached houses for every apartment,” Fotheringham says. But not everyone wants to live in a traditional detached home. Vincent Murray, 72, became interested in co-housing after being inspired by communities he had seen in France, where homes surround a village square with shared activities and spaces. He and his partner had long maintained separate residences but wanted another housing option as they aged. Vincent Murray thinks that co-housing provides a transition to life after work. Kate Geraghty “A lot of people have their work community but when you retire you lose all of that, so you need to have something else to put in its place. And so the village concept seems perfect for transitioning to a different sort of life after work,” says Murray, a retired academic.



When a flyer from a group called Agency Cohousing and Community – a development for over-50s in inner Sydney’s Balmain – landed in his mailbox, Murray thought he’d found the perfect solution. “I went along to the meeting and became more involved in it,” he says. He later became president of Agency. Related Article Housing affordability Melissa moved into a share house in her 50s. More people are doing the same “Before COVID a lot of people were very enthusiastic about it. We had these meetings with hundreds of people. And then COVID … Because we couldn’t meet because we’re more at the older end of the age spectrum … people became much more fearful about coming out and meeting people.” Dominik says co-housing had traditionally attracted older people. But recent moves to create more intergenerational communities has piqued the interest of younger people and families as housing affordability plummets and loneliness rises.



“The greatest saving is more that you can actually have a smaller house,” Dominik says, noting there can be communal facilities like guest rooms or shared dining rooms. McGee says “conceptually”, co-housing should deliver affordability benefits. “But in places where we have such a housing crisis and land so expensive, that doesn’t end up as the main driver, the main driver is really about the community-building,” she says. At Brougham Street, to ensure the community is diverse, the older members decided to lower the deposit for younger members. Emily Donaldson and her children will be younger members of the co-housing development. Ruby Alexander



“The collective is definitely age-weighted – it’s a bit of a Boomer paradise currently because of the cost,” says Emily Donaldson, 45, a married mother of three girls. Related Article Exclusive

Housing affordability Where first home buyers have been getting into the market this year The houses, while modest, are not exactly affordable, spanning $875,000 to $1,475,000, with an average cost across the 20 homes of $1.06 million. Setting up co-housing developments in Australia is not simple. Challenges include finding suitable land to build and land costs, as well as getting bank financing. Balmain’s Agency, for example, faced a range of challenges in its attempt to set up its community, and has now wound up after about 10 years.



The high cost of land and development building costs, and inability to borrow via conventional banking mechanisms, were some of the roadblocks. “When you’re in a community group with diverse backgrounds and abilities, some have difficulty, first of all, to visualise what it might look like, and also the financial side of it,” Murray says. Murray outside a site in Sydney’s inner west that was considered by Agency Cohousing and Community as an option for their co-housing development. Kate Geraghty Adam Russell, a partner of creative practice Saltbush Projects, which has worked with prospective co-housing dwellers, says from a legal perspective they can be complicated to set up, with roadblocks including approvals, loans and insurance. “Co-housing is, as a mindset, is establishing a habitat where people live in that sort of way, permanently,” he says.



“And legally it’s also a bit complex because the types of buildings that get customised or custom-designed for co-housing don’t have a very clear pathway or definition under planning codes.” Related Article Exclusive

Construction How Zac Efron is turning an Aussie bush block into his forever home Brougham Street faced this and other complications. The upfront costs were nothing to sneeze at. As their co-housing model operates in the private market, groups only have access to commercial debt funding and their own capital. The group also met resistance from locals. But it was the council’s reluctance to issue a building permit for a development they had not seen before that was the major issue.



Riley expected this, and factored VCAT costs into the project. However, the spend went beyond what he’d imagined. “We spent about $200,000 on additional architectural fees to alter our design to make it VCAT-proof, on lawyer fees and expert witnesses – we called traffic, planning and urban design witnesses. There were also the construction cost escalations,” Riley says. This masthead contacted Nillumbik Shire Council but did not receive a reply. VCAT took only 1½ weeks to rule in favour of the collective. It said this was the type of project that “could and should have been supported and fast-tracked”, an “exemplar of an innovative approach” to addressing the housing crisis. Ann Cox at Brougham Street, which is still under development. Ruby Alexander



The Victorian government has introduced a new planning pathway for apartments and townhouses that demonstrate great design. The Great Design Fast Track is available for apartment and townhouse proposals two to eight storeys in height, with eight or more homes. Related Article Housing affordability Cassandra grew up in a large family home. Then she found something better Projects are assessed against the design principles of being neighbourly, welcoming, landscaped, sustainable, healthy, adaptable and good value. “If you get a permit through the process, there is no chance of going to VCAT,” Riley says. In New South Wales, the NSW Housing Pattern Book and fast-track assessment pathways are not designed specifically for co-living developments, but may be applicable depending on the type of proposal.



“In NSW, co-living development proposals are assessed through existing planning approval pathways, depending on the type of housing proposed and the planning controls that apply to the site,” says a spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure. At Brougham Street as of June, all 20 homes on the about-7000-square-metre block have been purchased and are expected to be completed at the end of the year. Brougham Street members at the site of what will be their new homes. Ruby Alexander “We first heard about the collective over coffee at a cafe, and came to an information day,” says Shaun McLeod. He and his wife Suzanne are future residents of the Eltham development. “We were a little unsure at first but the more we read about it, the more we became convinced it was a great idea.”



For Murray, while Agency has closed down, the experience remains valuable. He has made new friends, some of whom are considering buying into a new development in Rozelle. Murray and his partner have purchased side-by-side units off the plan there. Those who still want to continue to meet up. The group also provides assistance to former Agency members in need. “There’s a group of us that meet once a month for dinner and we rotate it around people’s houses … So we’re still continuing on, in a more informal basis.”

World.title: Nelson City Council set to scuttle speed bumps on Tāhunanui Hills
World.content:
Residents divided by the council's decision to remove speed bumps on Nelson's Tāhunanui Hills agree that measures to calm traffic are needed - but are at odds over what that should look like.

"Speed cushions" were installed as a trial on Moana Ave and Bisley Ave in 2024 to slow traffic and reduce rat-running on the streets above SH6.

In March, the Nelson City Council decided to remove them after surveying public opinion and receiving complaints that they were noisy and disruptive.

A group of residents had since campaigned for them to remain, saying there was strong support for their retention and evidence they had improved road safety.

Last week, Mayor Nick Smith said that as no elected members had changed their position since the 8-5 vote to remove the speed bumps, the council's position was unchanged and the bumps would be removed next month.

He said it was a difficult issue with "quite different, valid, but polarised views".

"I personally view the problem as a symptom of inadequate capacity in our transport network into the city that has not kept up with the region's growth, resulting in this route being used for through traffic for which it was not designed, a problem that is affecting a number of neighbourhoods."

Pauline Puklowski, of the Bisley Moana Speed Bump Retention Group, said the decision showed a "shameful disregard for public safety".

It had left residents angry and pitted neighbours against neighbours, instead of enabling them to work together.

"Between all of us, we actually all want the same thing, we want a safe environment that we can all enjoy living in, and I think we should have been given an opportunity to work together better than this."

Puklowski lives on Bisley Ave, above a hairpin bend, and said the speed cushions had "worked perfectly" to reduce crashes and improve safety over the last two-and-a-half years.

Data from the New Zealand Transport Agency showed that between 2019 and 2023 there were 10 crashes on Bisley Ave and one on Moana Ave.

On Bisley Ave, 80 percent of crashes were attributed to loss of control on corners.

There had been two crashes since the speed cushions were in place.

Puklowski said since the bumps weren't perfect, drivers often swerved to try and avoid them, but she was worried that once they were removed, boy racers would return and more crashes would occur.

"Our main concern now is: where do we go? How do we get some form of protection?"

She said the council had not taken heed of the advice of its staff, nor that of residents who were seeking better safety measures, and it felt like there had been a lack of meaningful community consultation on the matter.

"Spending $70,000 removing a proven safety measure is mind-blowing, quite frankly.

"They've pulled the plug with no plan of how they're going to manage the safety issues."

Nicholas Lunn of the Tāhunanui Hills Residents Group is among those who campaigned for the bumps to be removed.

He was pleased the council had stuck to its position, but said residents wanted "21st century traffic calming solutions, not just bollards which create crashing and vibration and noise".

The reduction in crashes could not solely be attributed to the speed bumps, when there were other factors like the opening of Clarence Drive, which offered an alternative route into central Nelson, he said.

Lunn wanted to see the council work with residents to set up a working group to find a solution that worked on the Tāhunanui Hills, and could be rolled out in other parts of Nelson.

He said there were many initiatives that could be considered, and it was unfortunate the issue had created a rift in the community.

The group wanted to see the speed limit reduced on Bisley and Moana Aves and signage that reads "no through traffic for heavy vehicles".

Lunn said the council could also consider chicanes and putting a request to NZTA to install traffic cameras.

"I'm hopeful that we can actually repair that rift and work together with council to actually come up with a proper solution to this because right now we've got the noisy cushions removed, but we haven't actually sorted out the underlying problem.

"The cushions didn't sort that out anyway because they created other problems, and I know that when we put our heads together, we can create lasting solutions that don't impact negatively on people."
