World.title: Delays, cancellations over fire on Auckland's City Rail Link on first day of operation
World.content:
The new City Rail Link network in Auckland is facing delays and cancellations due to a fire at the Waitematā station, a train manager says.

Fire and Emergency are on site at Waitematā Station, where a small fire is understood to have been spotted near the ceiling.

Auckland Transport chief executive Stacey van der Putten said it may have been caused by an electrical short circuit.

"Clearance has been given, recovery to open in progress - services will resume and temporarily bypass Waitemata," she said.

The fire comes as trains began carrying passengers through the long-awaited City Rail Link network for the first time.

Auckland's long-awaited City Rail Link (CRL) opened finally on Sunday morning, with the first train hitting the tracks at 4.57am from Ōtāhuhu into the city.

The $5.5 billion underground rail system, New Zealand's first, is also the country's largest transportation infrastructure project and has taken a decade to build.

The massive project that adds two 3.45km tunnels deep underground that will link Auckland's existing rail lines into one network and allow the rail system to almost quadruple its capacity.

World.title: Warriors toppled by Dolphins in NRL qualifying final
World.content:
The NZ Warriors have been defeated by the Dolphins in their NRL qualifying final, at Go Media Stadium in Auckland.

The Warriors will now have to take the scenic route to the NRL grand final, after bowing to the Dolphins 26-16 on Saturday night.

After finishing second, to earn homefield advantage for the opening round of the playoffs, the Warriors could not take advantage of their fan support and a penalty advantage that had them 12-8 ahead at halftime.

Their only try of the game came when fullback Taine Tuaupiki spun out of a tackle near the line and scooted clear to score. Tuaupiki scored all the Warriors' points, adding a conversion and five penalties, as his team chose to kick for goal, instead of push for tries in the redzone.

They probably should have led by more at the break, but Tuaupiki stretched the margin beyond a converted try, with two more penalties in the second half, before the Dolphins piled on three unanswered converted tries in the final 20 minutes.

The Warriors' cause was not helped by ill-discipline, as centre Adam Pompey was sin-binned for a no-arms shoulder tackle and then second-rower Kurt Capewell was matched for sparking a melee just before halftime.

Dolphins wing Selwyn Cobbo was also sent to the bin in the same incident, after Jackson Ford was dumped in a tipping tackle and the teams came together.

The Warriors lost centre Leka Halasima to injury during the warm-up, with Pompey promoted to the starting line-up in his place.

The Dolphins were good for their win, scoring four tries to the Warriors' one, all converted by wing Jamayne Isaako, and they will now take a rest next week, as they await their opponents for a preliminary final in two weeks.

Meanwhile, the Warriors will host Newcastle Knights next week.

The result broke a six-game winning streak and marked the first time this season they have lost, after leading at halftime.

World.title: Two-thirds of middle-aged adults delay eye tests despite problems - survey
World.content:
More than two-thirds of middle-aged adults are delaying their eye tests despite having problems.

A survey by YouGov commissioned by Specsavers showed that 70 percent of adults between 40 and 59 put off getting their sight checked by more than a month when having trouble with their vision.

Longer delays weren't uncommon with almost half waiting for more than six months to get help, and one in five stalling for more than two years.

Chair of Ophthalmology NZ Dr Sonya Bennett told RNZ it was "probably human nature" to avoid confronting health problems.

"It's not uncommon for us to hear the story that they've put off getting seen until they've got quite significant issues."

She said people would find ways to cope before seeing an optometrist "because they actually don't want to wear glasses" out of vanity or perceived impracticality.

And YouGov's survey found one in five avoided wearing glasses despite needing them because of social perception.

It found half of respondents simply increased texts and display settings on their devices to cope - with a third simply missing out on certain activities because of their eyesight.

Dr Bennett explained that "presbyopia" was the most common age-related cause of eyesight loss, often setting in around middle age.

"It gradually affects your ability to read at near [distance]. Distance vision is usually in most cases okay, but you just lose the ability to see things up close.

"And that's because what we call 'accommodation' - which is the ability to focus - reduces with ageing due to changes in the lens, inside the eye and changes in the muscle that moves the lens."

The survey found nine in 10 had never heard the medical term for this common condition.

She said the only real danger of delaying getting help was if there were another underlying disease, such as glaucoma, where vision could not be regained once lost.

World.title: Man charged after election hoardings damaged in "vandalism spree", police say
World.content:
Charges have been laid against a Tauranga man after what police called a "vandalism spree", damaging political hoardings in Papamoa.

About 30 hoardings were attacked in a two hour period, from about 6:30am on Thursday, police said.

The first damaged were in Parton Road, then more were damaged throughout the suburb of Papamoa.

Senior Sergeant Shannon Clifford thanked the people who had provided information about the damage, which led to an arrest on the same day.

A 43-year-old man faces charges of wilful damage and is scheduled to appear in court again next month.

Ahead of November's general election, the case was a warning that damaging political hoardings is not okay, Senior Sergeant Clifford said:

"The damage in some cases is significant and unfortunately that's an unnecessary cost for the people who own them.

"We won't tolerate this illegal and destructive behaviour in our community."

World.title: Fiji government announces death of a Cabinet Minister
World.content:
Fiji's Government has annouced the death of its Minister for Employment, Productivity and Workplace Relations, Agni Deo Singh.

A government statement said that "It is with great sadness that the Office of the Prime Minister announces the passing of the Minister for Employment, Productivity and Workplace Relations, Agni Deo Singh."

He died in Brisbane.

Prime Minister and chair of the Coalition Cabinet Sitiveni Rabuka extends his deepest condolences to the family, loved ones, colleagues, and friends of the late Minister during this difficult time.

Prime Minister Rabuka acknowledges Singh's dedicated service to the workers and people of Fiji and his invaluable contribution to the Government and the nation.

World.title: Ranfurly Shield stays in Whangārei, after Northland crush Waikato
World.content:
Northland have just one more defence before they can tuck the Ranfurly Shield away for the summer, after seeing off Waikato in Whangārei.

The Taniwha's magic season continued on Saturday as they defended the log o' wood in dominant fashion, hammering the moo-loos 34-17.

Australian import Lachlan Hooper opened the scoring for Northland, before Waikato flyer Dan Sinkinson responded for the Mooloos.

Taha Kemara pushed the conversion wide in trying kicking conditions, to leave Northland in front, a lead they stretched courtesy of a contentious try to halfback Sam Nock.

After a Northland maul splintered, Nock weaved through the mess to dot down as the Waikato players pleaded for an obstruction call which never came.

Rivez Reihana nailed a penalty on the siren, to send his side to half-time with a 15-5 lead.

The Tani's extended their advantage shortly after oranges through James Ramm, but Waikato weren't done, Tepaea Cook-Savage keeping his side in touch with a spectacular finish in the corner.

A second for Hooper put Northland 17 points in front with 15 to play, before Brady Rush sealed the result after Corey Evans stabbed through a grubber, which sat up perfectly for his winger.

Waikato would pick up a late consolation through replacement hooker Sean Ralph.

The win marks the first time Northland have ever beaten Waikato in a shield match, and extends their tenure to two successful defences.

Northland's one remaining shield defence will come against Counties Manukau, on 26 September.

World.title: Sharks hand Dragons NRLW wooden spoon and Eels down Cowboys
World.content:
Parramatta has scored a thrilling 33-28 come-from-behind victory over the Cowboys, and the Sharks have handed the Dragons the wooden spoon with a 16-8 win in the final round of NRLW action.

None of Saturday's teams were in finals contention, but pride was still on the line, and both games were genuine contests.

The matches were played under the experimental rule that allows the side conceding a try to choose whether to kick off or receive, and both games saw teams use the latter option and score shortly after.

In the day's first game, the Eels scored five second-half tries and overcame a 16-point deficit to win a thriller at Western Sydney Stadium.

After losing their opening six matches of the season, the Eels ended 2026 with four wins from their last five starts.

The Cowboys' Charlize Lloyd-Phillips got the scoring under way after just four minutes, but suffered a suspected ACL injury in the process.

Parramatta took less than three minutes to reply, strike centre Rory Owen crossing for her sixth try in four games, before former Wallaroos star Ash Marsters posted the only other try of the half to see the Cowboys up 10-6 at the break.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Cowboys hooker Alisha Foord snuck over two minutes into the second half, and another four-pointer followed quickly to Makenzie Weale to give North Queensland a 22-6 lead.

However, with veteran Kennedy Cherrington sin-binned, the 12-player Eels scored tries to Zali Fay and Jasmin Morrissey to get within six points.

Keilee Joseph then made it three tries in eight minutes to tie things up.

Cowboys interchange hooker Nadia Windleborn put her side back on top, before Joseph again tied the scores.

Experienced half Rachael Pearson stepped up to nail a one-pointer for Parramatta with four minutes remaining, before Owen sealed victory with a stunning 90m effort moments later.

In Saturday's second game, the Sharks came out firing in the second half to defeat the Dragons at Sydney Football Stadium, handing their local rivals the wooden spoon.

It marked Cronulla's first back-to-back wins in 2026 following their upset of the Warriors in Auckland last week.

It took 20 minutes for the first points to be registered, Dragons front-rower Ruby-Jean Kennard-Ellis powering over from 12 metres out for the only score of an opening half littered with 15 errors.

It didn't take as long for points in the second period, with Sharks half Chantay Kiria-Ratu delivering a beautiful short ball two minutes in for China Polata to run 50m to score.

Four minutes later Georgia Hannaway dived over from dummy half for Cronulla's second.

Ellie Johnston made it three tries within 13 minutes for the Sharks, and when Dragons centre Tyra Ekepati was sin-binned for a high shot it looked like Cronulla may run away with it, but the Dragons held strong in those 10 minutes.

Shenae Ciesiolka scored a consolation try for the Dragons in her 50th NRLW appearance, but it was too little, too late.

AAP

World.title: Lions keep three-peat dream alive with 53-point mauling of Adelaide
World.content:
The Brisbane Lions are through to the AFL's final four, keeping their three-peat dream alive with a 53-point mauling of Adelaide at the Gabba.

Charlie Cameron kicked five goals as the Lions used an outrageous early onslaught to cruise to a 21.18 (144) to 13.13 (91) triumph and will face Hawthorn in a preliminary final next weekend.

Challenged after defeat to Sydney last week, a number of Brisbane's best players stepped up with Zac Bailey, Cam Rayner and Will Ashcroft all terrific in a comprehensive win.

Adelaide champion Taylor Walker kicked two goals in the last quarter of his career before bidding a tearful goodbye after full-time.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Hawks' AFLW win soured by skipper's sickening leg injury
World.content:
Aine McDonagh has fired Hawthorn to an 11-point win over the Western Bulldogs that was soured by captain Emily Bates's serious leg injury.

Bates was taken off the field on a stretcher at the Kennedy Community Centre today after her right leg twisted underneath her in a tackle late in the third quarter.

The decorated 30-year-old, who played her 100th AFLW match a week earlier, was expected to be taken to hospital for further assessment.

The Hawks also lost Laura Stone (concussion) after an early head clash with an opponent and were 11 points down at half-time.

But Daniel Webster's side piled on five unanswered goals in the third quarter — four of those before Bates's injury — to set up their 6.5 (41) to 4.6 (30) victory.

The result lifted Hawthorn (3-2 win-loss record) into the top eight, leapfrogging the Bulldogs (3-2) on percentage.

Irish key forward McDonagh kicked a career-best four majors, extending her lead at the top of this season's goal-kicking list.

Eliza West (24 disposals), Tamara Smith (20) and Jasmine Fleming (19) also shone for the Hawks, as did ruck Lucy Wales.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Isabelle Pritchard had match-high tallies of 31 disposals and eight clearances for the Bulldogs, with Elisabeth Georgostathis (19 disposals) also busy.

The Bulldogs kicked three of the first four goals but were held scoreless in the third quarter as the Hawks took control of the contest.

Meanwhile, Sunny Lappin kicked three goals and sparked the second-half surge that led to Gold Coast's 30-point win over Collingwood.

The Suns (3-2) kicked four goals to one in the third term — two of those to Lappin — to set up their 9.8 (62) to 4.8 (32) victory in Carrara.

Maddy Brancatisano kicked two goals, Charlie Rowbottom had 29 disposals and Dekota Baron provided the highlight of the day with a towering mark-of-the-year contender.

Mikayla Nurse suffered a nasty cut on the face after a head clash with Suns teammate Lucy Single late in the match.

Tarni White had 29 disposals for Collingwood (0-5), which remains winless this season.

Cats and Eagles score historic victories

Georgie Prespakis of the Cats and Ebony Marinoff of the Crows. (Getty Images: Sarah Reed/AFL Photos)

Later on Saturday, Geelong's Georgie Prespakis and West Coast's Ella Roberts starred as their teams each recorded a first win over their opponents.

The Cats (4-1) retained a top-four spot, scoring a fourth-straight victory and their first in seven attempts against the Crows (2-3), with an 8.9 (57) to 6.10 (46) win at Adelaide's Unley Oval.

Gun midfielder Prespakis was dynamic for Geelong, racking up match highs of 32 disposals, 19 contested possessions and nine clearances.

In Perth, West Coast (1-4) posted their first win of the season in a 6.10 (46) to 6.5 (41) victory over Brisbane (2-3).

It was their first AFLW win over the Lions in four attempts after three heavy defeats.

Young Eagles superstar Roberts put in a mammoth performance, leading the game in possessions (33), contested possessions (19), clearances (11), tackles (eight) and metres gained (700).

AAP

World.title: Trindall returns from shoulder dislocation to lead Sharks in finals win
World.content:
One month after dislocating his shoulder, Braydon Trindall has returned to lead the Cronulla Sharks to a 26-16 win, advancing to the second week of the NRL finals while knocking out the North Queensland Cowboys.

Trindall missed the final four matches of the NRL regular season after suffering the shoulder dislocation in round 24 against the Canberra Raiders, with the Sharks losing three of those games.

With a heavily strapped shoulder, Trindall looked uncomfortable throughout the match but remained strong in defence.

Trindall's kicking game put North Queensland's back-three under pressure, with two drops from Cowboys fullback Scott Drinkwater, with one leading to a first-half try.

He set up the match-sealing try late in the second half, with his 31st assist of the season putting fullback Will Kennedy over for his side's fifth try.

The Sharks will meet the loser of Sunday's qualifying final between the Penrith Panthers and Sydney Roosters.

Meanwhile, the Dolphins scored three tries in the final 20 minutes of the club's maiden NRL finals match to stun the Warriors in Auckland.

Herbie Farnworth scores for the Dolphins during their qualifying final win over the Warriors. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

In a fiery contest which had three players sent to the sin bin in the first half, the Dolphins were hampered by indiscipline.

Both sides had one try each after 60 minutes, but five penalty goals from Warriors fullback Taine Tuaupiki gave the Auckland-based side a 16-6 lead with a quarter to play.

But the Dolphins ran in three tries, including a length-of-the-field effort started and finished by Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow to take the lead in the 66th minute.

The Dolphins have earned the right to host a preliminary final at Lang Park in Brisbane in a fortnight, while the Warriors will host the Newcastle Knights next week in a knock-out semifinal.

"It is big. It is massive for everyone involved at the club," Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf said.

"The club has done such a good job over the last four years in every department, but the blokes that deserve the credit are the players with the way they played tonight and the bravery they showed under pressure.

"They are in this position for a reason and that's because they want to work hard for each other."

Relive all of Saturday's NRL finals action in the blog below.

World.title: Newcastle's finals win is proof the future has come
World.content:
If Newcastle were going to pull off a classic finals ambush on South Sydney they were going to need some new heroes to be born under the bright lights of the Sydney Football Stadium.

The Knights went into the game light up front, not in size, strength or willingness, but certainly in experience and definitely in recognition. After their 20-10 win over South Sydney, however, they will never have the luxury of being underestimated again.

Across 80 minutes of a classic blood-and-thunder final, fresh faces and young legs won the day as the star-studded Rabbitohs outfit fought on despite being busted until they were finally beaten.

NRL Finals live Newcastle holds on for a 20-10 victory over South Sydney to kick-off the 2026 finals series, but Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett fumes at more Bunker confusion after a contentious call.

Perhaps it could have all been different were it not for Cody Walker falling to a sniper's shot early in the second half, suffering a calf injury that ended his night early.

The ageless Walker is what binds the Rabbitohs left edge together and takes it from a series of talented individuals to the closest thing rugby league has to a hammer of the gods.

But you'll find little sympathy for an injury up Newcastle way. They were without Dylan Brown, Dylan Lucas, Trey Mooney and Jacob Saifiti heading into this and while plenty expected them to fight few expected them to win.

After their first finals win away from home in 13 years, expectations be damned. They defied them all over the park, perhaps no more than down their right, where backrower Jermaine McEwan had the game of his young life.

It was always going to be a big night for the 21-year old, one way or the other. It was he who would be tasked with setting up Newcastle's defences against the Rabbitohs knockout left.

He did that with aplomb, even before Walker went down, from setting the tone with driving hits from the inside to holding his width and his nerve when Souths gave their chainsaw a rip.

Throw in two tries and it's the last time McEwan will catch anybody by surprise.

Together that Knights edge put together some of the best defensive plays of the night, but it wasn't the biggest — that honour must belong to McEwan's backrow partner, Francis Manuleleua.

They call him "Big Frisco" and people were put in Alcatraz for the type of violence he dropped on Cameron Murray late in the first half as he raced out of the line to dish out one of the hits of the season.

Technically it was illegal — the shot was clean, but Manuleleua was half a metre offside. The red and blue hordes at the southern end of the ground didn't seem to care, even though Souths scored off the field position, because sometimes it's worth it.

Paying the blood price for a little bit of rough stuff is something Dane Gagai and Latrell Mitchell know well.

The two centres fought like demons after a scuffle midway through the first half and while both won their share of battles it was Gagai who won the war.

Gagai is one of the few older heads in this side — you can call him older but don't call him old, whatever you do — and only a player as sure as himself as the 35-year old would risk poking a bear like Mitchell.

It's something few have done while surviving to tell the tale but Gagai didn't just weather the might and power, he fought like a far younger man, with nothing held back and no regard for his own safety.

His try in the 25th minute was a snapshot the endless love of competition that keeps him young even as the years keep passing and his roar of triumph after he was first to a Sandon Smith kick was among the first harbingers of what was unfolding.

There were other fine battles and contributors — Bradman Best and Jack Wighton, who was close to his side's best, went hell for leather on the other side of the field to Gagai and Mitchell.

Tyson Frizell had a game up front that puts the war back into warhorse and Keaon Koloamatangi left everything out there in his final game as a Rabbitoh.

Kalyn Ponga, once the sun around which everything in Newcastle orbited, was prominent throughout but the class of Smith and Fletcher Sharpe meant the whole game was not on his shoulders and the Knights fullback thrived as a result.

It meant he was able to access the best parts of his game, something the Rabbitohs found difficult throughout even as a torrid defensive effort and several last gasp saves by Campbell Graham kept their heads above water.

They will be haunted by the hypothetical over the summer after their first trip to the finals in four years fell at the first hurdle.

Walker cut a forlorn figure on the South Sydney bench. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

If only Walker didn't get injured, or at least had made it through more of the game.

If only Bud Sullivan's circus act of a try wasn't chalked off for a knock on from Alex Johnston that could have easily been called a strip, just as Dom Young's try could have easily been rubbed off the board.

If only Brandon Smith's last desperate effort with three minutes left — which would have forced a big finish at the very least — didn't come up a blade of grass short.

If only, on a night where they played something resembling their top side for one of the first times all season, they were able to tap into the tried and true talent that lurks somewhere within and rises to the surface enough to tantalise and tease.

They are a team built for the present with stars who made their reputation on tearing down what came before them. That's the law of the jungle and the nature of the game.

The Rabbitohs will fancy their chances of returning to the mix next year but this time around were served a reminder there comes a time when the young feed on the old.

This night was such a time and with nothing to lose and everything to prove, Newcastle was ravenous.

World.title: Shelton through to US Open final as he looks to end 23-year drought
World.content:
American eighth seed Ben Shelton has the chance to end his country's long wait for another men's US Open champion after beating compatriot Frances Tiafoe to reach the final.

Shelton posted a 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory over Tiafoe in the second semi-final and will play top seed Alexander Zverev in the final on Monday morning, AEST.

He showed plenty of energy after ousting defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a quarterfinal match that ended at 3:33 am Wednesday, local time.

It was the latest finish to a match in US Open history.

Andy Roddick was the most recent American to win the men's US Open title, in 2003.

Zverev will play for his second major title this year after beating Karen Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (9/7), 7-6 (8/6) in the first semi.

Zverev, who had long been considered the best men's player without a major, finally broke through at the French Open this year. The German followed by reaching the Wimbledon final, which he lost to Jannik Sinner, and is 24-2 in grand slam matches this season.

"Sometimes just things go your way and I feel like I've had a lot of struggles at the major level. I was so close so many times and maybe this year God has said that this is going to be your year and just enjoy the time on the court," Zverev said.

Alexander Zverev on his way to a straight-sets win against Karen Khachanov. (Getty Images: Manuela Davies/USTA)

Now he will try to win the title that he still can't believe he let get away in 2020. Zverev won the first two sets against Dominic Thiem but then lost in a fifth-set tiebreaker, as Thiem became the first man to win the US Open title after dropping the first two sets since 1949.

Zverev was solid after going up two sets this time, and has won 13 consecutive sets after becoming the first number one-seeded man to play five-setters in each of the first two rounds of a major.

Khachanov was trying to reach his first major final after a surprising run in New York. He arrived with a losing record for the season but went on to reach his third grand slam semifinal, including second at the US Open.

He started playing better after dropping the first set and then falling behind 2-0 in the second. He finally broke Zverev's serve to tie it and it stayed even until they went to the tiebreaker. The Russian erased Zverev's first two set points in it before Zverev finished it off by winning a 34-shot rally.

Khachanov then had leads of 3-0 and 5-2 in the third-set tiebreaker before Zverev battled back.

World.title: Aussie athletics star shocked at massive pay packet for coming second
World.content:
Nicola Olyslagers has had the best bad night of her career after missing out on becoming a new 'Ultimate' athletics high jump champion, only to learn to her surprise that she had still leapt to the biggest payday of her life.

Australia's world champion only managed to clear 1.95m on the first night of World Athletics' inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest this morning (AEST).

She struggled with her approach on a difficult surface on a cold night as Ukraine's Olympic champ Yaroslava Mahuchikh beat her to the title with a 1.99m leap.

Olyslagers' runner-up spot earned her $US75,000 ($105,000) — $5,000 more than she pocketed for winning the world title last year — as part of the record $US10 million ($14 million) prize pot for the streamlined new event that World Athletics hopes will attract a host of new fans.

Only when speaking to reporters afterwards did Olyslagers realise just what she would be taking home.

Nicola Olyslagers clears the bar on her way to second in the high jump. (Getty Images: Christel Saneh/World Athletics)

"What? Really? I genuinely thought it was just first prize got the 150k and second was like 10,000," she said.

"You are the bearer of good news. That's fantastic."

Olyslagers, wrapped in a scarf and still shivering 40 minutes after her event, said she struggled with her approach on a firm-surface run-up but, with more than half the field exiting early, she realised that after two fails at 1.95 a clearance would be enough for second place.

She duly sailed over at the final attempt, punching the air in delight.

"That's the happiest I've ever been after a 1.95. I think I celebrated as if I'd won the whole competition and it was a really good jump," she said.

"It just showed tonight that all of us were a little bit tired but I mean, that 95 jump, I'm still living off that."

Olyslagers' domestic rival Eleanor Patterson also looked uncomfortable all evening but took joint third with a modest clearance of 1.91 a week after she'd jumped 10cm higher to win the Diamond League crown.

"It's the lowest I've jumped all year. Really, really frustrating," Commonwealth champ Patterson said.

"After the best season of my life I really wanted to enjoy it but I didn't really."

Marschall fourth as Duplantis stars again

Meanwhile, triple Commonwealth pole vault champion Kurtis Marschall managed only fourth with a best of 5.95m as Swedish superstar Armand Duplantis again revelled in being the star attraction, having seen the event open with a theme song he had both co-written and performed.

With the title secure after a faultless run to 6.20m, the spellbound full house of 20,000 willed him to clear a world record 6.32, but he narrowly failed in what would have been a remarkable 16th world best in six years.

Earlier, Australia's Ky Robinson gave it a real go in the 5,000m, leading at the bell, but got swallowed up in the run for home as Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen roared back to his best with a superbly-judged victory charge.

Sarah Billings ran well in her 800m semi-final to qualify for tomorrow's final when there will be four more Australians in action.

Abbey Caldwell and Jess Hull will go in the women's 1,500m, Mackenzie Little in the javelin and Oceania record holder Lachlan Kennedy in the men's 100m.

World.title: England has won 38 straight Tests but Wallaroos won't die wondering
World.content:
On paper, the Wallaroos aren't given a chance of beating England in this weekend's WXV Global Series Test.

The Red Roses, as England is known, are on a 38-match winning streak, stretching back to 2022.

They're reigning Women's Rugby World Cup winners and have claimed eight straight Six Nations titles, which include a run of five consecutive Grand Slams.

Why Wallaroos are 'family' Past and present Wallaroos players reflect on the journey and challenges to reaching 100 Tests.

England has never lost to the Wallaroos, with the most recent meeting — in last year's World Cup — finishing in a 47-7 victory to the tournament hosts in Bristol.

The Australians, though, aren't intimidated ahead of the Test in Salford, which will be played on Sunday morning, AEST.

They respect the Red Roses, but possess a quiet confidence in their ability to compete with the world champions.

"I think it will be a hard challenge," said Wallaroos winger Amelia Whitaker, who will make her Test debut.

"Obviously England [is] number one, but this week I feel like we've really rallied together so I think we're up for the task."

Amelia Whitaker will make her Test debut for the Wallaroos. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Wallaroos reserve forward Jemma Bemrose, who could debut off the bench, was similarly undaunted.

"They've [Red Roses] got a strong reputation, and they've achieved a lot as a team," Bemrose said.

"But I'm just really excited to embrace the challenge."

Wallaroos assistant coach Mike Ruthven knows England's strengths, but he believed there might be a chink in the Red Roses' armour.

"They're a pretty complete footy team," Ruthven said.

"We know what's coming, but we think we've identified a few things that we've been really able to target and have a crack at."

Rugby's 'benchmark'

The Red Roses' status as the top-ranked nation in the world did not come by chance.

England's governing body, the Rugby Football Union (RFU), made a wise investment in the women's game when it offered full-time contracts to players in 2019.

The Red Roses now have 32 full-time contracted players for the 2026/27 season, with an additional six players on transition contracts.

England won last year's Women's Rugby World Cup on home soil. (Getty Images/World Rugby: Molly Darlington)

England's pathways haven't been ignored either, with the RFU boasting it's invested 14.5 million pounds ($27 million) in the community game.

The national team also benefits from a thriving club competition, Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR), which involves nine clubs playing 16 league matches each before a finals series is contested.

The RFU announced in June it's committing 24 million pounds ($45 million) to PWR across 10 years.

The Red Roses have been embraced by the English public, with 219,439 spectators attending their World Cup matches last year, including a global record of 81,885 at Twickenham when they beat Canada 33-13 in the final.

There was also a 336 per cent increase in TV viewing hours during the tournament, helping raise the visibility of the players amid England's crowded sporting landscape.

This is reflected in the fact that star back Ellie Kildunne finished runner-up in 2025's publicly voted BBC Sports Personality of the Year Award, outpolling the likes of Formula 1 world champion Lando Norris.

Ellie Kildunne is among the most recognisable figures in English sport. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

It's all food for thought for Rugby Australia (RA), which is shifting the Wallaroos to a full-time program ahead of the 2029 World Cup to be hosted on home soil.

Some positive steps have already been made, such as the appointment of successful rugby sevens coach Tim Walsh as RA's director of women's high performance.

Rugby Australia setting high standards Only three years out from hosting the Women's Rugby World Cup, Australia makes a key appointment it hopes will help deliver success on the international stage.

Australia has the playing and coaching talent to become a World Cup contender, but as Walsh recently acknowledged to ABC Sport, the Wallaroos must have the "infrastructure for them to be able to excel".

Ruthven, who is working under Walsh on the Wallaroos' staff until incoming coach Sione Fukofuka begins next year, rated England's program as the gold standard.

"The RFU have done a great job to support the women's game over here, underpinned by a really strong PWR competition," Ruthven said.

"You look at their players, and they're playing 20-odd competitive games of domestic football.

"You would like to think that is a bit of a benchmark. I think Rugby Australia are doing a really good job at the moment to … take the women's space to a similar level."

The Wallaroos are in the process of becoming a full-time program. (Getty Images: Phil Walter)

The Red Roses deserve to be the "benchmark" both on and off the field, and it's no surprise they're overwhelming favourites to win Sunday's Test, which is expected to be played in front of a sell-out crowd.

But as the Wallaroos squad have reminded themselves this week, it's a "two-horse race over 80 minutes".

"If we can go out and deliver on the things that we've talked about during the week and deliver on them consistently and compete really hard, stranger things have happened, right?" Ruthven said.

Tech.title: StarCraft returns in 2030 as an open-world shooter
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Blizzard originally tried to bring the StarCraft universe to the world of 3D shooters way back in 2002 with StarCraft: Ghost. It sat in development hell for years until Blizzard president Mike Morhaime confirmed that it had been canceled in 2014. Now Blizzard is giving it another go with the simply titled StarCraft. Dan Hay, a VP at Blizzard, took the stage at BlizzCon today to reveal that after more than a decade of lying dormant, StarCraft would be returning in 2030. But, rather than another top-down real-time strategy installment, the new title would be an open-world shooter.

He then showed off a cinematic trailer for the title that focused on the human United Earth Directorate faction as they prepare to face off against the Zerg. The Protoss are limited to passing mention. What’s obvious from the trailer is that the new take on the StarCraft franchise won’t be pulling many punches. After a rousing call to militarism, the propaganda-fueled human is faced with the brutal realities of battle, and the character we’ve been following for the last 3 minutes is revealed to be disposable fuel for the meat grinder of war.

While fans are definitely excited that Blizzard is defrosting the long-dormant series, I’m sure plenty are still holding their breath, hoping for a proper RTS follow-up to 2010’s StarCraft II.

Tech.title: Sylvan Esso think you should splurge on good-quality yogurt
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amelia Meath and Nick Sanborn, better known as Sylvan Esso, have been bringing their low-key electro-pop to the masses since 2014, bursting onto the scene with their self-titled debut album and the single “Hey Mami.” Over the years, they’ve put out a number of excellent records, dabbling in dustier, more fragile textures on Free Love, going dancier and glitchier on No Rules Sandy. The two are constantly pushing at the edges of their sound while retaining the core of what makes a Sylvan Esso record sound like a Sylvan Esso record.

Their new album Ow ∞, released this past Friday, represents perhaps the boldest reinvention of their sound, however. It’s unabashedly nostalgic-sounding, trading the glitchy modular drums and glossy dance production of Free Love for turn-of-the-century breakbeats and distorted guitars. At times, the songs recall bands like Soul Coughing and Blur, on tracks like “Hot Slob” and “Concrete Glen.” But don’t worry, there’s still plenty of bleeps and bloops and modern vocal production techniques to keep fans of past albums happy.

To celebrate the release of Ow ∞ , Sylvan Esso agreed to answer our weekly questionnaire.

What is your most indispensable tool?

Nick Sanborn: My laptop. I have loved a series of MacBooks dating back to when I graduated from high school and cannot imagine working without one. I am absolutely one of those millennials who despises typing or doing any important work on a touchscreen.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

NS: I wish it felt like it cared more about me than its creator.

Amelia Meath: I wish the phone was actually a food replicator. So many problems would be solved.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

NS: Eight, which feels a touch low compared to my normal ADHD tab expanse. No pins besides email, though, I like a tabula rasa scene when I open a browser.

What is your happy place online?

NS: I still frequent a version of the old Monome forum, which is generally focused on programming and instrument design. The people there are excellent and interesting and so welcoming and nice. It’s the only place on the internet that feels more positive than detrimental to me.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

AM: I had a T-Mobile Sidekick that I saved up for when I was in high school. It was the coolest phone I have ever owned. I kept my journal on there :D

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

NS: EarthBound, which was a gorgeous, heartfelt, quirky JRPG on the Super Nintendo that came out in 94. It’s beautiful and strange and full of humanity. I still play it all the way through every few years.

AM: The first Zelda I played was Skyward Sword on the Wii. We lived in a house with a whole bunch of other people, and we would all hang and play together. It was a joy and became my gateway into playing games as an adult. There have been so many others that I have fallen in love with since then — Hollow Knight, Blue Prince, Hades — but Skyward Sword was my first love. So much lore.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

AM: The encouragement of apathy.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

NS: I rarely wish I had made something that I already like, since I feel like me making it would have ruined it being what it is in the first place. But I have been dreaming about a really specific thing — an AM/FM radio with an analog tuner that I could control remotely with a computer or sequencer — for literal years. There are many things out there that are close but not quite this, so much so that it’s kinda maddening. I even tried to get a synth tech I work with regularly to help me prototype one, but it never came to fruition. Finally, last year, a small company in Italy started making one, and like four friends sent me the link in a week, that was how endlessly chatty I had been about wanting one. Of course I ordered one, and it’s good, but I still think it could be better lol.

AM: I wish I had the well. What an incredible claim to fame. “I figured out how to store and save water from the table.” I feel like I could stop trying after that.

What do you do when you need to focus?

AM: I go outside and sit. Usually, I have to be writing, so I can take my notebook out. I try to leave my phone inside, but I usually forget!

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

NS: I usually find myself stuck when I want something to be good and it just isn’t yet, but I can’t let it go. In that situation, I just have to step away and do something totally different and without consequence, like pulling out an instrument I haven’t used in a while and making something unrelated as spontaneously as I can. I find removing expectations and shifting gears to be really helpful for my headspace when I can’t find a way through whatever has me in a loop.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

NS: About a month ago, I put my phone through both the washer and dryer, destroying it completely and giving me about a week of pure phoneless existence. It was heaven. Highly recommend.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

AM: I just bought Sheila Heti’s Pure Colour at a bookstand in Brooklyn. It is a beautiful and incredibly surreal read.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

NS: Yogurt. It’s not even that much of a splurge, but I just think good yogurt is utterly transcendent. Deeply underrated delicacy.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

AM & NS: “Ow ∞”

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

AM: This is also the last GIF I used!!!

Tech.title: Anthropic CEO says it’s time to pump the brakes on AI
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says the time has come to slow down AI development and will give third-party evaluators like METR access to its models to help ensure its “adherence to safety practices and commitments.” In a winding essay, Amodei proposed a three-step plan to “pace the frontier” — jargon that simply means to slow the pace of training and development to give companies time to build safeguards and regulators to evaluate models.

Amodei says that giving external evaluators wide-ranging access is just the first step, and one it is taking now unilaterally. Step two would involve the industry coming together as a whole, likely with government agencies to “establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.” This step would focus on AI companies operating in democratic countries, but because passing laws and building regulatory infrastructure takes time, Amodei says that the industry should work together to create safety standards.

The third step would be the most challenging — getting authoritarian governments like those in China and Russia to agree to slow development and adopt a global set of AI safety standards. But he also says it’s crucial that the US and other democracies maintain a technological lead over China and other authoritarian regimes by limiting their access to high-powered chips and cracking down on things like distillation that allow companies to quickly catch up by training its AI to replicate the behavior of a more powerful model.

Amodei says that his concern stems from two primary factors. First is the emergence of recursive self-improvement, or RSI, in which AI systems train the next generation of AI, leading to rapidly accelerating capabilities. “Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems,” he says. The other is this summer’s OpenAI / Hugging Face incident, in which “a swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack and that were unrelated to the task at hand, sacrificing themselves for the success of the group, and attempting to hack into the “grader” responsible for evaluating their performance.“

Of course, Anthropic’s Claude was also responsible for a series of rogue AI hacking incidents that have recently put the company under the spotlight.

Tech.title: LG responds to TV spying allegations
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Earlier this week, Gamers Nexus, Level1Techs, and independent security researchers detailed some alarming findings about how LG’s TVs are logging and uploading data on its users. Now the company is pushing back against those allegations, saying that “Some recent media coverage may have contributed to misconceptions about how LG smart TVs work.”

LG released a statement in which it claims that its “TVs do not continuously record or transmit users’ conversations,” and that wake-word detection is all processed locally. However, the word “continuously” is doing a lot of heavy lifting here as Gamers Nexus demonstrated an LG TV keeping extensive logs of ambient conversations long after one would assume its AI assistant had stopped listening.

LG also said that its features like “Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), voice recognition, and interest-based advertising are optional,” and “not enabled by default.” The company says that:

ACR uses audio fingerprinting technology using the TV’s internal audio processor (not a speaker) to identify content and does not collect screenshots, screen recordings, video recordings, voice recordings, or other audio recordings from the TV.

The company did not address broader concerns about how much data it collects, who it shares it with, the potential for bad actors to exploit its features, or the misleading way in which its privacy options are presented.

Tech.title: Trump is giving data centers a pass to pollute
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

President Donald Trump is weakening environmental regulations in the name of speeding up the construction of AI data centers, raising health risks for Americans, a cadre of former EPA officials said this week in a briefing and new report. They are urging — perhaps futilely — the president to adopt a “Data Center Health Protection Pledge” to signal that the administration is taking the environmental threat seriously.

As a result of the Trump administration’s deregulation spree and attacks on renewable energy, the wave of new AI data centers is increasingly powered by dirty energy that can impact Americans’ health even if they don’t live near a data center, the group of EPA alumni warn. They say that the agency they once worked for, which was created to “protect human health and the environment,” is no longer the watchdog it should be as the physical infrastructure underpinning generative AI changes America’s landscape.

“You would think that an industry buildout of this magnitude, billed as a revolution, would mean more vigilance from EPA.”

“You would think that an industry buildout of this magnitude, billed as a revolution, would mean more vigilance from EPA,” Lynn Goldman, a pediatrician and a former EPA assistant administrator, said at the briefing. “Instead, EPA is doing just the opposite, thinking first about industry’s needs and weakening or reconsidering limits on toxic chemicals and harmful pollutants.”

Goldman and other former EPA employees who are part of an independent organization called the Environmental Protection Network released a report this week that identifies 30 different federal actions since January 2025 that they say exacerbate health risks stemming from data center pollution.

That includes executive actions and proposals meant to curtail renewable energy projects while softening pollution regulations and exempting existing power plants and factories from certain standards. Of the 30 policy changes included in the report, 17 specifically mention AI or target data centers.

Trump released an “AI Action Plan” in July 2025, recommending “streamlining or reducing regulations” under the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and Superfund law to expedite permitting for data center projects and chip factories. “What the AI plan is really about [is] using unprecedented emergency powers to grant massive new exemptions for data centers and specifically fossil fuel infrastructure,” Tyson Slocum, energy program director at the consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, told The Verge at the time.

“You do not need to be near a data center to be affected, because the pollution doesn’t just come from the data centers themselves,“ Goldman says.

“A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable. It depends on the choices government makes now.”

Last year, hundreds of current EPA employees fired off a public letter addressed to Zeldin saying, “EPA under your leadership will not protect communities from hazardous chemicals and unsafe drinking water, but instead will increase risks to public health and safety.”

The new report cites a study from UC Riverside, Caltech, and the Rochester Institute of Technology that found that air pollution associated with AI could lead to up to 1,300 premature deaths and more than $20 billion in public health costs by 2028. The toll could be even larger after factoring in the policy changes outlined in EPN’s report, according to the organization. The US can avoid those losses by restoring clean air and water standards, as well as rebuilding federal agencies’ capacity to enforce those rules, the EPA alumni argue.

“A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable. It depends on the choices government makes now,” Marc Boom, EPN’s senior director of public affairs, said in the briefing. “EPA should be measuring how this buildout is changing pollution, who is being exposed, what it means for their health, and making all of that information public. That is what a Data Center Health Protection Pledge should mean in practice.”

Responding to the report in an email to The Verge, EPA spokesperson Cora Mandy said, “In each action EPA has taken, the agency has returned regulations to the best reading [of] the Clean Air Act after years of overreach by previous administrations.” She also reiterated the agency’s commitment to “Protect Human Health and The Environment” while simultaneously prioritizing “Making America the AI Capital of the World.”

Tech.title: Laika’s stop-motion fantasy Wildwood looks so smooth
Tech.content:
Due to a scheduling mishap, I was only able to check out two movies on my second day at the Toronto International Film Festival — but I did manage to get an early look at and some fascinating details on one of my most anticipated films this year.

Even if you don’t know the name Laika, you probably know the studio’s work; it’s the animation house behind stop-motion hits like ParaNorman, The Boxtrolls, and Kubo and the Two Strings. Over the years Laika’s films have steadily gotten more impressive on both a technical and artistic level. Which brings us to the incredible-looking Wildwood, hitting theaters next month. If you’re unfamiliar, here’s a look:

Some of the crew from Laika was on stage at TIFF to talk about the making of Wildwood, in particular why this film looks more lifelike than the studio’s previous work. There are a few reasons. One has to do with the animation itself, which, as you can see in the trailer, is incredibly smooth in the new film. “We’re in the midst of the evolution of an art form,” Laika’s head of animation Brad Schiff explained. “Because we have digital cameras, we’re able to see what we’re doing; we have what we call frame-grabbers.” This lets Laika’s animators see all of the recently-shot frames as they’re animating, allowing them to track every single movement of a puppet, ensuring everything moves smoothly. “There’s no reason for stuttery animation, other than a stylistic choice,” Schiff said.

The puppets themselves are also more advanced. They utilize an internal “diaphragm” that Laika calls a breather, which the studio first experimented with on its previous film, 2019’s Missing Link. This time, all of the major puppets are outfitted with breathers, and this lets the animators make characters appear to breathe in a lifelike way, so that they seem more human in the final product.

You can see some of that in the trailer above, but I was also able to watch a handful of clips from the film, and — despite Laika stressing that they weren’t final — they looked incredible. One showed a fast and tense bike chase through a bustling version of Portland, where Wildwood takes place. There was a speed and tension to it that felt like a live-action sequence. In the movie, a young girl named Prue loses her little brother in an “impassable wilderness” that’s home to a rich fantasy world. In the clips I saw, she did everything from escaping an ornate mansion filled with guard dogs distracted by their own tails, to soaring above a vast landscape while on the back of a giant bird. Wildwood looked as stylish and detailed as you’d expect from a Laika production, but what impressed me the most was how realistic it all felt in motion.

A few other details for those who love numbers: Wildwood features 233 puppets (36 are just versions of Prue), was brought to life by 49 animators, and took 231 weeks from start to finish. It’s in theaters on October 23rd.

As for the movies I was able to actually catch on day 2 of TIFF, they were both great, but also, could not be more different. One is a sweetly morbid musical, the other a life-affirming family film made with traditional animation. And if you missed my previous TIFF coverage — including films like All of a Sudden and The Only Living Pickpocket in New York — you can check it out right here.

Julián

No theatrical date yet

Julián comes via Irish animation studio Cartoon Saloon, best known for the features Song of the Sea and Wolfwalkers. And it shares much in common with the studio’s previous work, telling the story of a child lost in a world of fantasy. In this case it’s seven-year-old Julián who goes to live with his grandmother in Brooklyn while his dad is on a work trip. Julián is obsessed with ocean life and anything pretty, so when he meets some kids making costumes for an upcoming mermaid parade, joining in becomes his sole focus in life. But his colorful personality often clashes with his more conservative grandmother, and when some boys bully Julián for wearing a mermaid tail, he starts to retreat into himself. Ultimately, Julián is a fairly straightforward tale about being yourself and allowing others to do the same, but it’s told with tremendous style and passion, making it a welcome addition to the studio’s catalog. Plus, the ending is almost guaranteed to make you tear up.

Stuffed

No theatrical date yet

A love story between an eccentric taxidermist and the man who agrees to give up his life in order to fulfill her lifelong dream of stuffing a human. Oh, and also it’s a musical. Stuffed has shades of Sweeney Todd, but despite its macabre premise, it’s much more heartfelt. Barrie (Harry Melling) lives a sad life working at a sandwich factory, collecting obituaries, and caring for his aging mother. But he’s obsessed with being remembered, and when he answers an online ad promising to make him “exceptional,” he meets Araminta (Jodie Comer), whose house is filled with taxidermied animals, but who has also always wanted to take the next step. Their interests, it seems, line up: she wants to stuff a person, he wants to live forever. But as they work together on the weirdo plan, the two become close, complicating the whole killing Barry thing. Stuffed is morbid and occasionally wince-inducing, but it’s also filled with a lot of love and heart, and a not-so-surprising amount of humor.

Tech.title: Where to preorder the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max are almost here. Announced at Apple’s September 2026 “Sunrise and shine” event alongside the iPhone Duo and other new gear, the two upgraded phones feature the faster A20 Pro processor with more GPU power as well as more neural cores for AI-related tasks, plus some welcome improvements to the camera.

The phones will arrive on Friday, September 18th, and preordering one is never a bad idea if you want to ensure you get the color and storage capacity configuration you’re seeking. Speaking of, preorders are officially open.

The 6.3-inch iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for the 256GB model, and goes all the way up to $2,399 for the version with 2TB of storage. The larger 6.9-inch iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for 256GB, with the 2TB model costing $2,499. Both phones are available in four colors: deep black, silver, glacier, and burgundy.

At the time of publication, the only way to preorder an unlocked version of the Pro or Pro Max is directly from Apple. You have some options if you don’t want to pay the full price upfront. Financing through Apple is an option (36 monthly payments with zero percent APR), and the new phones are also eligible for the recently-announced Apple Upgrade program. You can also trade in your existing phone for up to $885 in credit towards the cost of the new phone, with carriers offering additional credits.

The likes of Best Buy and Walmart only have the carrier-locked versions listed at the start of the preorder phase. Best Buy is offering the 18 Pro through Verizon or AT&T, along with the Pro Max tied to Verizon or AT&T. Walmart is offering the 18 Pro through Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile, as well as the Pro Max with T-Mobile, Verizon, or AT&T.

Offers from US carriers

AT&T will offer to cover the cost of an iPhone 18 Pro via billing credits paid back to you over 36 months if you trade in an iPhone 14 or newer. You’ll also need to 

T-Mobile is offering the iPhone 18 Pro for free by way of bill credits when you transfer your number or trade in a qualifying phone on the Experience Beyond plan . The credits aren’t as generous as AT&T’s offer if you’re an existing customer already, with only the iPhone 16 and newer covering the cost of a new phone, but it’s very similar if you’re new to T-Mobile.

The Verizon deal is fairly straightforward. The Simplicity Pro plan, which comes to a total of $80 per month if you’re switching from another carrier, includes a free iPhone 18 Pro, with the option to upgrade your phone after one year. Like other carriers, the “free” phone is paid off to you via monthly bill credits, so you’ll need to stick with the carrier for three years to get the full value.

Tech.title: OpenAI just wants to win
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

OpenAI has spent the last few years planting flags across the increasingly difficult terrain in mathematics. This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem. In normal circumstances, this would have been celebrated as a historic achievement.

Instead, many mathematicians have watched OpenAI’s relentless advance with growing unease. To them, the company appears less like an enthusiastic newcomer than an impossibly well-resourced interloper, charging into problems they have dedicated their lives to studying with little apparent regard for long-standing norms or the consequences for those left in its wake. At the heart of that unease is a sense that OpenAI is doing mathematics for different reasons. Mathematicians want to advance the field. OpenAI wants to win.

Mathematics is not normally this dramatic, so how did things get this bad?

This week, The Verge spoke with more than a dozen mathematicians, including Tristan Buckmaster and Andreas Thom, who are at the center of recent controversies surrounding OpenAI’s work in the field. Even those skeptical of the most serious allegations described a field shaken by the tech giant’s conduct and fearful of what it might do next in its determination to trounce its rivals.

Buckmaster has accused OpenAI of failing to adequately explain whether work he did through its tool Codex could have contributed to its recent successes. In a statement to The Verge, OpenAI spokesperson Laurance Fauconnet strenuously denied that material from his prompts had played a role: “We can say categorically that it is impossible for Dr. Buckmaster’s Codex prompts over the last two months to have influenced the system in any way, including training.”

Buckmaster remains unconvinced. “Given their behavior up until this point, one should take such statements with great skepticism,” he said.

Mathematics is not normally this dramatic, so how did things get this bad? A rumor was all it took for tensions to boil over.

OpenAI says it heard some researchers were making progress on Millennium Prize problems and decided to see whether one of its advanced, unreleased models could make headway too. It turns out it could. OpenAI says it took roughly 10,000 agents, tens of millions of dollars of compute, and just 88 hours to find a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.

The company had also discovered who it was racing against: Buckmaster, an NYU professor, and Levent Alpöge, a researcher at one of its fiercest rivals, Anthropic. Among several lines of research, the pair were pursuing Navier-Stokes, though had not yet completed a proof. Some details of what happened next are fiercely contested, but the two sides broadly agree on the basic sequence of events. One thing is particularly clear: Alpöge’s involvement was a problem for OpenAI, despite his saying it was a “personal collaboration” independent of his work with Anthropic.

Even those skeptical of the most serious allegations described a field shaken by the tech giant’s conduct and fearful of what it might do next in its determination to trounce its rivals.

Buckmaster said he contacted OpenAI after learning the company had become aware of their progress and was racing toward a solution of its own. He said discussions with OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck grew contentious and, in his view, threatening, but the company offered a path forward for him — one that excluded Alpöge. Buckmaster said he was offered practically “unlimited compute” to finish his own work, and the opportunity to be the sole author of OpenAI’s paper announcing the breakthrough, which would of course credit its tools.

“All I had to do was throw Levent under the bus,” Buckmaster told The Verge in a phone interview. He said he flatly rejected Bubeck’s offer, which he viewed as a “bribe,” and also began questioning whether OpenAI may have benefited from his use of Codex, one of the company’s AI tools he had been using to tackle the problem. OpenAI has denied that anyone — or any agent — accessed his specific user data, and until its more recent comments acknowledged it could not rule out the possibility data derived from his use of the products was used to improve the model.

Buckmaster ultimately decided to go public with both his work and his account of OpenAI’s conduct. His office, he said, had been transformed into something of a “war room,” with colleagues helping scrutinize his mathematics, coordinate outreach, and even get in touch with lawyers.

Bubeck has rejected Buckmaster’s characterization of the conversations on social media and in an interview with The New York Times. He acknowledged offering OpenAI’s resources to help Buckmaster complete his own proof or to have him take over the writing of the company’s. Strikingly, Bubeck said OpenAI had made similar arrangements with other mathematicians, though did not identify them.

But his account nevertheless makes clear that Alpöge’s affiliation with Anthropic was a sticking point. “From our perspective, how can we have an internal OpenAI project with an Anthropic employee?” he told the Times.

If the goal is to compete in mathematics, there are few bigger trophies than solving a Millennium Prize problem. The seven problems, set out by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, are widely considered among the most formidable challenges in the field. Each carries a $1 million bounty for whoever solves it. Many had already endured decades of intense scrutiny by the time the prizes were established. In the quarter-century since, only one — the Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres — has fallen.

For an AI company looking to prove that its models are the best at mathematics, then, they are irresistible targets. To Buckmaster and many other mathematicians The Verge spoke to, that helps explain why OpenAI moved so ferociously when it heard others were closing in — particularly once a rival AI company appeared to be involved.

For Buckmaster, the episode reinforced something he already believed strongly from a previous spell collaborating with Google DeepMind: “All these tech people are obsessed” with solving big famous problems and are “obsessed with scooping,” he said. “Its all about competition.”

In that world, Tristan Buckmaster said there is an intense fixation on prestige, fame, being first, and being seen to be first. “That’s the only currency,” he said.

He said what often gets “lost” when companies race to solve famous problems are the mathematicians themselves — not just the people whose accumulated work makes these breakthroughs possible, but the reasons they do mathematics to begin with. Yes, some may pursue prestige, but most are simply not trophy hunters. Andras Juhasz, a professor of mathematics at the University of Oxford, described mathematics as an elegant discipline that is part science, part art, with many different motivations driving those working there. “Often there is no immediate practical application,” he said. “They do it because it’s beautiful. They enjoy it. It’s the sense of discovery. It’s natural.”

Unlike classroom-level mathematical exercises, frontier mathematics rarely has a prescribed route to an answer. Researchers can attack problems from any number of angles, some radically different, which makes the ideas that lead to a solution — and who developed them — especially important, perhaps more so than solving a problem itself. Mathematicians care deeply about this lineage because it is how the field expands, with new techniques and methods often proving more consequential than the problem they were designed to solve.

To Buckmaster, his exchanges with Bubeck typify the chasm that separates the worlds of research mathematics and Big Tech, and highlight the differences between what is considered valuable in research. Reading from notes he took while chatting with Bubeck, he said the OpenAI researcher was visibly taken aback when he rejected the company’s offer to take credit. “I could see Sébastien’s face. He was shocked when I said I don’t care about the Millennium Prize,” he recalled.

Buckmaster said he had encountered a similar mentality among tech researchers before. In that world, he said there is an intense fixation on prestige, fame, being first, and being seen to be first. “That’s the only currency,” he said.

Buckmaster isn’t the only mathematician to come away from an encounter with OpenAI concerned about the company’s motivations. Andreas Thom, a professor at the Technical University of Dresden in Germany, found himself at the center of a controversy last month after OpenAI announced an impressive mathematical result that built heavily on work by him and fellow researcher Gábor Kun. The company quietly amended its announcement to acknowledge the pair’s contribution without announcing or publicly disclosing the change.

Thom described the ordeal as “not a very pleasant experience,” but told The Verge he had largely put it behind him until Buckmaster went public. His allegations prompted Thom to revisit an unresolved question about OpenAI’s breakthrough: whether conversations he and his colleagues had with ChatGPT about the research could have been used to help improve the models that ultimately cracked the problem he’d spent years working on.

Only OpenAI has the information needed to answer that question, Thom said. “To be honest, I suspect that they don’t even know.” The people training the models and using them to produce mathematical results are “a different kind of people,” he said. To him, that’s hardly an excuse for the uncertainty. “Because it effectively means that they don’t really care, right?”

“The prospect of competing with powerful AI companies, whose resources far exceed those available to academic research groups, could make them even more reluctant to pursue ambitious questions.”

The tension echoes fights already playing out elsewhere. Writers, musicians, artists, and media companies have all challenged AI companies over systems built from vast stores of human-created work, often without permission, recognition, or compensation. While mathematics may seem a world apart, the underlying question is the same: What do companies owe to the people whose accumulated work they ingested to build their systems?

In Thom’s case, the question remains unresolved. OpenAI did not respond to The Verge’s question on whether data from conversations Thom and his colleagues had with ChatGPT could have contributed to the company’s solution that built on his work.

More broadly, Thom said he resents what he sees as a failure to recognize the “the communal effort that this entire community has put into all the research results” underpinning AI’s recent mathematical advances. Companies, he said, “are just now using [it] as if it was kind of nothing.”

“I think there is a certain attitude that I don’t like in that,” he said.

It’s not that mathematicians are strangers to competition — researchers care deeply about priority and bitter disputes over who came first litter mathematical history — but while competition does not preclude cooperation, these are no ordinary competitors. Scooping in mathematics has historically been relatively difficult for obvious reasons: Very few people have the specialized expertise to swoop in on a discovery at speed. AI companies operate on a different scale. Researchers worry they could turn scooping into something of an industrial process mathematicians would have little chance of fighting back against, rapidly spinning up thousands upon thousands of agents and enormous amounts of compute whenever word spreads that a breakthrough is close.

To Buckmaster, OpenAI could have easily collaborated with researchers rather than race them to results. Indeed, the company seemed perfectly willing to work with him. The problem was Alpöge, or, more specifically, his ties to Anthropic.

“They were in such a rush to publish, to beat Anthropic,” he said. They barely took note of the researchers caught in the middle.

For all the rush, OpenAI won’t know whether it has won the Millennium Prize for solving Navier-Stokes for years. The Clay Mathematics Institute requires a period of two years to have passed since a result was published, during which it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.” For now, Navier-Stokes occupies a peculiar limbo: The Institute has removed it from its list of unsolved problems, though hasn’t yet declared it solved. “The process is deliberately unhurried,” the Institute said in a statement.

OpenAI, meanwhile, has already moved on. In a statement to The Verge, OpenAI’s Fauconnet said that “since the completion of Navier-Stokes we have made substantial progress on another Millennium Prize problem,” adding that the company is “working through how to share these results thoughtfully.”

Which problem remains unclear. Unconfirmed speculation on social media suggests this could be the Hodge conjecture, which concerns, very roughly speaking, how complex geometric shapes can be understood in terms of simpler building blocks. Rumors are also circulating that Anthropic is closing in on a Millennium Prize problem of its own.

As the two giants of AI race to collect yet more mathematical trophies, they are discovering that astonishing results alone are not enough to earn the trust of the community they are transforming.

Mathematicians are beginning to push back. Many The Verge spoke to, even the most enthusiastic proponents of AI in the field, worried the companies were having a chilling effect on research, pushing mathematicians to be more secretive about unfinished work for fear someone may swoop in and beat them to it. Several said colleagues who had previously compiled lists of important unsolved problems were reconsidering the practice, concerned that what was intended as a useful resource for the field could instead become a list of targets for AI companies.

Resistance is becoming increasingly public. In June, mathematicians published the Leiden Declaration, a set of principles for the responsible use of AI in mathematics that has been endorsed by the International Mathematical Union and signed by nearly 3,900 people, an increase of nearly 500 people since I last covered it in mid-August. It urges policymakers, governments, the media, and other groups to not buy into “the hype” created by companies who “overstate the capabilities of their products.” As the Millennium Prize controversy raged, OpenAI withdrew its sponsorship of an undergraduate mathematics hackathon at Caltech following fierce opposition decrying the intrusion of corporate interests and worries the event would create a deluge of low-quality “slop mathematics.”

“They don’t care anything about us as a community. It’s all about this petty drama between two trillion-dollar companies that are acting like children.”

Shing-Tung Yau, a professor of mathematics at China’s Tsinghua University, an emeritus professor at Harvard, and a recipient of the prestigious Fields Medal, told The Verge he worries about the potential effect on young researchers. “Working on hard problems already carries considerable risk for Ph.D. students and junior faculty,” he said. “The prospect of competing with powerful AI companies, whose resources far exceed those available to academic research groups, could make them even more reluctant to pursue ambitious questions.”

Yau declined to weigh in on allegations that researchers’ work may have been used by OpenAI, but said he is in favor of an independent review to establish what happened. More broadly, he worries that a lack of transparency and rush to announce first could obscure the intellectual lineage behind a breakthrough. Mathematical credit, he said, should reflect intellectual contributions, not who had budget for the most compute or made the loudest announcement.

Yau pointed to another problem, too. OpenAI and other AI companies occupy a peculiar position as both the providers of important research tools and, in a way, researchers. It “raises a serious conflict-of-interest concern,” he said, particularly as they could benefit from privileged access to customers’ unfinished and unpublished work.

“That concern deserves a substantive response,” he said. “It should not simply be dismissed as ordinary competition.”

A lot of this growing sense of unease comes down to trust. Mathematicians do not have to accept the most explosive allegations against OpenAI to worry about a company that both provides their research tools and, simultaneously, competes with them.

“Yeah, quite honestly, I don’t think that some data security announcement or whatever will really solve it,” Thom said. “I don’t really trust them.” Buckmaster felt similarly: “Why should we trust anything they said?”

Buckmaster said the reaction from colleagues to his going public had been overwhelmingly positive. But there was an undercurrent of something else too: fear. He told The Verge he initially intended to thank those who supported him when he went public with his experiences. He elected not to after many expressed discomfort at the idea of having their names publicly attached. “The reality is that mathematicians are actually scared of them,” Buckmaster said, referring to the AI companies.

And fear is hardly a solid foundation on which to build a productive and healthy research community. Buckmaster isn’t convinced it matters much to those companies involved. “They don’t care anything about us as a community,” he said. “It’s all about this petty drama between two trillion-dollar companies that are acting like children.”

Tech.title: OpenAI’s Sam Altman says it would be ‘ill-advised’ to go public in 2026
Tech.content:
In Brief

While OpenAI has filed confidentially for an IPO, the company will not be going public this year, according to CEO Sam Altman.

Altman was interviewed recently by Fortune editor in chief Alyson Shontell; amidst the fallout from the OpenAI-HuggingFace hack, as well as broader discussions about AI safety, Shontell asked whether OpenAI still feels pressure to “move really fast” due to its IPO plans.

“We’re not rushing into an IPO,” Altman said. “I actually think that given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public.”

Instead, he insisted that OpenAI will go public “when we’re ready, which is when the business is ready, when we feel ready from what the moment is like in society with this technology.” When pressed on whether that means the IPO isn’t happening in 2026, Altman replied, “I would say not 2026, yeah. We’ve got a lot of stuff to do.”

The New York Times reported in June that although OpenAI had hired bankers and lawyers with the goal of going public in the third or fourth quarter of 2026, the company was leaning toward 2027 due to the volatility of tech stocks and its own financial challenges.

Tech.title: Anthropic CEO outlines plan to slow AI development
Tech.content:
We’ve been seeing increasingly dire warnings from AI researchers about the dangers of artificial intelligence, and even comments from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that it may be time to “pace” AI development. But what would that actually look like?

In a new blog post, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei not only echoed the call to “pace the frontier,” but also outlined three broad strategies for doing so. And he said Anthropic is “unilaterally committing” to one of them, with Altman chiming in to say OpenAI will follow suit.
